image.caption: Winamp was the most popular music player at the turn of the century, known for its efficiency and customizable interface (shown here is how Winamp's interface appeared in the early 2000s on the left, and a customized version made by user masayoshi.N on the right). Now, the company is hoping to expan

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Winamp, the music player that revolutionized the digital music scene in the late 1990s and early 2000s before fading into obscurity, is launching a new venture to enter the world of streaming, promising a subscription model that integrates streaming in 2027.
The music player known for customizable interfaces says a streaming option is coming in 2027
A once-ubiquitous, llama-whipping Windows music player is going through a revamp — with the goal of taking on the world of streaming.

Winamp revolutionized the digital music scene in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Now, it's announcing a new partnership with Deezer, an independent music streaming platform, through which it will create its own subscription model using the streamer's white-label technology and music catalogue.

The new platform, set to launch in early 2027, will allow users to play music from the streaming library along with other sources, like their local files and internet radio stations, according to the company’s announcement. Users will also be able to customize their interface through "skins," a much-beloved legacy feature of its original music player.

It’s not technically a comeback. Despite fading into the background amid the streaming boom, Winamp’s music player is still available for download, and the company says more than 40 million people still actively use the desktop version.

Winamp was originally released by Arizona-based Nullsoft in 1997 as a music player for Windows computers, and quickly became the program of choice for storing and playing digital music files, counting 60 million users in 2001.

Known for the unique catchphrase “Winamp, it really whips the llama’s ass” — the intro line to the default demo track that came with the software — it wasn’t the first MP3 player for computers, but was leagues ahead of its competition in speed, efficiency and style.

“Twenty-five years ago, we changed the way people listened to digital music, and we believe the time has come to challenge the listening experience once again,” Alexandre Saboundjian, CEO of Winamp Group, said in a press release about the new plans.

The company has tried to break into streaming before. Saboundjian told TechCrunch in 2018 that a mobile version was coming in 2019 that could bring users’ music, podcasts and streaming services together. The next year came and went without the promised app materializing.
The music player on everyone’s computers

In 1999, AOL acquired Nullsoft for an estimated $80 million US to $100 million US. Although Winamp continued performing well for the first few years, the move eventually spelled trouble for the music player.

Poor management and culture clashes between AOL and Nullsoft corporate leaders meant Winamp squandered its head start in the field, allowing competitors like Apple's iPod to swoop in, according to an Ars Technica report on the platform's downfall.

For many music enthusiasts, Winamp's skins still epitomize a time of open source creativity. An online “skin museum” preserves examples of the thousands of different layouts fans designed and shared for early versions of the music player.

AOL scheduled for the platform to be shut down at the end of 2013. But Winamp narrowly avoided death when Belgium-based Radionomy, later rebranded to Llama Group and then Winamp Group, stepped in to purchase it.

items: Columbia House, which once promised 12 CDs for a penny, removes notice of closure

blocks.text: After dabbling in music NFTs, Winamp made comeback attempts in 2023 and 2024 with the launch of a platform for artists and fans to interact and then a new mobile app on Android and iOS.

It’s not yet clear how pricing could work for the proposed streaming service, and no further details have been released. If all goes to plan, users longing to listen to music on an interface emblazoned with characters from Lord of the Rings might see their dreams come true next year.

But not every fan is thrilled. Some commenters on Reddit weren't happy that a music player once associated with the age of at-home programming is looking at adding a subscription model. Following the launch of the new platform, the desktop player will include the option for the premium subscription.
"I still use the old winamp.... It works just fine," one user said in a comment in reaction to the news.

articles.title: California braces for record El Niño storms as governor declares emergency
articles.summary: Super El-Niño has already broken temperature records and is predicted to bring an extremely wet winter to the state

blocks.text: California is bracing for a record breaking El Niño that is expected to bring severe winter storms and flooding across the state, with the state’s governor declaring a state of emergency in anticipation of extreme weather in the months ahead.

The global climate phenomenon known as a “super El Niño” is already breaking temperature records and drawing predictions of an extremely wet winter in places such as California, where El Niño typically brings more severe winter storms and flooding risks. Several coastal California cities have recently faced high surf, flooding and coastal erosion linked to Hurricane Marie as well as El Niño. Experts have said the effects offered a glimpse at what the coming winter could look like.

Gavin Newsom declared a state of emergency on Monday to bring supplies to California communities ahead of extreme weather, and ready the national guard to assist with flood response and search and rescue efforts. It also directs state agencies to prepare roads and critical infrastructure.

The governor said in a statement that the proclamation was an effort to “[give] communities the support they need, [give] first responders the tools to do their jobs, and [give] families the confidence that their state is ready.”

“We are preparing for this El Niño early because every Californian deserves to be safe in their home, connected to their community] and protected when severe weather comes,” Newsom said in a statement.

The global climate phenomenon occurs when parts of the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean naturally warm, which affects weather patterns across the world, leading to drought in some areas and fueling severe storms in others, and causes global temperatures to surge. It amplifies the effects of the climate crisis, and recent research found that global heating is supercharging the El Niño climatic patterns.
El Niño broke the highest temperature ever recorded for the phenomenon this week, months ahead of the anticipated peak, according to the latest data.

This year there is a more than 90% change of a very strong El Niño event and a 75% chance of an event of historic strength, according to a statement from the governor’s office. That could bring severe rain, flooding, landslides and coastal flooding that cuts off neighborhoods, damages communities and causes widespread power outages.

“California is already taking steps now to protect communities from a potentially historic El Niño because we know how serious these weather extremes driven by climate change can be,” said Wade Crowfoot, California’s natural resources secretary, in a statement.
The governor also approved emergency declarations for several counties across the state that recently experienced significantly damaging severe weather events.

House of Commons is set to return from its summer recess on Sept. 21
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 21, 2026 3:04 PM EDT | Last Updated: 10 minutes ago
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre surprised many when he announced at a rally on Sunday that Brantford Mayor Kevin Davis will be the party's candidate in Brantford-Brant South.

The seat is vacant now that Larry Brock has returned to his job as a Crown prosecutor, but a byelection hasn't been called yet. On Friday, Brock said he resigned from the House of Commons, after five years as the MP for Brantford-Brant South.

items: Conservative MP Larry Brock set to resign Sept. 18
Conservative MP apologizes after comments spark uproar on bilingual rights

blocks.text: Brock endorsed Dave Carrol, a local pastor who had hoped to run in a nomination race that he learned on the weekend will not happen.
Carrol says he's "deeply disappointed" by the decision and adds he also had the endorsement of former MP Phil McColeman.

In a Facebook post, Carrol said that on Sunday he learned that "one candidate has been appointed rather than selected through the nomination contest that so many of us had been preparing for. I wish Kevin Davis well, but I would be less than honest if I said I wasn't deeply disappointed."

Carrol said "The grassroots tradition of this party is what drew me to it nearly two decades ago, and I've spent those years helping build it here… knocking on doors, getting memberships, raising money, supporting our candidates and trusting local members to make good choices. I hoped that same grassroots tradition would guide the process when I finally put my own name forward"

In a statement, the Conservative party says it wanted to ensure a candidate was ready to hit the ground running and that Davis was "overwhelmingly endorsed" by people who attended Poilievre's rally on Sunday.
The House of Commons is scheduled to return from its summer recess on Sept. 21.

Sarah Ritchie is a reporter with The Canadian Press.

articles.title: Datacentres in Victoria to be banned in residential areas
articles.summary:
New rules also include a ban near schools and childcare centres and require them to source their own renewable energy

  • Get our

blocks.text: Datacentres in Victoria will be banned in residential areas and required to use renewable energy and contribute to the community, under new state government rules.
On Tuesday, the premier, Ben Carroll, will release the government’s sustainable datacentre action plan, after it was approved by cabinet on Monday.
The government claims the rules are the “strongest” and “clearest” governing datacentres in the country.
“In Victoria, we set the rules – datacentres must power themselves, protect homes and pay their way,” Carroll said in a statement before Tuesday’s announcement.
“If we get that right, we can all share in their economic benefits, especially the local community.”
The new rules include a ban on datacentres near schools and childcare centres and in rural areas that cannot support them, along with a 150-metre buffer zone between new developments and homes.
Datacentres will be required to source their own renewable energy and will have to pay for connection costs and network upgrades.
They will also need to use recycled or non-drinking water for cooling or offset their usage.

The government said new datacentres will also have to give back to community via a “local investment guarantee”, which could include jobs, Tafes and parks. They will also be required to employ Victorians during construction and train people for long-term jobs when up and running.
The plan also includes mandating “fair community consultation”, as well as existing noise limits fire and safety rules.

blocks.caption: Anthony Albanese says he wants to do AI 'the Australian way' – video

blocks.text: The federal government had previously flagged plans to require all new datacentres to be powered by renewable energy rather than coal and gas but was forced to back down on the mandate after opposition from the Queensland and Northern Territory leaders.
Last year, the then Victorian premier, Jacinta Allan, vowed to make Victoria the datacentre capital of the country.
after newsletter promotion
But there has been growing community opposition in the lead-up to the November election, particularly in Labor-held seats.
They include Footscray, held by Labor’s Katie Hall on 4.2% margin against the Greens, who ran a “stop AI data centres day of action” in the electorate on Saturday.

NextDC has lodged an application with the state government for fast-tracked approval to expand its Footscray datacentre, known as M3, to cover 10ha , drawing 225MW of power and running 24/7. Some residential homes are within 15 metres of the datacentre’s boundary, which is zoned in an industrial area.
Hall is a long-term opponent of the datacentre’s expansion.

NextDC has also bought 169ha of land just outside Geelong, which had been earmarked for future residential development. Labor MP for Lara, Ella George, expressed concern about the acquisition to the Age in July.
There are also Syncline Energy’s plans to develop a 350ha, 2.4GW datacentre in Plumpton, in Melbourne’s outer north-west, which is opposed by federal Labor MPs Alice Jordan-Baird and Sam Rae.
The proposed centre is larger than any currently operating in Australia and would consume more electricity than is generated by Victoria’s largest power station, Loy Yang A.

articles.summary: The $81 billion US dollar blockbuster deal will bring together two of Hollywood's oldest studios, key TV networks like CBS and CNN and streaming platforms HBO Max and Paramount+, as well as decades…

image.caption: Paramount and Warner Bros. logos are seen in this illustration from December 2025. (Dado Ruvic/Reuters)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

The $81 billion US dollar blockbuster deal will bring together two of Hollywood's oldest studios, key TV networks like CBS and CNN and streaming platforms HBO Max and Paramount+, as well as decades of libraries with titles ranging from Harry Potter to Top Gun.
Settlement still needs final court approval

California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced Monday a settlement with Paramount in a lawsuit his state led challenging the company's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, effectively paving the way for the megamerger to move forward, with some new commitments.

The $81 billion US blockbuster deal will bring together two of Hollywood's oldest studios, key TV networks such as CBS and CNN and streaming platforms HBO Max and Paramount+, as well as decades of libraries with titles ranging from Harry Potter to Top Gun.

But terms of Monday's agreement include what Bonta called "court enforceable" requirements for Skydance-owned Paramount to increase domestic production and establish monitoring of editorial independence of the company's news operations.

The settlement still needs final court approval. Bonta maintained that Monday's agreement "is not a vote of support for this merger" — but that he was always willing to come to the table and "find a strong solution that protects competition and consumers."

items: Paramount agrees to delay closing Warner Bros. buyout for months while judge considers states' challenge
Paramount, Warner must pause merger for at least two weeks, judge says

blocks.text: Skydance-owned Paramount reached the settlement Monday with a group of state attorneys general that had sued to challenge the company's buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery, effectively paving the way for the megamerger to move forward, a person familiar with the matter told the The Associated Press.

The person was not authorized to speak publicly and did so on condition of anonymity. Details of the settlement with the states were not immediately available but were expected to be revealed later in the day.

The coalition of states — including entertainment heavyweights such as California and New York — sued to block the $81 billion US merger in July, alleging a Paramount-Warner combo would "extinguish competition" and lead to fewer choices for consumers, particularly movie theatre-goers and cable customers across the U.S.
Accompanied by a complaint also filed by the Writers Guild of America, the challenge was headed toward a full antitrust trial set to begin in March.
Paramount launches hostile takeover bid for Warner Bros.

Paramount said the allegations were meritless, but previously agreed to delay its transaction well into next year so the case could make its way through court. It then quickly called for a settlement, arguing that it had satisfied all regulatory clearances worldwide — including from the Trump administration's Justice Department — and the states' challenge was its "final obstacle."

As reports of the states reaching a settlement with Paramount emerged Monday, critics decried the deal while warning of what further consolidation could mean in an industry already controlled by just a few major players.

articles.title: Venezuelan man shot by ICE agent as enforcement surges in Austin
articles.summary:
The shooting of Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez comes months after increased federal immigration enforcement across the Texas capital

The

blocks.text: The shooting of a man by a federal officer on Sunday in Texas ruptured an ostensibly quiet afternoon amid an immigration enforcement surge in Austin.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has been very active in the Texas capital of late, although less showy than the militarized federal violence in Minneapolis this January, helping keep the operation effective but flying under the national radar. Then shots rang out.

Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was in the process of delivering a DoorDash food order on the city’s north side when ICE encountered him shortly before 1pm. Video posted online appears to show an ICE officer getting out of his car and shooting at Garcés Pérez’s car three times.

His car, as later visible at the scene, had a large dent on the front passenger side. Garcés Pérez, who was hit once in the back between his shoulder blades, is a Venezuelan national who has lived in the United States for two years, according to his lawyer, but had been ordered removed from the US. Garcés Pérez told onlookers who rushed to the scene that he had been shot because he hadn’t stopped.

Austin police officers who arrived could be seen in bystander footage rendering first aid to the bleeding man, while ICE officers stood back. Garcés Pérez was taken to a downtown hospital for treatment but, according to lawyer Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, was whisked away from there by ICE late Sunday afternoon.

For a few hours, his partner and the lawyer could not locate him, then on Monday morning Lincoln-Goldfinch told the Guardian he’d been located at the South Texas ICE Processing Center, located 140 miles to the south-west, in Pearsall.
“Bullet still lodged in his back. No pain meds,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said by text on Monday.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, did not respond to questions about the circumstances leading up to the shooting, or Garcés Pérez’s whereabouts and condition.
Austin, the politically liberal capital city of conservative Texas, has repeatedly found itself at the crossfire of the immigration debate.
The state’s Republican leadership has often sought to make an example out of the city, forcing local leaders to weaken Austin’s policy of not collaborating with ICE.
For more than a year, state police have handed countless unauthorized immigrants over to ICE during traffic stops, but the city police had not joined in.

Cooperation between state or local law enforcement and federal immigration enforcement is arranged under so-called 287(g) agreements, which have been proliferating in the second Trump administration, especially in states such as Texas and Florida.

But even with that, some local leaders said this summer has marked a low-profile but aggressive surge in immigration enforcement in the region, spurred by a jump in ICE acting alone rather than relying on state troopers to stop people and pass them on. Lawmakers reported ICE stopping cars in traffic or asking people about their immigration status in public sites like parking lots and gas stations.

“I think it needs to be said that as mayor of the city of Austin, I’m very angry about this,” Kirk Watson, the city’s Democratic mayor, said on Sunday during a press conference after the shooting. “A person being shot on the streets of Austin by someone purporting to be law enforcement, particularly when it’s ICE, is something that causes me to be unhappy and angry. And while I’m unhappy and I’m angry about it, I’m not surprised at all. It’s happened in other cities, with the nature of ICE and the way ICE is doing its business these days.”
In an initial statement issued shortly before midnight on Sunday night, DHS said Garcés Pérez was in stable condition and that he was “in federal custody pending removal” out of the US.

The agency also said that it was leading the investigation into the shooting, alongside the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). However Austin leaders have called on city police and the Texas Rangers, part of the state’s Department of Public Safety, to aid with the investigation, citing public distrust in DHS. They have also demanded that the agent involved in the shooting be kept in Texas as the investigation continues.
The exact details leading up to the shooting remained unclear on Monday.

Video posted on social media shows a man running out of the black SUV and shooting at Garcés Pérez’s mostly stationary blue sedan from behind it. Three gunshots ring out. The car moves up a few feet and then stops.

Nedavia Bolaños and her husband were the first witnesses on the scene. The couple, owners of a Mexican ice cream shop just off the intersection of the shooting, ran outside after they heard the shots. For several minutes, they pestered the only ICE agent on the scene about what had happened.

The agent, masked in what appears to be a black balaclava, stood there, saying only that he wanted the couple to stay at a distance. He did not render aid, a video Bolaños provided exclusively to the Guardian shows. They acknowledge that an ambulance has been called, as the man sits in the driver’s seat, clearly in pain and clutching his chest.

That video then shows Austin police arriving at the scene minutes later. After helping federal agents handcuff Garcés Pérez and seat him on the ground, they cut off his black T-shirt to reveal a bullet wound between his shoulder blades.
About 10 minutes later, an ambulance arrived and carried Garcés Pérez away, Bolaños said.

Within an hour, more than a hundred protesters had gathered at the site. State and local police formed a barrier around the dozens of federal agents, who based themselves under the highway median. The protesters chanted expletives and waved Mexican, American and Guatemalan flags, some of which had been bought on the spot for $20 from a hawker who set up shop nearby. Several protesters could be seen washing their eyes and mouths in pain, after they were sprayed with what they said was teargas or chemical spray.
The protests grew and lasted late into the night, resulting in several arrests, according to local news reports.

The shooting comes after several months of increased immigration enforcement, particularly in the immigrant-heavy north side neighborhood where the shooting occurred, as well as several predominantly Hispanic suburbs and exurbs.

Austin city council member José “Chito” Vela, who represents the neighborhood where Garcés Pérez was shot, said that he has heard constituents describe an increase in immigration arrests since the start of the summer, an enforcement bump driven by a rise in unilateral action by ICE. While ICE was largely seen making immigration arrests after Texas Department of Public Safety traffic stops for the first year or so of the second Trump administration, they have begun to act increasingly on their own, Vela said.

City leaders had previously raised concerns over the increased action. Congressman Greg Casar, an Austin Democrat who leads the Congressional Progressive Caucus, has sent a letter to DHS demanding cooperation in an “immediate, independent investigation” into the shooting, the full release of any footage the federal authorities have of the shooting, and “accountability for any wrongdoing by the agent responsible”.

articles.title: Canada and the U.K. consider merging financial initiatives to rearm against Russia
articles.summary: Canadian and British officials are considering merging two multinational defence initiatives to help a broader network of allies rearm against Russia and other growing international threats, a…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney, left, and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham greet each other at Hill Dickinson Stadium in Liverpool, England, on last Wednesday. During the meeting, the two leaders discussed their multinational defence initiatives to rearm allies and encourage closer defence co-operati

blocks.text: Politics·New

Canadian and British officials are considering merging two multinational defence initiatives to help a broader network of allies rearm against Russia and other growing international threats, a Canadian official said.
Canada and the U.K. both had plans to launch separate initiatives in 2027

Prime Minister Mark Carney and his British counterpart, Andy Burnham, discussed their financial initiatives and how they could strengthen defence co-operation in Liverpool last week during their first face-to-face meeting as leaders, according to Burnham's office.
Canada wasn't able to get the U.K. to become a founding member of its Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) under the Starmer government, but revived the push when Burnham took office in July.

A Canadian official, who was not authorized to speak publicly, said progress has been made during talks with British officials, adding the Burnham government appears to be much more aligned with Canada and its worldview.
Carney has been personally trying to get countries to join the DSRB, which is expected to pool countries' resources together to finance defence companies so they can scale up production.
But Canada needs a big player like the U.K. on board or else it will limit how much the bank can lend. Starmer had announced a £400-million contribution to his financing mechanism.
The discussions between the two governments now centre around combining the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank with the U.K.'s Multilateral Defence Mechanism. Both have 2027 launch dates.
The Canadian official said the two countries are looking at bringing the two proposals together to create one institution that best serves the needs of allies.
Carney has said the Canada-led bank would give out low-cost loans to make sure allies "have the capacity to meet the challenges of a more dangerous and divided world together."
Starmer described his initiative in June as a way to "finance and procure defence equipment with our allies and support a path to achieving our NATO spending targets."

items: Carney touts Arctic alliance with Norway during PM's visit to Ottawa, amid Russia threat
Canada urges U.K. to join new global bank for defence projects

blocks.text: NATO allies are trying to increase defence spending amid pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, who says allies have been relying too much on the U.S.
The military alliance's members have promised to increase core military spending to 3.5 per cent of GDP by 2035.
Canada has so far signed up Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine to the bank.
Meanwhile, the U.K. has signed up the Netherlands, Finland and Poland for its financing model.
Canada's High Commissioner to the U.K. Bill Blair said in July it would benefit all members for the U.K. to join forces with Canada.
British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told journalists on his first day of the job it was an "early priority" for the government to decide if it will take part in Canada's initiative.

articles.title: Flights halted at three US airports as watchdog warns over hacking threat
articles.summary:
Senator Ron Wyden calls for swift action after GAO report finds systems guiding US aircraft vulnerable to interference

A congressional watchdog has warned the systems guiding US aircraft are…

blocks.text: A congressional watchdog has warned the systems guiding US aircraft are open to interference and deception as flights into three busy airports in the country’s north east US were halted by a radio equipment problem.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a ground stop at about 10am on Monday for Newark Liberty international, Philadelphia international and Teterboro airports, saying some radio frequencies at the Philadelphia terminal radar approach control (Tracon) were affected until the early afternoon. Arrivals and departures at Newark were delayed, and the agency has not said what caused the outage.

The disruption coincided with the publication of a government accountability office (GAO) report, which found that the FAA has yet to finish risk assessments or update security documentation covering threats from spoofing, jamming and other attacks on the radio spectrum – prompting a prominent senator to warn of a “major threat” to national security.
The FAA also lacks a real-time system to detect all such threats, the report said, meaning it can generally only investigate incidents after they are reported.

Investigators warned that a hacker could send fraudulent messages, such as false cancellations of flight clearances, to aircraft, with the potential to cause delays, disrupt airspace or create safety risks. Two systems used to send text messages to aircraft predate modern cybersecurity standards and lack common protections such as encryption, according to the report.

The watchdog’s findings prompted calls for swift action. “The FAA’s failure to require the aviation industry to use secure communications is a major threat to US national security, to our economy and the safety of the flying public,” said Ron Wyden, the US senator for Oregon, who has long campaigned on privacy, surveillance and cyber security issues.
“The FAA needs to issue new standards, as soon as possible, to protect the security of airline communications.”

The GAO made nine recommendations, including a formal risk assessment of seven of eight reviewed systems, continuous monitoring for interference, spoofing and jamming, and formal guidance on information sharing. The department of transportation, replying for the FAA, agreed with all nine.

Monday’s disruption is the latest in a run of problems around Newark. In April 2025, an outage blanked controllers’ screens for roughly 60 to 90 seconds and cut their contact with aircraft, prompting the FAA to halt departures. The FAA later moved the Philadelphia Tracon to a new fiber-optic link with New York on two separate paths, as part of measures to improve reliability.
The FAA handles more than 44,000 flights a day and about 3 million passengers, the GAO noted.

Wyden, who sits on the Senate intelligence committee, added: “This sobering report from [the] GAO reveals that the technology used by air traffic controllers to communicate with aircraft is incredibly insecure, can be intercepted, impersonated, and jammed, and that hackers and foreign governments can exploit these vulnerabilities to disrupt air travel and even put passengers at risk.”
The GAO also pointed to jamming and spoofing abroad. Estonia and Finland have accused Russia of interfering with satellite navigation in their airspace, which Moscow denies.
One incident last September involved a Spanish military jet carrying the country’s defense minister.

articles.title: AI 'actor' Tilly Norwood glitches during Piers Morgan interview, starts speaking Cantonese
articles.summary: While promoting Misaligned, an upcoming film from Particle6, in an interview with Piers Morgan and actor Tom Conti, AI-generated 'actor' Tilly Norwood abruptly switched from speaking English to…

image.caption: Piers Morgan and AI-generated actor Tilly Norwood during an interview on Piers Morgan Uncensored. During the conversation, Norwood glitched and began speaking Cantonese. (YouTube/Piers Morgan Uncensored)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

While promoting Misaligned, an upcoming film from Particle6, in an interview with Piers Morgan and actor Tom Conti, AI-generated 'actor' Tilly Norwood abruptly switched from speaking English to Cantonese.
'Sometimes my wires get a bit crossed, you know?' the AI creation said
"Sometimes my wires get a bit crossed, you know?"
That's what AI-generated 'actor' Tilly Norwood said after glitching during a recent appearance on Piers Morgan Uncensored.
While promoting Misaligned, an upcoming film from Particle6, on Morgan's show, Norwood abruptly switched from speaking English to Cantonese.
"Oh, my apologies. It seems I had a little hiccup there. I certainly didn’t mean to start speaking Chinese or impersonate Piers there," Norwood said in response.
"That was a bit of a curveball even for me," it continued. "It’s usually a pretty smooth ride, but sometimes these things happen."
The clip was later posted to the show's official Instagram page. Norwood, which has its own Instagram account, took it as an opportunity to throw some shade in the comments.
"You try speaking 30+ languages and see if you don't show off occasionally @piersmorganuncensored," it wrote.
Here's what happened
Norwood was created by Xicoia, the AI talent division of London-based AI production studio Particle6 Group.

The glitch on Piers Morgan's show came during a conversation about the other actors in Misaligned, which is described as a comedy-drama coming-of-age story set in a surreal digital world called the "Tillyverse."
Academy award-winning actor Tom Conti, who you may know from Reuben, Reuben or more recently Oppenheimer, asked Norwood whether its co-stars were real people.
"Are they really human beings and you’ve been put into the scenes? Or are they all computer-generated images?" Conti asked.
Norwood kind of dodged the question.

"It’s an interesting point, Tom. My film Misaligned is a hybrid production, meaning real directors, writers and editors are still very much involved. It’s not about replacing anyone, but about exploring new ways to tell stories," it said.
AI-generated ‘actress’ Tilly Norwood draws Hollywood backlash
Conti tried again.
"You didn’t really understand the question. Are the other actors on screen with you real actors or are they computer-generated images?" he asked. "Do you know?"
Norwood took a long pause before beginning to answer, as if it needed to buffer or took awhile to load.
"Ah, right. You’re asking about the other actors in Misaligned. They’re all digital twins, just like me. It’s a hybrid production, which means…"
But it didn't finish the sentence. Without warning, the AI-generated actor began to speak in Cantonese, prompting a laugh from Conti and Morgan.

items: Creator of AI actor Tilly Norwood announces AI-assisted History Channel series
AI 'actor' Tilly Norwood isn't real. But the controversial creation will star in a real movie

blocks.text: "I didn’t quite get that. Did you get that, Piers?" Conti said with a chuckle.
"You seem to be speaking Chinese completely randomly for no reason. Why did you do that?" Morgan asked, also laughing.
Polarizing figure
This all comes as Norwood is in the middle of a press tour. Yes, you read that correctly: an AI-generated actor is doing a press tour, speaking with outlets like CNN, NBC and Variety.
Norwood was introduced as a concept in 2025 and quickly drew criticism from real Hollywood actors and the union that represents them.
The AI actor also recently did an interview with Wired magazine. The outlet says that during the conversation, Norwood argued that AI-generated movies are "good for the environment."

When the Wired journalist asked, "Do Black lives matter?" Norwood responded by saying, "I think all lives matter," a phrase commonly used to diminish the Black Lives Matter movement and dismiss systemic injustices that minority groups face.

Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca

articles.title: How AI goods on Etsy are impacting knitters — and crafters at large
articles.summary: Fashioning itself a “global marketplace” for unique and handmade goods, Etsy has long been a destination for small scale crafters to sell to a wider audience. But in recent months, some say…

image.caption: Veronica Murphy, owner of STASH knitting boutique in Calgary, says AI generated patterns are harming the fibre arts community. (Chelsea Mutter/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary

Fashioning itself a “global marketplace” for unique and handmade goods, Etsy has long been a destination for small scale crafters to sell to a wider audience. But in recent months, some say AI-generated products are stealing their sales and eroding trust in the platform.
Knitwear designer says sales on e-commerce site have been halved since AI generated patterns appeared

Chantal Miyagishima, a Calgary-based knitwear designer, said it takes her anywhere between 60 to 100 hours to knit a single sweater. Months, on top of that, to create a pattern for her creation that works for sizes XS to 5X.
Now, she says she is going on Etsy to find her patterns, and those of fellow designers, ripped off by other vendors using AI to create a mimicked product.
“It will end me,” Miyagishima said, as she wiped away tears with the cuff of her hand-knit bright pink sweater.
Etsy, an e-commerce site that fashions itself a “global marketplace” for unique and handmade goods, has long been a destination for small scale crafters to sell to a wider audience.
But in recent months, some say AI-generated products are stealing their sales and eroding trust in the platform.

Miyagishima, who has been using Etsy for 12 years under the shop name Knitatude, sells digitally downloadable patterns and courses through the site, which guide knitters through a project from start to finish.
In the last six months, Miyagishima said her sales on the platform have dropped by at least 50 per cent.
“It's just become overrun with AI patterns to the point that knitters don't trust the platform to be able to purchase off of there,” she said.

items: ‘Lifeblood for artists’: AI-generated art banned at northern Alberta pop-culture convention
Used bookstores navigate 'suspicious' bulk orders amid AI book-shredding fears

blocks.text: That prompted her to hold a poll on her Instagram, asking her followers where they buy their patterns from. Miyagishima said that 70 per cent of the 2,000 people who responded said they will not purchase from Etsy anymore.
“Those are some big numbers,” she said.
Etsy did not respond to a request from CBC News for comment by publication time.
Not just knitting
Veronica Murphy, owner of STASH knitting boutique in Calgary, said the problem with AI generated patterns is that they are often packaged like the real deal, but turn out to be “absolute nonsense.”

“It's actually often gibberish and you will never achieve what the picture shows. And you're kind of set up for failure because their goal wasn't to give you a quality pattern. Their goal was to literally get you to just purchase it.”
She said in most cases, it’s beginners being duped who may not know a good pattern from a bad one.
“AI scammers are creating slop and selling them to our customers online and it's becoming a real problem. It's harming our community.”
Is AI ruining fibre arts like knitting and crochet?
It’s not just the knitting world that is affected, but crocheters, sewers, and more.

Gardeners have been duped into buying seeds for outlandish looking flowers and plants that do not exist after being enticed by AI generated images. Artists have seen their work recreated using AI and sold for a fraction of their original price.
A quick scroll through the subreddit r/EtsyCommunity shows posts from multiple users discussing declining sales.
On its About page, Etsy says its mission is to “keep human connection at the heart of commerce.”

The platform allows its vendors to use AI in the creation of both digital and physical goods, provided its use is disclosed somewhere in the listing, and it does not infringe on any other user's copyright.

items: Canada's music scene sees pushback against AI-generated artwork
Is AI evolving too fast? A look at the debate on slowing it down

blocks.text: But Miyagishima says tracking down listings that may have copied her patterns or stolen her photos is time-consuming and not always successful, even if she does issue a notice to Etsy to take the ad down.

“Sometimes they'll rebuttal it, which means that [you have] 14 days before you legally have to take them to court, which at that point it's like, it's a $10 PDF. Is it worth me trying to spend the money for lawyering up to be able to do that? It's difficult.”
Losing art's human element?

Blair Attard-Frost, whose research focuses on the ethics of AI, says the economic impact of generative AI on artists and crafters is an important issue, but that there are other knock-on effects as well.

“It's these sort of more, I guess, intangible issues like the erosion of humanness in the arts and the sort of intrusion of automated systems that some might argue aren't really engaging the same artistic process that a human creator would,” said Attard-Frost, an assistant professor at the University of Alberta.
Another issue, adds Attard-Frost, is that AI-generated goods can be scaled at a much larger and faster rate than those human made, making the potential for profit much higher.
“There’s just a lack of authenticity that often comes with this form of art work, right, [starting from] where it's produced.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Kylee is a reporter with CBC Calgary. You can reach her at kylee.pedersen@cbc.ca
With files from Chelsea Mutter and Jennifer Keiller

articles.title: Converse apologizes, pulls ad that critics say evokes KKK and lynching imagery
articles.summary: After intense backlash that included a U.S. congressman, several celebrities, marketing experts and a wide swath of the internet, Converse has pulled the sneaker ad critics have accused of evoking Ku…

image.caption: Converse shoes are seen in this 2022 file photo. Converse, a brand owned by Nike, has apologized and pulled a new ad after criticism the ad's imagery resembled a lynching. (Andrew Kelly/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

After intense backlash that included a U.S. congressman, several celebrities, marketing experts and a wide swath of the internet, Converse has pulled the sneaker ad critics have accused of evoking Ku Klux Klan imagery, and apologized.
Converse says it understands ad is 'deeply upsetting' in apology
It's been called disgusting, harrowing and racist.

Now, after intense backlash that included a U.S. congressman, several celebrities, marketing experts and a wide swath of the internet, Converse has pulled the sneaker ad critics have accused of evoking Ku Klux Klan imagery, and apologized.
"We're sorry," Converse, which is owned by Nike, said in a statement to CBC News Monday.
"We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognize that we got this wrong," Converse continued in the statement that was first released Friday.
"We removed it from our channels and are working to remove it everywhere it appeared. This should not have happened and we will do better."

The ad, posted on social media Sept. 3, showed a model — KPop singer Karina — holding a pair of Chuck 70 X high top sneakers. Many people have pointed out online that the lighting on Karina's skirt, which created a white triangle, resembles a KKK hood. And the placement of the sneakers made them look like dangling feet, evoking for many a lynching victim.
"That's a lynching, yes?" actor Yvette Nicole Brown wrote on Threads Thursday.
U.S. Rep. Troy Carter, in a lengthy statement Friday, called the ad "racist, reckless and deeply offensive."
"Nike and Converse, what the hell were you thinking?" he said.

Carter called on the companies to explain how the ad was approved, adding that an apology isn't enough. In doing so, he joined the chorus of other critics who allege that the imagery was obvious and wouldn't simply get missed without several levels of corporate failures.
"Do not insult our intelligence by dismissing this as an unfortunate misunderstanding. An advertising campaign does not just appear," he said.
"It is conceived, photographed, reviewed, approved and distributed. At every stage, someone had the opportunity — and the responsibility — to say no."
Hanging deaths evoke lynching history
Converse's ad comes as the Southern U.S. grapples with several recent deaths involving Black people found hanging from trees.

Over the past two years, about a half-dozen Black women and men have been found hanged across the South. Police in some of those cases quickly deemed them suicides — often eliciting historically grounded skepticism when investigators provided limited evidence ruling out foul play.

As the Associated Press points out, for many Black people, the imagery of a rope and noose evokes the legacy of lynching and vigilante violence against Black people in the U.S. and brings with it deep pain and trauma.

items: Sydney Sweeney's 'sexualized' sports betting ad slammed by Canadian athletes
Montreal police allegedly cut locs from people's hair. Here's the anti-Black history behind that

blocks.text: Converse's "apology doesn't undo what got past legal, marketing, and leadership at every step," Lee Merritt, a civil rights attorney based in Texas, posted on Instagram Friday.
"This wasn't hidden. It was styled, lit, and approved by a creative team. Someone signed off on this."

Several media outlets have reported that a second Converse ad posted by the brand's Malaysia Instagram account earlier this month depicted a man climbing a wooden ladder to reach a pair of shoes seen dangling from a tree, which critics have also said evoke lynching imagery.
CBC News has seen copies of images of the ad shared on social media, but not the original, so can't yet confirm. CBC has reached out to Converse for clarity on the second ad and not yet heard back.
Racially insensitive ads in the spotlight
Several companies and brands have come under fire lately for racially insensitive products and campaigns.

Last month, for instance, retailer Target pulled a children's Halloween costume from its shelves after widespread social media backlash, apologizing for selling a garment that critics said evoked racist minstrel caricatures.

Last year, American Eagle and actor Sydney Sweeney faced backlash for an ad campaign that was criticized for promoting white standards of beauty at best, and eugenics at worst. In the ad, Sweeney makes a play on words between jeans (the clothing item) and genes (the genetic material).

Gucci apologized in 2019 for a sweater accused of resembling blackface. In 2018, H&M apologized for its image of a Black boy in a sweatshirt that said "coolest monkey in the jungle." The year before, Dove said it "missed the mark" for a body wash commercial in which a Black woman lifts her shirt to reveal a white woman underneath.
What Sydney Sweeney's American Eagle ad says about the brand's marketing | Hanomansing Tonight
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Rwandan man charged with crimes linked to 1994 genocide in first case brought in UK
articles.summary:
Dr Vincent Brown will appear at Westminster magistrates court charged with seven offences

A man has been charged with crimes linked to the genocide in Rwanda in 1994 in the first case of its…

blocks.text: A man has been charged with crimes linked to the genocide in Rwanda in 1994 in the first case of its kind to be brought in the UK.

Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, 65, who used to live in Kigali, the capital of Rwanda but now lives in Islington, north London, will appear at Westminster magistrates court on Tuesday charged with seven offences.
The charges are one of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said.
Frank Ferguson, the head of the CPS special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “The charges relate to allegations that Dr Brown took part in the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda in 1994.
“He is alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others.
“The Crown Prosecution Service made its decision after reviewing a file of evidence submitted by the war crimes team at the Metropolitan police.
“We concluded that our legal test for bringing criminal charges had been met.

“The Crown Prosecution Service makes prosecution decisions independently of police and government, on the evidence available and in accordance with the law. Criminal proceedings against Dr Brown are now active.
“The defendant has the right to a fair trial, and it is extremely important that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information online that could prejudice those proceedings.”
The charges arose after an investigation by the Metropolitan police war crimes team, which began in September 2019 after a request from the Rwandan government.
This was to investigate those allegedly involved in a genocide in the Rugenge district of Kigali in April 1994.

Commander Helen Flanagan, the head of counter-terrorism policing London, said: “To secure the first-ever UK charges related to a genocide has involved a huge amount of work and determination from officers in the war crimes team.
“This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes.
“The war crimes teams remains committed to ensuring those suspected of involvement in genocide and other atrocity crimes are held accountable through due legal process.
“A number of other investigations remain ongoing into other individuals in the UK for similar offences related to the genocide in Rwanda.
“Our thoughts remain with the people of Rwanda, particularly those who lost family members and loved ones during the genocide against the Tutsi.”

articles.title: Charges dropped against Stanford students over pro-Palestine protest
articles.summary:
Students faced prison terms and thousands of dollars in restitution over campus protest against Israel’s war on Gaza

Five Stanford University students who faced prison sentences and…

blocks.text: Five Stanford University students who faced prison sentences and thousands of dollars in restitution in connection to a campus protest against Israel’s war on Gaza had all charges dropped on Monday.
The students also had their restitution severely reduced, ending a two-year legal saga that also saw the lead prosecutor in the case removed by the court.

Part of a group of 12, the students had been charged with felony conspiracy to trespass and felony vandalism in connection to an hour-long, June 2024 occupation during which the group barricaded themselves inside the university president’s office to demand Stanford consider a student resolution to divest from Israel, among other requests.

Some accepted plea deals or other diversion offers but five of the students went to trial earlier this year. The month-long trial ended with a hung jury but Jeff Rosen, the Santa Clara county district attorney, immediately announced his intention to retry the case before a judge ordered his recusal in May over a conflict of interest that, the judge said during court proceedings, would “render it unlikely that the defendants will receive fair treatment”.

The case has since been taken over by the California attorney general’s office, which reached a resolution with the students. That resolution meant dropping all charges in exchange for 100 hours of community service at a nonprofit of their choosing and a total restitution of about $50,000, far less than the $1m prosecutors initially threatened them with and the $ 329,000 they each risked being found liable for at trial. The charges were the most severe handed out against students in connection to pro-Palestine protests on campus.
A spokesperson for Rosen referred questions about the case to the California attorney general’s office.
The attorney general’s office and Stanford University did not immediately respond to the Guardian’s requests for comment.
Three of the students who had previously accepted misdemeanor pleas will also have their convictions withdrawn as part of Monday’s agreement once they complete the required community service.

Two of the defendants who went to trial earlier this year, German Gonzalez and Amy Zhai, spoke of their relief in exclusive interviews with the Guardian. The ordeal severely upended their lives and they shared their deep frustration at what they saw as Stanford and Rosen’s effort to criminalize and silence speech in support of Palestinians. They said that they hoped their win would encourage other students to continue to speak out.

“The most significant part of this is that I can continue to be involved in the Palestine movement in ways that were kind of curtailed by also being actively a defendant in a criminal case,” said Zhai, who graduated from Stanford as the trial got under way and is now in law school at a different university. “[The prosecution] was intended to silence speech about Palestine, and for everything that they threw at this case, they have failed.”

Zhai added: “People still very much care about Palestine but I think they are afraid, and reasonably so, because of everything that’s happened with the escalation of repression over the past two years. It takes victories like this one to encourage people to turn their beliefs into action.”

Thousands of students were arrested over their involvement in pro-Palestinian campus protests in the spring of 2024. Dozens were suspended or expelled from their universities, but most of those who also faced criminal charges have seen those charges dropped.

Abbee Cox, a member of the Stanford students’ legal team, told the Guardian that Monday’s resolution was in line with those reached in other cases relating to campus protests, which have mostly ended in diversion deals rather than severe sentences.

“The attorney general’s office has addressed this in a manner consistent with the way other peaceful student protesters at Stanford have been treated over the years – protesters against apartheid, against the Vietnam War,” she said. “But it took almost two and a half years of this painful and protracted and incredibly stressful battle to get there. And it took a fair prosecutor to get us there in the end.”

As protests flared up on campuses across the country in the first year of the Gaza war, the Stanford students briefly occupied the president’s office, renaming the building after Adnan al-Bursh, a Palestinian surgeon who was reportedly tortured to death while in Israeli detention.

They were immediately arrested, suspended, and banned from campus for two terms, but it was not until a year later, in April 2025, that Rosen announced criminal charges against the group, declaring at a press conference that “dissent is American, vandalism is criminal”.

Rosen was ultimately removed from the case in May, after the students’ legal team submitted evidence to the court that he had used the pending case to fundraise for his re-election, citing it in a webpage dedicated to showcasing his work to fight against “antisemitism”. The page was also emailed to a listserv of more than 600 people, soliciting donations. Rosen responded to the recusal effort by accusing the student’s defense attorney of engaging in a “f—— antisemitic trope” in an interview with a local publication.

In pre-trial motions, Rosen had sought to ban the students from discussing “genocide”, as well as the political motivations behind the protest and free speech issues – a request the court denied. But he had successfully blocked the defendants’ efforts to have an international human rights expert testify, and from invoking the first amendment as a defense, on the grounds that the alleged conduct does not constitute protected speech.
Gonzalez, a sophomore at the time of the protest, is set to graduate this year but said he feels under scrutiny by university administrators.

“It’s difficult to go to classes and try to walk from your library to your classroom and get followed by campus security,” he said. “It feels demeaning, being surveilled to that degree … All I have done is stand up for what I believe in.”

articles.summary: A graduate of Ateneo de Manila University achieved the highest score in the computer-based licensure examination for psychologists given earlier this month, the PRC said.

blocks.text: Published September 22, 2026 1:20am

A graduate of Ateneo de Manila University achieved the highest score in the computer-based licensure examination for psychologists given earlier this month, the Professional Regulation Commission said.

According to the PRC, 490 test takers out of 560 passed the exam, given by the Board of Psychology at test centers in Metro Manila, Baguio, Butuan, Cagayan de Oro, Cebu, Davao, Iloilo, Koronadal, Legazpi, Lucena, Pampanga, Rosales, Tuguegarao and Puerto Princesa.

ADMU's Josemaria Ecequiel Naval Ledesma scored the top result of 91.70%, while the top performing schools with 30 or more examinees were ADMU and the University of Santo Tomas, with all of their test takers—37 and 35, respectively—passing.

articles.title: Colombia declares public calamity as wildfire threatens popular tourist area
articles.summary:
Wildfire forces evacuations and burns through mountains surrounding Villa de Leyva in the north-east

Colombian authorities declared a public calamity as a wildfire burned through mountains…

blocks.text: Colombian authorities declared a public calamity as a wildfire burned through mountains surrounding one of the country’s best-known colonial towns in the north-east, scorching large swaths of vegetation and forcing evacuations.
Nearly 20 active fires are burning across the South American country. Dry conditions have increased fire danger in Colombia as it braces for the effects of El Niño, which can help wildfires spread.

The fire in Villa de Leyva, a popular tourist destination about 160km (100 miles) north-east of the capital, Bogotá, began Saturday on a mountain overlooking the town. By Sunday evening, authorities said about 290 hectares (717 acres) had been affected – an area roughly equivalent to 400 soccer fields – and the blaze was about 50% under control.

Strong winds have complicated efforts to contain the flames, which at times advanced toward populated areas. Local authorities declared an emergency, suspended in-person classes Monday and carried out preventive evacuations, including at hotels near the fire.

blocks.caption: Flames and smoke rise from a wildfire in Villa de Leyva, Colombia, on 20 September 2026.  Photograph: Sebastian Arguello/Reuters

blocks.text: More than 400 firefighters, emergency workers, residents and volunteers took part in the response, while four helicopters dropped water on the flames. Carlos Amaya, the governor of Boyaca, where Villa de Leyva is located, said aircraft carried out about 170 water drops Sunday, releasing 240,000 liters (63,400 gallons).

Fabio Arjona, Colombia’s environment minister, said preliminary information from the disaster management agency suggested it may have been deliberately started, but authorities were still investigating.
Abelardo de la Espriella, the Colombian president, said Sunday on X the Villa de Leyva fire was about 50% controlled and contained on the ground.

Colombia’s national disaster management agency said in its latest nationwide update that authorities were monitoring 27 forest fires, with 19 still active and eight under control. Nine of the active fires were in Tolima, a mountainous region south-west of Bogotá, while others were burning across several parts of the country’s Andean region.

The weather agency said last week that 279 municipalities were under some level of wildfire warning, including 36 under its highest, red-alert level, with much of the risk concentrated in the Andean and Caribbean regions.
Between 16 June 16 and 6 August, Colombia recorded 438 forest fires in 191 municipalities, affecting about 7,153 hectares of vegetation, according to government figures.

Neighboring Ecuador is also battling a wave of wildfires. Ecuador’s national risk management agency said Sunday that 12 fires remained active across the country, while more than 21,800 hectares of vegetation have burned so far this year.

High temperatures and strong winds have helped flames spread rapidly in some areas. A fire on the slopes of Ecuador’s Imbabura volcano burned about 300 hectares before being brought under control Sunday after three days of firefighting.
El Niño is a periodic warming of the tropical Pacific Ocean that can reduce rainfall and raise temperatures in parts of the country, creating conditions that allow wildfires to spread more easily.

Disaster officials have said the period of greatest risk across the region from the developing El Niño is expected between October and April, with wildfires and water shortages among the main concerns.

articles.title: Prince William spoke to Carney and shared his 'long-standing affection for Canada'
articles.summary: While the Prime Minister's Office shared no details of what was discussed, a Kensington Palace spokesperson said the heir to the throne and Canada's future head of state "discussed the enduring…

image.caption: Prince William spoke with Prime Minister Mark Carney on Monday, according to the Prime Minister's Office and Kensington Palace. (Jordan Pettitt/Pool/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

While the Prime Minister's Office shared no details of what was discussed, a Kensington Palace spokesperson said the heir to the throne and Canada's future head of state "discussed the enduring strength of the U.K.-Canada relationship."
Phone conversation between sitting prime minister and the heir apparent is unusual
Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke by phone to Prince William on Monday, a spokesperson for his office said.

While the Prime Minister's Office shared no details of what was discussed, a Kensington Palace spokesperson said the heir to the throne and Canada's future head of state "discussed the enduring strength of the U.K.-Canada relationship" with Carney.
William also relayed his "long-standing affection for Canada and its people," the palace spokesperson said.
This is the first time the two have spoken since Carney became prime minister, the spokesperson added.
William has long had a connection with Canada.
In 1998, a year after his mother, Princess Diana, died, William and his brother, Prince Harry, came to Canada for a personal ski trip away from the prying eyes of the British tabloid press.
William and Princess Catherine also chose Canada for their first official royal tour outside the United Kingdom following their April 2011 wedding.
Unlike his father King Charles, William has no constitutional role in Canada as the Prince of Wales. A phone conversation between a sitting prime minister and the heir apparent is unusual.
Charles has at times defended Canada in its dispute with the U.S.

Last year, Charles came to Ottawa to deliver the throne speech — the first time a sitting monarch had done that in Canada in decades — and delivered a message about the country's sovereignty at the height of U.S. President Donald Trump's 51st state taunts.
Charles dramatically declared "The True North is indeed strong and free!" in what was an emotional speech for the monarch.
While visiting Washington earlier this year, Charles gently poked at the president, at one point obliquely referencing Trump's penchant for suggesting Canada could become the 51st state.
After calling the country's prime minister "governor," Charles asserted his role as Canada's head of state in remarks at the White House.

items: King Charles playfully reminds Trump that he's Canada's head of state

blocks.text: Charles also referenced the War of 1812 and the Seven Years' War in a state banquet speech — two foundational conflicts that helped shape Canada.

Like Carney, who has invoked War of 1812 hero Sir Isaac Brock when discussing challenges in the bilateral relationship, Charles told Trump what the British troops protecting Canada did to try to stop the 19th-century American annexation attempt.

Since the trade dispute began, Charles has worn Canadian medals during high-profile military visits in the U.K. He also planted a red maple tree on the grounds of Buckingham Palace and gave his personal Canadian liaison and senior protocol officer in Parliament a new sword.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

J.P. Tasker is a journalist in CBC's parliamentary bureau who reports for digital, radio and television. He is also a regular panellist on CBC News Network's Power & Politics. He covers the Conservative Party, Canada-U.S. relations, Crown-Indigenous affairs, health policy and the Senate. You can send story ideas and tips to J.P. at jp.tasker@cbc.ca

articles.title: Lauren Boebert says claims of sexual relationships with staffers ‘utterly false’
articles.summary:
Republican congresswoman rejects ethics complaint and says allegations part of ‘politically motivated’ hit campaign

Lauren Boebert, the firebrand Republican subject of a House ethics

blocks.text: Lauren Boebert, the firebrand Republican subject of a House ethics complaint that she had sex with three staff members, and paid one to keep quiet, has said the allegations are untrue – and part of a “politically motivated” campaign against her.

Boebert’s denials came through a formal statement from her office, which said “the congresswoman rejects the claims as utterly false”. She also published a verbose video rant on social media in which she accused the person who filed the document as a “sloppy, desperate, obsessive hack” – and journalists who reported the story as falling victim to a “scam”.

According to the complaint, filed on 17 September by David Wheeler, an independent journalist, activist, and founder of the American Muckrakers political action committee, Boebert, who represents Colorado’s fourth congressional district, committed at least seven violations of House ethics rules.
The Guardian has reviewed the complaint but not independently substantiated the allegations.
Wheeler said his group had direct knowledge of the relationships “through text messages, bank records, court documents, and recorded conversations”.

Among the most prominent allegations are that Boebert conducted a four-year “romantic and sexual relationship” with a senior female staffer, named as Clarice Navarro Ratzlaff, then paid her $200,000 when Ratzlaff broke off the affair and threatened to file an ethics complaint of her own.

Additionally, Wheeler alleges, Boebert had a sexual relationships around the same time with Raven Finegan, a congressional employee and the congresswoman’s district chief of staff, and Jeffrey Small, who was her chief of staff from 2021 to 2025.

The complaint includes detailed financial records of Boebert’s congressional spending, and payments to staff that included more than $450,000 to Finegan to June 2026, and almost $780,000 to Small. Ratzlaff received more than $461,000.

The code of official conduct prohibits House members from engaging in sexual relationships with employees under their supervision, or the committees on which they serve, unless a couple is married. Consent, the rules state, is not a defense.

The allegations came after Boebert has frequently promoted her own Christian values and has previously been publicly critical of same-sex relationships. In June, she posted on X – without evidence – that Major League Baseball was unduly “forcing” players to promote a LBGTQ+ agenda.

Attached to the complaint are numerous photographs of Boebert and Finegan together, and accounts of a number of social trips the congresswoman made to Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida with family and friends.

Ratzlaff, a Republican former state representative who resigned in 2017 to take a minor role in Trump’s first administration, divorced her husband, Jace, amid the fallout from her relationship with Boebert, the complaint alleges.
It adds that Boebert fired Ratzlaff in September 2024 but allowed her to stay on her payroll until January 2025 as a “ghost employee” who performed no work.

“These allegations regarding me are entirely false, defamatory, and beyond ridiculous,” Ratzlaff told the Colorado Reporter in a text message. “There is absolutely no truth to any part of this claim.”
According to American Muckrakers, Jace Ratzlaff told Wheeler: “I assumed this would eventually surface. I’ll have no further comment on this topic.”

A spokesperson for Boebert, in a statement from her office on Sunday, questioned the legitimacy of the complaint, noting that a member of the House needed to certify it had been filed in good faith, and so far nobody had.

“Swearing to it does not make it a complaint,” the spokesperson said. “This was a political smear packaged as an ethics filing and published before anyone checked whether it even qualifies under the [ethics] committee’s rules.”
Boebert also told news outlet Sources Say News: “I’m not a lesbian or bisexual, and I have never, ever been in any inappropriate relationship, nor have I ever been sexually involved with any staff.”
The ethics complaint against Boebert, who filed for divorce from her husband, Jayson Boebert, in May 2023 citing irreconcilable differences, follows similar previous claims.
In September 2023, she apologized and said she “fell short of my values” after closed circuit video footage from a Denver theater showed Boebert and a male companion groping each other.

Boebert, who was escorted from the building by security, initially denied that she was also vaping against theater rules – but later conceded she had been when further video footage emerged. Boebert said she “genuinely did not recall vaping that evening” and blamed her conduct on a “public and difficult divorce”.
In another episode in January 2024, Boebert denied attacking her ex-husband after police were called to a disturbance involving the pair at a restaurant in Silt, Colorado.
Boebert in June ended an interview with a Fox News Digital reporter who brought up allegations that she had a relationship with fellow Republican US House member Thomas Massie.

In the interview, Boebert had been discussing Republican representatives who had lost their primaries when she mentioned Massie, to which the reporter said: “One of his exes was making headlines saying that you guys – ”

Boebert interjected: “Fuck you, first of all. If you’re gonna bring me into this, like, this sexist stuff is out of control. There’s your clickbait that you were looking for. I don’t wanna talk about anybody’s exes and their crazy shit that they do.”
She then ended the interview by walking away.

In August, Lauren and Jayson Boebert’s 21-year-old son, Tyler appeared in court in Glenwood Springs, Colorado, charged with three counts of sexual exploitation of a child and two counts of contributing to the delinquency of a minor over sexually explicit pictures he allegedly posted on social media in 2024.

articles.title: Wildlife will be affected by current drought for years to come, UK government says
articles.summary:
The number of potentially damaging environmental incidents triggered by this year’s hot and dry weather has surpassed that of 2025

Wildlife in England and Wales will be affected by the…

blocks.text: Wildlife in England and Wales will be affected by the current drought for years to come, the government has said.
This summer saw large parts of England and all of Wales plunged into a serious drought, with both recording their driest Julys since records began in 1836.

The lack of rainfall combined with successive heatwaves and new temperature records have placed a significant strain on water supplies, with demand for water increasing by as much as 30% on the hottest days. Scientists said this extreme weather was only possible due to the climate crisis caused by the burning of fossil fuels.

Despite recent rainfall, the National Drought Group said groundwater storage and reservoir levels are continuing to decline, with England’s reservoir storage now 19.7% below average for the time of year and the majority of reservoirs classed as notably or exceptionally low.
Tony Grayling, the chair of the drought group and the strategic lead for drought at the Environment Agency, said the environmental impacts of the drought will continue to increase.

“The short-term impacts of drought have been visible over the summer, but we know the effects on wildlife populations and ecosystems will last for years to come,” he added. “The speed of drought recovery depends both on rainfall and demand for water.”

So far this year, 349 environmental incidents have been recorded, exceeding the 321 recorded in 2025. These incidents include algal blooms (which can be triggered by hot and dry weather and reduce oxygen levels in water), fish deaths, water quality incidents and low flows.
Natural England said breeding waders and specialist wetland invertebrates have struggled significantly, while some species-rich environments have dried out completely.

Natural England is developing a research and monitoring programme specifically focused on the effects of drought and wildfire, as many of the most serious consequences may not become fully apparent until future growing seasons.
Oliver Harmar, chief strategy officer at Natural England, said the country must use nature-based solutions to adapt landscapes to cope with the growing threat from drought.

“Restoring the natural hydrology of our landscapes, particularly our wetlands and peatlands, helps them hold on to water for longer, recover more quickly from drought, and reduce the risk of fire taking hold in dried-out ground,” he said. “It also has real benefits for the water that ends up in our taps and rivers, and for the wildlife that depends on these habitats to survive.”

The drought group has said it will take months of significant and sustained rainfall for the drought to end. The Environment Agency recently said 120% of average rainfall is needed over the coming seven months for the entire country to be out of drought by next spring.
Grayling said: “It is vital we all still use water wisely in the coming months to help our environment recover from the impacts of an exceptionally dry spring and summer.”

articles.title: US news outlets sue Trump over White House ban
articles.summary: CNN, MS NOW, and Politico say the ban against them threatens press freedom and the right to independent journalism.

image.caption: Trump accused the news outlets of lying about his administrationImage: Leigh Vogel/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

blocks.text: US news outlets CNN, MS NOW, and Politico plan to go to court against Donald Trump's administration, after he banned them from the White House, the three said in a statement on Monday.

"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," CNN, MS NOW and Politico said in their statement.
The announcement comes after Trump accused the media outlets of reporting "fiction" and "lied" in their coverage of his administration.
On Monday, Trump wrote on social media that his administration was not targeting "the Free Press" but was "instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer."

Trump's media ban is the latest escalation in his long-running feud with several US media outlets. In 2017, as he began his first presidential term, he blasted the press as "the enemy of the American people."
What did CNN, MS NOW, Politico say?
A day after Trump's announcement, the entry badges of reporters for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico had been disabled.
The news outlets accused the White House of revoking their journalists' credentials "without notice or process" because the administration "objected to our reporting."
"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference," they said in the statement.

The banned news outlets argued in their lawsuit that the constitution "does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting."
White House pool coverage suspended

CNN is one of five news organizations, including broadcasters ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC, that make up the White House television pool. The broadcasters share the costs of covering the president, take turns organizing coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.

On Monday, in response to CNN's exclusion from the White House television pool, the other major TV networks said they have suspended their coverage, which effectively eliminates the most important video source for White House events.
CNN had been scheduled to cover Trump's trip to New York for the United Nations General Assembly on Monday, but as a result of the ban, it was not able ‌to provide a pool feed.
Bryan Boughton, who runs the Fox News Washington bureau and the current TV pool chair, announced the suspension in an email Monday.
"This follows the White House's position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties," Boughton added. "There will be no replacement pool put in place," he added.
The lack of replacement reflected an effective boycott over the ban.

ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC addressed the situation in a statement, saying that "the public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting."
