articles.title: Discovery of new Australian stick insect species reveals case of mistaken identity
articles.summary:
New study describes two species, Anchiale robusta and Anchiale mabiensis, both found in far north Queensland

  • Get our
articles.byline: Donna Lu Assistant editor, climate, environment and science

blocks.text: Two new large stick insect species have been identified by Australian researchers, in a discovery they say illustrates how little we still understand about insect diversity.
The two species, both found in far north Queensland, are described in a study published in Austral Entomology.

One, named Anchiale robusta, was hiding in plain sight: the stick insect has long been popular among enthusiasts and scientists, but analysis has only now revealed that its previous designation was a case of mistaken identity.

“When we went out into the field, and we saw a whole bunch of different individuals that looked morphologically different, and they were also living in … different habitats, that was our first hint that there was a bit more of a complicated story here,” said the study’s lead author, Dr Braxton Jones of the University of Sydney.
Combining analysis of DNA and museum collections, citizen science records and surveys, the team discovered the insect had been misidentified for decades.

Anchiale robusta females grow to a body length of 12 to 16cm; males reach 9 to 10cm in length. “Mostly their wings are black but some of them have a little bit of purple on the underside of their hindwing,” Jones said.
“Males are always smaller than females – it’s incredibly rare for a female to be able to still fly because they are quite heavy with … eggs.”

blocks.caption: A female Anchiale robusta, during a threat display. Photograph: Paul D Brock/Natural History Museum

blocks.text: The team also described Anchiale mabiensis, a species that lives in the critically endangered Mabi rainforest of Queensland’s Atherton tablelands. Females of the species are about 11 to 12cm long.
The eggs of the species have an unusual structural “lid”, which detaches when the insects hatch, Jones said.

In describing two new species and confirming the existence of a third, the research revealed that what were once considered two species are in fact five species in habitats stretching from northern New South Wales into tropical north Queensland.
That finding had important conservation implications, Jones said, given that the species are found in smaller habitat ranges than previously thought.

Jones said animals of the Anchiale genus were one of the most documented stick insects on citizen science platforms, because “there’s quite a lot of them and they can hatch in large proportions and population sizes”.
Despite this, he said, “there’s so much we don’t know about them”.
The study also identified another probable new species in Cape York, but more specimens are needed for confirmation.

Last year, also on the Atherton tablelands, scientists discovered a 40cm-long new species, Acrophylla alta, which weighs slightly less than a golf ball and which they noted could be the heaviest insect in Australia.
Australia’s longest species, the gargantuan stick insect, is also found in northeastern Queensland; females of the species can grow to more than half a metre in length.

articles.title: Man and police officer wounded in exchange of gunfire near Ontario synagogue
articles.summary:
Officials say man was critically injured and officer was wounded in Yom Kippur incident near Belleville synagogue

A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire on Sunday…

blocks.text: A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire on Sunday near a synagogue in Ontario as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. The man was hospitalized in life-threatening condition.

The Canadian province’s special investigations unit said the exchange of gunfire happened near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, about 110 miles (160km) east of Toronto. Belleville police said the officer encountered the man at about 7.10pm and that both were taken to a hospital.

Police have not said what led to the shooting or whether the synagogue or Jewish community was targeted. They said there was no risk to public safety and asked people to avoid the area while officers investigated.
The special investigations unit, the civilian agency that investigates serious incidents involving police, said it sent investigators to the scene.
Belleville police said they would not provide further information while the investigation was under way.
Doug Ford, Ontario’s premier, said the shooting took place outside the synagogue as people gathered for Yom Kippur.

“I’m disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur,” Ford said in a post on social media.
Ford said Jewish people “have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear” and called for those responsible to be arrested and prosecuted.
“My thoughts are also with the police officer who was shot, along with their family and loved ones,” Ford said.
York regional police said there was no known threat in the region but residents should expect increased patrols at places of worship.
Sunday’s shooting comes months after Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, warned that the country was failing its Jewish community amid a surge in antisemitism.

Carney cited shootings at Jewish schools, firebombings of synagogues, and attacks on community centers and Jewish-owned businesses. His government announced millions in additional funding to help faith-based institutions pay for security infrastructure, training and personnel.

Synagogues in the Toronto area have also previously been targeted by gunfire. In March, shots damaged the entrances of synagogues in Vaughan and Toronto. No one was injured. Police later arrested three suspects in connection with those shootings.

articles.title: Airlines criticise air traffic control as second glitch causes more disruption in UK
articles.summary: EasyJet says the latest incident "once again calls into question the resilience" of the system.

blocks.text: Airlines have criticised the UK's air traffic control system after a second technical problem in two weeks caused major disruption to UK flights

EasyJet said Monday's incident "once again calls into question the resilience" of how the service works, while Wizz Air said there was a "national confidence crisis" in National Air Traffic Services (Nats), which runs the UK's air traffic.
The technical problem at Prestwick in Ayrshire caused disruption at airports across Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England, delaying dozens of flights.

Nats said a "connectivity issue" was to blame for the disruption, and that it had "nothing to do" with a separate software defect at Swanwick that led to the cancellation of 2,000 flights earlier in September.
The underlying issue causing Monday's disruption has since been resolved, with Nats saying it was running at "full capacity" although officials warned of knock-on effects.
A spokesperson said they were now "focused on working with our customers to recover their residual delays and help get their operations back to normal".

According to aviation analytics company Cirium, as of 13:45 BST, at least 200 flights had been cancelled or did not fly on Monday. This includes 100 flights scheduled to arrive in the UK and 99 that were due to depart from the UK.
Easyjet was the worst affected airline, with 47 of its 670 scheduled departures cancelled, while British Airways has seen 11 cancellations from its 513 scheduled departures.
The UK Civil Aviation Authority said passengers who had flights disrupted were "unlikely" to be entitled to compensation.

It said the technical issue is "likely to be considered the result of 'extraordinary circumstances' under passenger rights rules", meaning that "although passengers should be looked after by airlines, they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident".
Industry representative body Airlines UK said both passengers and airlines "deserve better" service after "yet another Nats failure".
Managing director of Wizz Air UK, Yvonne Moynihan, called for "urgent reform" of Nats, adding that she did not have confidence in its current leadership.

When asked by BBC Radio 4's World at One programme whether Nats chief Martin Rolfe should resign, Moynihan said: "We need to look at the leadership at the top. But more than that, what are the board of directors doing?"
Jet2 boss Steve Heapy called for "urgent and accountable" action to bolster the UK's air traffic control infrastructure.

Ryanair reiterated its calls for Rolfe to resign, saying he had failed to deliver" either a reliable system or an effective back-up". The latest outage affected 140 of the airline's flights and 25,000 passengers.
British Airways said "yet another technical fault with Nats" was "disappointing".
A Nats spokesperson apologised for the disruption, saying: "In the real world, we accept technology can and sometimes does fail. Our job is minimising disruption where possible.
"What isn't acceptable is any incident where safety is compromised - this is always our first priority."
They added that it was working to return air traffic to normal as quickly as possible and urged passengers to check their flight status with their airline.
Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander acknowledged the problems with flights were "deeply frustrating" for passengers.
Steve Davies, 74, told the BBC he was "cheesed off with air traffic control" as technical issues with its systems seemed to be "happening a lot".
He and his wife Sadie became stuck at Birmingham airport after being told to disembark their easyJet flight to Edinburgh on Monday morning.
Nicole McCloskey, from Kilmarnock, had been due to go to Disneyland Paris with her family before their flight was cancelled.
She told the BBC her family got a message to say the flight was delayed while they were travelling to Glasgow airport, but only found out it had been grounded altogether once they arrived.
Nicole said they have been rebooked on another flight on later on Monday and were hopeful "it's sorted in time".

articles.title: Pakistan jails sisters of Imran Khan before protest seeking his release
articles.summary:
Police crack down on family and political supporters of former PM who say authorities are ‘slowly killing’ him in prison

Three sisters of Pakistan’s incarcerated former prime minister Imran…
articles.byline: Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad and Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi

blocks.text: Three sisters of Pakistan’s incarcerated former prime minister Imran Khan have been arrested amid a heavy-handed government crackdown on plans for a nationwide protest to demand Khan’s release.

The lawyer for the three sisters – Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi – said on Monday that they had all been detained and jailed for 30 days under a warrant that accused them of being a threat to public order.

Leaders from Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) condemned the “illegal harassment” of his sisters. Since Khan was arrested and held in prison on corruption charges in 2023, his sisters have been vocal advocates for his release.

His family and party allege that Khan is being kept in solitary confinement and has been denied visits and calls from his family for six months, as well as being allegedly prevented from accessing vital medical treatment for an eye condition.

The arrest of Khan’s sisters marked a dramatic escalation of a crackdown on PTI members and supporters in the run up to a nationwide demonstration due to be held on Sunday – described as a “long march” – to demand the release of Khan and to protest an alleged erosion of democracy and the constitution under the ruling coalition government.

Khan’s sisters hold a political position in PTI. Since protesting against their brother’s detention – including by camping outside the prison where he is held, demanding to see him – they have been named in various court cases. This is the first time they have all been held in prison.

Aleema was arrested in Lahore on Sunday as she was travelling to a private club; her driver was also picked up by police. Uzma and Noreen were then arrested at around 3am on Monday morning, after they held a press conference to condemn Aleema’s detention at her house in Lahore.

According to their lawyer, Rana Mudassir Umar, hundreds of police officers later surrounded the family home as more than 100 entered to arrest Uzma and Noreen, as well as their children, grandchildren – who are four and six years old – and the household staff. The house was raided and all their phones were taken.
By 7am on Monday morning, the children and grandchildren had been released but the three sisters were held and charged under the country’s Maintenance of Public Order law, according to Umar.
He said: “They have not been allowed any family access, no legal counsellor access and they were not even allowed to bring clothes or basic things.
“We have challenged their arrests in the high court in Lahore and [are] hoping we will get a hearing soon.”

While Pakistan is ostensibly ruled by a civilian coalition government, the army is widely regarded as the country’s most powerful establishment, led by Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshall Asim Munir, who fell out with Khan while Khan was prime minister. The current government was brought to power in an election in 2024 which was widely documented as rigged, allegedly by military intervention, to prevent Khan’s party returning to power.

Speaking to the Guardian last week, Khan’s two sons, who are based in London and fighting for his release, accused Munir of a “personal vendetta” against their father and alleged the Pakistani authorities were “slowly killing” Khan in prison.
Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi said on Monday taht the government would “find a permanent solution” to prevent to march going ahead and shutting down swathes of the country “once and for all”.

Despite Khan’s lengthy incarceration, he is still regarded as Pakistan’s most popular politician and there are fears among officials that large numbers could turn out to support PTI’s march on Sunday. It is being held as discontentment is rife on the streets amidst an economic crisis and crippling petrol shortages due to the turmoil in the Middle East and the Gulf. Disgust at the alleged mistreatment of Khan is also widespread.
Khan’s party has faced constant harassment over the past three years, with most senior PTI figures either in jail or pressed to leave politics.

Sheikh Waqas Akram, a senior PTI leader, said the government feared that hundreds of thousands of people may turn out to the long march and “topple the government”, as protest movements have done recently in neighbouring countries such as Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka.

Over the weekend, the capital of Pakistan, Islamabad, was transformed into a fortress of heavy security, with barriers and heavy armed security lining the roads and shipping containers placed to block the entrances into the city.

“Punjab police are raiding houses, harassing families, bulldozing houses and arresting workers and families,” Akram said. “They are going to insane levels to crush the long march and stop it with violence and arrests. This illegitimate government know they can’t survive if people are allowed to protest and march on Islamabad in huge numbers.”

articles.title: Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war
articles.summary: The BBC's Frank Gardner speaks to some of those who have fled the war by crossing the Red Sea to Djibouti

blocks.text: Watch: Inside a camp for Yemeni refugees in Djibouti
ByFrank Gardner
Security correspondentReporting fromMarkazi camp, Obock, Djibouti
Ibrahim Issa, 50, is from the Yemeni coastal town of Dhubab, right on the front lines of the war between Yemen's Houthis and the Saudi-backed pro-government forces fighting them.

Today he sits, surrounded by his family, on a tarpaulin spread over a sandy floor inside a vast open-sided warehouse at Markazi camp in Obock, northern Djibouti, packed with Yemeni families who have fled by boat across the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait.
After their sea crossing, Yemeni refugees have made their way by truck and on foot to this camp, jointly administered by the government and the UN.

"How could I just sit there when my kids are screaming and shaking in terror?" says Ibrahim Issa. "When the sound of the planes start, and the kids hear the planes, they begin shouting and screaming. As parents it is our responsibility, what can you do when you see this? That is why we fled, to save them."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ibrahim Issa escaped on his fishing boat with family and several goats

blocks.text: Image source, Ed Habershon/ BBC
Ibrahim Issa escaped on his fishing boat with family and several goats
As a fisherman, Ibrahim Issa already owned a boat large enough to bring out his family from Yemen.

He even brought several of the family's goats which I can now see nibbling at scraps nearby, foraging amidst the discarded canisters of cooking gas and empty plastic bottles. Some families have been able to bring small bundles of possessions with them from Yemen – one family has even brought a "jeraak", a tall metal shisha pipe – but others have arrived, exhausted, in just the clothes they left in.

In just the last few days more than 3,000 refugees have arrived here from Yemen, many entire families. The UN estimates that in all, more than 120,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting along Yemen's Red Sea coast.

This month, the country's Houthis, who had already seized most of the populated parts of Yemen years ago, made a lightning dash down the coast towards Bab al-Mandab, the narrow, maritime chokepoint where the southern Red Sea flows into the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean.

Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised UN-recognised government of Yemen, has responded with hundreds of air strikes along the flat, coastal plain where the Houthis are now digging in. The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia.
"We don't care which side it is that's attacking," is the message I got loud and clear in Arabic from everyone here I spoke to. "It's the bombs falling all around us that have caused us to flee."

blocks.caption: Regional map showing south west corner of Yemen to the east and Eritrea and Djibouti on the west side of the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Places labelled in Yemen include Mokha and the island of Perim in the strait. A small inset globe in the top right shows the region’s location.

blocks.text: Djibouti, a tiny former French colony that sits just across the water from Yemen, has made it clear it has no intention of involving itself in the war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.

And yet Djibouti is one of the most militarised nations in Africa. Since 2003, the US has run a huge multinational base here, Camp Lemonnier, once home to the French Foreign Legion. China too has a major base here, its largest military presence on the Indian Ocean and recently upgraded.
Back in Markazi camp, one of those I spoke to is Qassim Abraham Abssy. Once also a fisherman, his identity card shows him to be 100 years old.
"What led us to come here?" he asks rhetorically.

"It was the planes. The sounds of the planes, boom! That's what made us flee, for the sake of our children. It burns ours hearts. We don't know which side they are from. They are bombing everywhere, because the Houthis are everywhere, in the mountains, in the roads. A plane comes, bombs everywhere."

blocks.caption: Image caption, More than 120,000 Yemenis are estimated to have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting

blocks.text: More than 120,000 Yemenis are estimated to have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting

Outside in the blazing 37C heat, close to the neat lines of tents supplied by the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, I met Mohammed Abdullarim from Aden, a 63-year-old former tour guide old enough to have been born when Aden was still a British protectorate.

Unlike the new arrivals, Mohammed has been here since 2015. He fled to Djibouti soon after the fighting first flared up between the Houthis and the government of the now-ousted President Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi.
He has been at the camp ever since but suddenly, as we were talking, the sadness of what is happening to his country overwhelmed him and he turned his head away, choking back tears.

"Most of the people here are in the worst condition, inside the tents here. I am very touched, I'm crying for these people, for my people, for their suffering. I want our voices to be heard by the NGOs and the Djibouti government. And I'm thankful to them for accepting us."

How long will they have to stay here? That depends, of course, on the fighting. Yemen has been wracked by a horrific civil war that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions since 2014.
A shaky, UN-brokered 2022 truce between the Saudis and the Houthis has broken down spectacularly in recent months, with the two sides trading missiles, drones and air strikes.

blocks.caption: Image caption, "We are willing to go back in peace if peace returns to our country," says Aisha Abdulkadir Mohammed

blocks.text: Image source, Frank Gardner/ BBC
"We are willing to go back in peace if peace returns to our country," says Aisha Abdulkadir Mohammed

Yemen's war may be a remote one to most people but the effect of choking off Saudi Arabia's oil exports through the Bab al-Mandab strait are well publicised. But as ever, it is often the human cost that goes unnoticed.

Sitting beside his wife on their tarpaulin, amid the cacophony all around them, Qassim Abssy the fisherman is wary of leaving the safety of Djibouti: "If the war continues then we're not going back because we have peace here."

His wife, Aisha Abdulkadir Mohammed, agrees. "We are willing to go back in peace if peace returns to our country, and we are praying to God that peace does return. All we need is peace, even for our children's future, they get safety first, then food, water and an education.
"As you see we just fled with our clothes, and left everything behind, because [in Yemen] there is no peace."

blocks.caption: Regional map showing Yemen, Saudi Arabia, Eritrea, Ethiopia and Djibouti. About a quarter of the country from the Res Sea coast is shaded red and keyed as Houthi controlled territory. A more zoomed-in map below shows the south west where the Houthis have maid gains in their September offensive -…

articles.title: Eleksyon 2028 may have longer lines if 9,300 voting machines excluded in 2027 budget
articles.summary: Voters may experience longer queues in the 2028 National and Local Elections (NLE) if 9,300 voting machines are excluded from the 2027 national budget.

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 10:13pm
Voters may experience longer queues in the 2028 National and Local Elections (NLE) if 9,300 voting machines are excluded from the 2027 national budget.
Quezon 4th District Rep. Mike Tan, sponsor of the Commission on Elections' (Comelec) 2027 budget, made the statement during the plenary session of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill.
"Yun po yung nirerequest nila na ibigay po yung P23.16 billion kasi kukulangin tayo ng 9,300 na machines at magiging resulta nito ay longer lines, longer queues sa ating mga presinto," Tan said.
(They're requesting the additional P23.16 billion because we will be short of 9,300 machines. The result will be longer lines, longer queues at our polling precincts.)
Comelec is seeking a P44.7-billion budget for 2027, which was reduced by 34% to P29.5 billion.
The poll body is currently drafting the terms of reference for the voting machines to be used for the 2028 NLE as it plans to procure new units.
Comelec earlier expressed its hope for clarity by September on whether the BSKE will push through as scheduled.

Comelec chairperson George Garcia said an early decision would allow the poll body to adjust its preparations, particularly as it also needs to gear up for the 2028 National and Local Elections (NLE).
Last week, the Senate approved on third and final reading a bill seeking to "fix" the term of office of barangay officials and SK members to five years.
With 13 affirmative votes, five negative votes, and no abstentions, the upper chamber approved Senate Bill No. 2387 during its plenary session.

The measure seeks to amend Republic Act No. 12232 by fixing the current four-year term of barangay and SK officials to five years and moving the next BSKE from the first to the second Monday of November 2028.

It also provides that no elective barangay official shall serve for more than two consecutive terms in the same position, while no elective SK official shall serve for more than one term in the same position.

Senator Francis “Chiz” Escudero, the measure’s principal author and sponsor, said the five-year term would give barangay and SK officials more time to plan, implement, and evaluate programs before the next elections. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: CNN, MS NOW, Politico suing Trump over White House ban
articles.summary: The lawsuit aims 'to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,' the three organizations say in a joint…

blocks.text: BANNED. MS NOW White House correspondent Vaughn Hillyard reports from a street corner just outside the White House after US President Donald Trump banned three major news outlets (CNN, MS NOW and Politico) from the White House, in Washington, DC, US, on September 21, 2026.
Kevin Lamarque/Reuters

The lawsuit aims 'to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,' the three organizations say in a joint statement

items: CNN, MS NOW, and Politico are suing President Trump and his administration for banning them from the White House, claiming it violates their First Amendment rights.
The lawsuit seeks to challenge the ban, which the news organizations argue threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism.
Trump defended the ban, labeling the media as a security threat and asserting that it is necessary to combat what he calls 'fake news.'

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON, DC, USA – CNN, MS NOW and Politico said on Monday, September 21, they are suing President Donald Trump and other members of his administration to protect their rights under the US Constitution’s First Amendment after he banned the news outlets from the White House building grounds.

The three news organizations said they have notified the government that they were filing their lawsuit in the US District Court for the District of Columbia and could see emergency hearings in the case as soon as this week.

“Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference,” they wrote in a joint statement.
The lawsuit aims “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” they added.
The First Amendment protects the freedom of the press and speech.
Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump first announced his action on Friday, September 18, in a social media post. The Republican president defended the ban in another social media post on Monday after the lawsuit was announced, calling the news media a security threat, without providing any evidence.

“The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS,” Trump wrote. “It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

His administration has upended decades of tradition in dealings between the White House and press, denying the access many major news organizations have had to the president while elevating new media outlets seen as more sympathetic to the administration. He has also filed a number of lawsuits against news organizations.

CNN had been scheduled to cover Monday’s White House events for the broader press corps, including Trump’s trip to New York for the United Nations General Assembly. It was not immediately clear what television footage of the president would be provided to the public.
“The ban is unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained,” the news outlets said in a copy of their lawsuit, adding that the ban was already impeding coverage that could have wider impact.

“The ban inflicts an injury on all news media organizations — who now risk a similar fate if they engage in reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable,” the three wrote in their complaint, which seeks a temporary restraining order to block Trump’s action.

Trump’s latest move comes as his fellow Republicans seek to defend their narrow majorities in Congress in the November midterm elections as polls show the public souring on Republicans and Trump’s own approval ratings stand near historic lows.

On Saturday, September 19, all three outlets said their journalists were turned away from the White House grounds and their press credentials confiscated, a day after Trump initially announced his ban in a social media post and threatened to block other outlets.
MS NOW and CNN over the weekend instead set up their journalists across the street from the White House and continued to broadcast coverage.

Trump on Friday addressed what he called his “ban on the free press” with reporters at an event in the Oval Office and said there was no particular incident that provoked the move. Asked what other news organizations could be targeted, Trump cited The New York Times and The Washington Post as “fake news” but said they had not been removed yet.

The Associated Press, the White House Correspondents’ Association and others have criticized Trump’s ban, citing the fundamental American right to free speech and calling for access to be immediately restored.

“The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably,” the correspondents’ association said in a statement.
The AP filed its own lawsuit after being barred, along with Reuters, in 2025 from the group of reporters that cover the president’s daily movements.

During his first term in office, Trump sought to revoke or suspend White House credentials of two correspondents for CNN and Playboy magazine, but federal judges ordered their press passes restored. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Millions urged to evacuate as powerful Typhoon Dujuan hits Japan
articles.summary: The country's meteorological agency had warned of an "imminent threat to life," but this has now been downgraded in most areas.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
ByJamie Whitehead and Kelly Ng
Almost two million people are under evacuation orders in Japan as Typhoon Dujuan batters a number of the country's prefectures.
Japan's Meteorological Agency had warned of an "imminent threat to life", but several warnings have now been downgraded, with the danger to life warning remaining in place in Oshima Town.
Strong winds caused power cuts for more than 50,000 people, while hundreds of flights have been cancelled and rail services have been suspended.

Dujuan has had sustained winds of 130km/h (80.8mph) and gusts of 194 km/h. It is the latest in a series of storms in the Pacific, made more intense by the "super El Niño", which has warmed the ocean, fuelling the formation of storms.

blocks.caption: Several people in Japan wait to cross a road during a storm. They are all under umbrellas.

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
The level three warnings, for heavy rain, and the level four warnings, for landslides have now been either downgraded or lifted by the Japan Meteorological Agency in most areas.
The level four warnings remain in Shinagawa Ward, Toshima Village, and Niijima Village.
Authorities have advised the public to pay attention to weather information.
Dujuan, which is Japan's 25th typhoon of the year, has hit in the midst of a five-day holiday and forced the cancellation of several events.
Concerts scheduled for Monday at the Rock in Japan music festival have been cancelled, while the Tokyo Game Show, a video game convention, has also cancelled Monday's programme.
Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has reportedly delayed her trip to the United States this week to monitor the effects of the typhoon.
She had been due in New York on Tuesday to meet with US President Donald Trump and speak at the UN General Assembly.

blocks.caption: A man rides a bike almost completely submerged in rain water.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
The Yokosuka City Fire Department told the BBC that a woman who lived in the house, aged in her 60s, may have been swept away and is believed to have been buried alive.
Separately, Sodegaura City Fire Department in Chiba prefecture told the BBC a man in his 50s was rescued after getting trapped while working to clear debris at a landslide site.
The department said the worker fell into a bamboo thicket, along with some heavy machinery. He was then taken to hospital.
Firefighters in Kanagawa prefecture said they received a call from a man who reported his house had been crushed by a landslide.

blocks.caption: A woman holding an umbrella being blown into the wind,.

blocks.text: Some research suggests that Japan has become more exposed to destructive storms, but climate change is not thought to be increasing the number of these storms globally, and could even make them less common in some regions.
As temperatures rise, typhoons that do form are likely to become more intense on average, however.
Warmer ocean waters mean storms can pick up more energy, leading to higher wind speeds.
And because a warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, these storms could also bring heavier rainfall.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A satellite view shows Typhoon Dujuan approaching Japan

blocks.text: A satellite view shows Typhoon Dujuan approaching Japan
This year, El Niño - the natural weather phenomenon bringing warmer water to parts of the tropical Pacific - is another factor.
El Niño doesn't have a clear effect on the total number of typhoons, but it can affect where typhoons form, their strength and which countries they hit.
Some El Niño events may expose Japan to stronger typhoons, for example.
The typhoon is continuing to travel along the country's Pacific coast, heading north. The extent of the damage today may not be known until Tuesday.
Additional reporting by Mark Poynting, climate reporter

articles.title: SC: Anti‑political dynasty ban up to 4th degree has basis
articles.summary: The Supreme Court said there is a basis to extend the prohibition on political dynasties to relatives up to the fourth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity.

blocks.text: The Supreme Court said there is a basis to extend the prohibition on political dynasties to relatives up to the fourth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity.

In its decision compelling Congress to enact an appropriate anti-political dynasty law at the earliest opportunity, it said, “certain circumstances can be considered if the evils of concentrating power and political opportunity were to be truly addressed.”
Still, the SC said the High Tribunal “will not instruct on how the legislation will be crafted and how the scope and extent of the prohibition will be defined.”

“The following discussion does not in any way impose upon Congress the substance on what to legislate but merely highlights key aspects for Congress's deliberation,” read the 86-page unanimous decision penned by Associate Justice Ramon Paul Hernando.
“First, there is basis to extend the prohibition on political dynasties to relatives up to the fourth civil degree of consanguinity and/or affinity,” the decision said.

The House of Representatives in June passed an anti-political dynasty bill banning relatives up to the second degree of consanguinity or affinity from running for or occupying a post in the same constituency or jurisdiction on final reading.
Lawmakers voted 267-20-7 to approve House Bill 8389 on third reading, two weeks after the measure hurdled second reading approval.
It has been criticized as a measure expected to perpetuate political dynasties rather than ban them.

In defense of the bill, House Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez of South Cotabato’s 2nd District said, “There are fair criticisms. But an imperfect reform is still reform. This is better than a permanent paralysis.”

On the basis for prohibition up to the fourth degree, the SC said that several laws that impose limitations recognize that familial ties and their influence extend up to at least the fourth civil degree.
These include:

items: Article 38(1) of the Family Code on marriages deemed void for reasons of public policy;
Article 1027 of the Civil Code on persons incapable of succession;

Section 3(k) of Republic Act No. 6713 or the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees on the requirement to disclose family relatives in government service in the Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth; and
Article 11 of the Revised Penal Code, on the defense of a relative as a justifying circumstance.

blocks.text: “Significantly, Article VII, Section 13(2) of the Constitution prohibits the president's spouse and relatives by consanguinity or affinity within the fourth civil degree to be appointed as members of the Constitutional Commissions, the Office of the Ombudsman, or as secretaries, undersecretaries, chairpersons or heads of bureaus or offices, including government-owned or controlled corporations,” the SC said.
The decision also said that:

items: covered persons can be prohibited from running for an elective office both simultaneously and successively for the same or any other covered position
relatives can be prohibited from occupying both local and/or national elective positions
the prohibition can optimally extend to all covered persons residing within the same administrative region

blocks.text: “The concentration of political power within a narrow few has distorted democracy, weakened accountability, and fostered conditions conducive to corruption and political patronage,” the SC said.
“When a clear constitutional mandate is left unimplemented for generations, the resulting harm begins to reflect in diminished public trust and stagnant governance,” it added.
Last week, the SC directed Congress to enact an anti-political dynasty law at the earliest opportunity, saying its failure to do so for 39 years constitutes grave abuse of discretion.
It found that Article II, Section 26 of the Constitution requires Congress to enact a law prohibiting political dynasties.
However, the SC said it is leaving it up to Congress to define what constitutes a political dynasty and determine the scope of the prohibition.
Justices’ opinions

In his concurring opinion, Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen cited the Duterte and Romualdez families as examples of “fat” political dynasties in the country, which refer to those family members who hold public office simultaenously.
Meanwhile, Associate Justice Henri Jean Paul Inting said that the delay on Congress’ part must be deemed presumptively unreasonable.
He also stressed that bills are not laws.

“[T]he constitutional mandate of the Legislature is to enact a law prohibiting political dynasties, not merely to introduce bills on the subject matter. Bills are not the same as laws; they do not produce any legal effect until they are passed into law,” he said.
For his part, Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda said that recognizing a constitutional duty is different from determining the remedy for its nonperformance.

“I sincerely believe that the constitutional command against political dynasties deserves enforcement. My concern lies with the institutional means by which the Judiciary addresses that duty,” he said.
“Constitutional enforcement does not mean that every branch of government must perform its constitutional responsibilities in whatever manner another branch considers appropriate,” he added.
Zalameda said that the Constitution binds all branches of government.

Associate Justice Japar Dimaampao, meanwhile, said that if the SC has the constitutional authority to command Congress to act in this case, it inherently possesses the corollary authority to ensure that its command is not left arbitrarily flouted.
He said that pragmatic, yet still effective, mechanisms to promote compliance are worth exploring.

“Because leaving the enforcement of this Decision solely to the hope that Congress will eventually act, or waiting for a future petition to challenge a continued inaction, would be to perpetuate the same ‘legislative paralysis’ that brought this controversy before the Court,” he said.
For her part, Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh said she did not agree with the grant of mandamus.
Singh said that the Court may pronounce the constitutional breach, but it cannot mandate the legislative response.

“While the Court may declare that Congress has unreasonably failed to discharge its constitutional obligation, it cannot compel Congress to discharge such function without arrogating unto itself legislative power,” she said.

“To issue a writ of mandamus in this case would be, in effect, to dictate not merely that a law be passed, but to intrude upon the substance, timing, and policy choices inherent in that law. This, the Court cannot do lest it ventures into lawmaking,” she added.
Meanwhile, Associate Justice Raul Villanueva said that until Congress complies with its ministerial duty, it should be “unrelentingly urged to finish the job.”

“Although not time-bound, the framers of the Constitution surely did not envision that the legislative department would take too long a time to give the Filipino people an anti-political dynasty law that promotes equal access to public service to everyone willing and qualified to serve in a political office, and not dominated by politically entrenched families,” he said.
Meanwhile, Villanueva said that not all political dynasties are bad.
He said that there are political dynasties that have contributed to the growth and progress of many localities and provided political leadership on a local and national level.

“Still, this is simply not enough reason not to prohibit political dynasties. In the end, it is because of the opportunity to allow public service freely accessible outside of political dynasties that the Constitution fundamentally prohibits it,” he said. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Turkey launches AI initiative ahead of COP31 climate summit
articles.summary: 'We must openly discuss AI’s growing energy consumption, and it is time for governments to start setting the terms,' says COP31 president-designate Murat Kurum

blocks.text: AI. The words 'AI Artificial Intelligence,' a keyboard and a robotic hand are shown in this illustration created on June 5, 2026.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
'We must openly discuss AI’s growing energy consumption, and it is time for governments to start setting the terms,' says COP31 president-designate Murat Kurum

NEW YORK, USA – Turkey, which will host the COP31 climate summit in Antalya in November, launched a push on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Monday, September 21, to address AI’s skyrocketing energy demand through a political pledge that countries would adopt to align their AI infrastructure build-out with global climate goals.

The new Antalya Pledge on Artificial Intelligence is being developed with the UN’s International Telecommunication Union, and a draft will be shared ahead of COP31, the incoming Turkish COP presidency said.

“We must openly discuss AI’s growing energy consumption, and it is time for governments to start setting the terms. We expect companies to be transparent about their energy use and to power their operations with clean energy,” said COP31 President-Designate Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Minister for Environment and Urban Planning.

Turkey also formally launched its flagship initiative ahead of the annual UN climate summit, a push for a global pledge to increase electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035, which will include efforts to electrify buildings, transport and industry.
The 35×35 initiative aims to encourage countries to use clean power, storage and modernise grids and support developing countries as they shift away from fossil fuels.
Currently, around 20% of the world’s total energy ​demand is met by electricity. The rest comes mostly from fossil fuels, plus around 10% produced ​by biofuels and waste.
The voluntary pledge would also include a global mechanism to track collective progress on electrification.

Turkey said the COP will have a day dedicated to technology and AI, and will launch an initiative to develop “a portfolio of AI-enabled clean-technology pilots” that will connect technology developers, industry partners and investors in cars and heat pumps. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Senate approves school safety bill after fatal shootings
articles.summary: The comprehensive school safety bill consolidates protections under existing child protection, mental health, and disaster policies into a singular operational framework for public and private schools

blocks.text: SIMULATION. Students take cover during an active shooter drill at Carlos F. Gonzales High School in San Rafael, Bulacan, on September 3, 2026.
Eloisa Lopez/Reuters

The comprehensive school safety bill consolidates protections under existing child protection, mental health, and disaster policies into a singular operational framework for public and private schools

items: The Senate approved Senate Bill No. 2426 to establish a comprehensive school safety framework following recent school shootings.
The bill prohibits various forms of violence and abuse in schools and mandates the Department of Education to lead the implementation of safety protocols and infrastructure.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Senate on Monday, September 21, approved on third and final reading a bill that institutionalizes a comprehensive school safety framework, following three fatal school shootings that shocked the country in the past months.
There were 17 affirmative votes, zero negative votes, and zero abstentions for Senate Bill No. 2426, or the proposed Comprehensive School Safety Act.
“Nananawagan tayo sa pamahalaan na madaliin ang pagtiyak na ligtas ang ating mga paaralan at mga komunidad para sa ating mga estudyante at guro,” said Senator Bam Aquino, the bill’s sponsor.
(We call on the government to expedite efforts to ensure that our schools and communities are safe for our students and teachers.)
Aquino also urged the House of Representatives to pass its version of a school safety bill.
“‘Wag tayong masasanay sa ganitong karahasan. ‘Wag natin hayaang maging normal ang school shooting sa ating bansa,” he added.
(Let’s not get used to this kind of violence. Let’s not allow school shootings to become normal in our country.)

On Friday, September 18, a Grade 9 student opened fire at a public high school in Banga, South Cotabato. Three students, including the alleged perpetrator, were killed, while eight others were injured.
It was the third such tragedy following the Tacloban City school shooting in June and another in Zamboanga City in August.

According to Aquino, the comprehensive school safety bill consolidates protections under existing child protection, mental health, and disaster policies into a singular operational framework for public and private schools.

blocks.caption: Philippines still among top countries in bullying – PISA 2025

blocks.text: Under the bill, the following acts committed by students or school personnel against other students or school personnel are prohibited:

items: Violence
Child abuse
Neglect
Exploitation
Bullying
Cyberbullying
Online abuse
Cybersecurity risks
Other forms of digital harm
Discrimination
Harassment
Gender-based violence
Corporal punishment
Retaliation

blocks.text: Primarily, the bill directs the Department of Education (DepEd) to lead a national comprehensive school safety framework, which would set clear crisis protocols, standardizing campus safety infrastructure and screening procedures, and implementing a whole-of-community protection strategy that supports both students and teachers.
Schools are expected to develop localized school safety plans, which must be communicated to parents and guardians through annual orientations.
The DepEd would be told to establish a national school recovery and support program to help schools heal from incidents concerning safety and student well-being.

Under the bill, schools must be equipped with security equipment such as CCTV cameras, metal detectors and other screening equipment, a visitor management system, security personnel, and perimeter fencing and other measures to secure and regulate access to campus grounds.

The bill also prohibits both students and teachers from using phones and other digital devices within school premises during class hours. Bag inspections are also mandatory. Such measures are already in place under current DepEd policies.
Every two years, the DepEd would be tasked to submit a national school safety report to Congress.
Ongoing discussions on school safety in the Philippines have been linked to responsible gun ownership and online influences.

On Monday, senators also approved on third and final reading the SAGIP BATA bill, a measure which seeks to strengthen the law on online sexual abuse or exploitation of children and child sexual abuse or exploitation materials.
Another Senate bill proposing a social media ban for children 16 years old and below is still pending on second reading. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Nuclear power is back on Southeast Asia's energy agenda
articles.summary: Rising electricity demand, shocks in energy security and climate commitments are reviving long-stalled plans for nuclear power across Southeast Asia. But proponents of nuclear energy still face…

image.caption: Advances in nuclear power technology are making it more tempting for Southeast Asian nationsImage: China National Nuclear Corporation/Handout via Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: Southeast Asian governments are revisiting nuclear power as electricity consumption raises, exposing the region's dependence on fossil fuels.
The rise is largely driven by new factories, electric vehicles and the region's rush to host data centers against the backdrop of countries trying to reduce carbon emissions.
No Southeast Asian nation currently operates a commercial nuclear power plant, but several are now placing their bets on nuclear energy and reviving plans that had been stalled for years.

On September 8, Vietnam's state-owned Petrovietnam and South Korea's KEPCO agreed to deepen cooperation on the planned Ninh Thuan 2 nuclear plant. Six days later, Singapore's government said it was studying nuclear power and small modular reactors (SMRs)with an "open mind", though it stressed that it had not made a decision.
Vietnam also wants to bring its two Ninh Thuan plants into operation by 2035 and pursue at least one SMR project.

Indonesia plans an initial 500 megawatts of nuclear capacity, with units targeted to begin operating in 2032, while the Philippines is working towards its first 1,200 MW of nuclear capacity from the same year.
Thailand's latest draft power plan proposes its first SMR in 2037, while Malaysia and Singapore remain at the study stage.
Can nuclear power cover AI's energy demands?
Energy shocks vs. the shadow of Fukushima
The renewed interest marks a sharp reversal from the caution that followed Japan's Fukushima nuclear disaster in 2011.

The incident stalled several Southeast Asian countries' plans to pursue nuclear energy, Alvin Chew, a senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS) at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, told DW.
But a string of geopolitical shocks in recent years has changed the energy debate.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) says Southeast Asia's electricity generation has risen by around 60% since 2015, but coal supplied most of that increase, pushing its share of regional generation from 37% to 47%.

The war in Ukraine and the current Middle East crisis have heightened energy-security concerns for developing countries, even as most Southeast Asian governments have committed to net-zero emissions by 2050 or 2060, Chew said.
The region's electricity demand is forecast to grow by an average of 5.3% a year between 2026 and 2030.
"Nuclear energy is deemed to be the viable solution to address both challenges of climate and energy security," Chew said.
Middle East conflict is firing up China's electric future
Appeal of modular reactors
One reason governments are reconsidering nuclear power is that today's technology is starkly different from what was used 15 years ago in Fukushima.
SMRs have broadened the range of possible projects. Unlike conventional reactors, SMRs are designed as smaller units that can potentially be added in stages.

"In the past, deploying nuclear energy generally meant building very large conventional reactors, involving long construction periods, enormous upfront investments and requiring electricity grids capable of absorbing very large generating units," Jie-Sheng Tan-Soo, assistant professor and director at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy in Singapore, told DW.
"SMRs have changed the nuclear conversation in Southeast Asia because they potentially make nuclear compatible with smaller grids, smaller countries and more incremental investment," he added.

blocks.caption: China has started implementing SMRs Image: Zhang Boqun/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: That does not mean SMRs will solve nuclear power's economics. Many designs remain at an early stage of deployment, meaning promises of cheaper construction through mass production have yet to be demonstrated on a broad commercial scale.

Another force pushing nuclear energy back onto the agenda is the rapid expansion of data centers, which require large quantities of reliable electricity, Julius Cesar Trajano, a research fellow with the Centre for Non-Traditional Security Studies at RSIS, told DW.
The IEA expects electricity consumption from Southeast Asian data centers to more than double by 2030.
More than 70% of existing regional data-center capacity is concentrated in Singapore and Johor in southern Malaysia.
"Countries are therefore approaching nuclear energy with greater emphasis on governance and regulatory capacity than during earlier attempts," said Trajano.
Building a nuclear safety net

The hardest problems, however, remain much the same. Nuclear plants, even SMRs, still require a lot of time and money, and newcomer countries must establish independent regulators, train specialist workforces and develop credible systems for radioactive waste and emergency response.
Geography adds another layer of difficulty. Parts of Southeast Asia are vulnerable to earthquakes, volcanoes and tsunamis, making site selection and emergency planning particularly sensitive.
Nuclear power also places unusually heavy demands on state institutions, Tan-Soo said. Governments need institutions that take a long time to establish and must remain reliable for decades.
"For countries developing nuclear power for the first time, building this ecosystem can take as much effort as building the plant itself," he added.
Does nuclear energy make financial sense?
Long road to wielding nuclear power
Public support is another matter. A Philippine government survey released last year found that more than 70% of respondents supported nuclear energy's potential role in providing electricity.
By contrast, the Indonesia Energy Transition Outlook 2026 reported that 78% of respondents placed nuclear as their least-preferred energy source.
"The biggest obstacle is the political will to proceed with adoption of nuclear energy, which, to a certain extent, is dependent on public perception," said Chew.
Southeast Asia's highly varied national capacities and electricity systems also make a common pathway unlikely, Trajano said.

Vietnam has revived plans for large conventional plants, Indonesia and Thailand are giving greater attention to SMRs, while Singapore is still building the expertise needed to determine whether nuclear power is suitable at all.
"There is clearly much more political momentum behind nuclear power in Southeast Asia today than there was a decade ago, and I think some countries could ultimately deploy it," Tan-Soo said.
"But moving from announcing a nuclear ambition to financing, licensing, constructing and safely operating a reactor is an enormous step."

articles.summary: The Ministry of Education, backed by international and local organizations, has moved ahead with the 2026-2027 academic year, establishing dozens of temporary schools made of tents, tarpaulins, sheet…

blocks.text: BACK TO SCHOOL. Palestinian students attend their first day of the new school year inside a tent classroom at a school in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip, on September 19, 2026.
Ramadan Abed/Reuters

The Ministry of Education, backed by international and local organizations, has moved ahead with the 2026-2027 academic year, establishing dozens of temporary schools made of tents, tarpaulins, sheet metal, and wood to accommodate pupils

items: Hundreds of thousands of children in Gaza returned to in-person schooling for the first time in nearly three years, despite many schools being damaged or in makeshift conditions.
UNICEF reports that 98% of schools in Gaza were destroyed or damaged during the conflict, leaving around 660,000 students without regular education.
The reopening of schools is a fragile milestone amid ongoing challenges, including high costs for essential school supplies and fears of violence.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Hundreds of thousands of children in Gaza returned to in-person teaching on Saturday, September 19, for the first time in nearly three years, albeit in damaged or makeshift school buildings and tents, and with uniforms, notebooks, and pens unaffordable for many families.

The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) says 98% of schools in Gaza were either destroyed or damaged during the war, and Gaza education officials say about 660,000 students have been deprived of in-person learning and regular participation in education.

The reopening is a fragile milestone for Gaza after a conflict that has killed around 22,000 students and more than 770 education workers, including 532 teachers, according to Ibrahim Ramadan, director of education for East Khan Younis.
“The last time I have been to school was three years ago. Now, we are starting the school year, it is year of joy, happiness, and success,” said Moayed Abu Mustafa in Khan Younis.
Mustafa said he was determined to learn even though he will sit on the floor in a tent lacking ventilation, he has no decent shoes, nor a notebook and pen, and lost friends during the war.
“Despite all of this, we will learn, we will learn even in a tent.”
Fifteen-year-old displaced student Samar Abu Salmi, who lives with her family in a tent, is also returning to class.
“We studied on phones, and we haven’t seen our teachers…. Now, we are back pursuing our dream…from one tent to another,” she said, speaking in the yard of her new makeshift school.
She also lacks much of the essential equipment, which has become unaffordable for her family.
“Before the war, everything was available for us — notebooks, pens, goods, clothes, outings, things that we could get cheaply,” Salmi said.

Despite the devastation in the enclave, the Ministry of Education, backed by international and local organizations, has moved ahead with the 2026-2027 academic year, establishing dozens of temporary schools made of tents, tarpaulins, sheet metal, and wood to accommodate pupils.
Some are built on sandy ground, others have classrooms with only some mattresses and a blackboard, into which students cram. Others are still housing dozens of displaced families.
Attending another school was 14-year-old Yamen Abu Samra.
“We used to wake up happy to go to school… Now, when we come to school, we’re afraid of stray bullets, rockets, strikes, everything,” he said.
“Now, I’m sitting in a tent that has absolutely nothing, just the sun and the heat,” he added.

At least 540,000 students are expected to attend in-person classes this year in makeshift private schools, temporary learning centers and educational points, with UNICEF support, according to education officials. Online learning will continue for those who can’t attend classes or who left Gaza during the war.
Israeli forces remain in control of more than 60% of Gaza despite last year’s ceasefire, which halted major fighting but failed to end the conflict.
Palestinian authorities say more than 73,000 people have been killed in Israel’s assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel in October 2023.
Stationery trader Khaled Aliyan, 30, said Israeli import restrictions have reduced supplies and hiked prices.
“This notebook, which used to cost 3 shekels ($1), now costs 15 (shekels). All stationery items are expensive,” he said.

Israel’s COGAT military agency, which controls access to Gaza, did not respond to a Reuters request for comment on restrictions on supplies and strikes on schools. Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of using schools for military purposes, which Hamas denies. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Why gender-based violence persists in Southern Africa
articles.summary: A series of killings in South Africa has renewed scrutiny of efforts to combat violence against women. Activists say laws alone are not enough without effective implementation.

image.caption: Violent crime in South Africa remains a major source of public concern ahead of municipal elections in NovemberImage: Themba Hadebe/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: On Thursday, police in South Africa found the body of Dineo M. stabbed, beaten and partially naked in Ekurhuleni, a municipality on the outskirts of Johannesburg, South Africa's largest city.
The 38-year-old's death is one of a series of killings of women in their 20s and 30s in Ekurhuleni over the past two months.
But for Dineo's sister, Carol, it is more than another statistic in a country where gender-based violence was declared a national disaster in 2025.

"We sit here today and we will never see her walk through the door. Her 2-year-old has no idea what is going on," Carol told DW. "How do you explain to her … that your mother was brutally murdered, dumped behind shrubs, left unrecognizable?"
A community on edge

Authorities said it was not yet clear whether all of the killings were linked. However, they said they have identified similarities in some of them and have issued an alert for women in Ekurhuleni to take precautions.

Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said on Sunday that so far there was no conclusive evidence that the killings were carried out by a serial killer, "but nothing has yet been excluded while investigations continue."
For families and communities, the deaths have raised fresh questions about whether existing measures are enough to protect women.

South African Minister in the Presidency for Women, Youth and Persons with Disabilities, Sindisiwe Chikunga, said at a protest march in Johannesburg that violence against women often starts behind closed doors.

"Please, stop it. Stop raping women. Stop insulting women. Stop financially abusing women," she said, warning that abuse can escalate. "They start with insults. They proceed to assault and then to murder. It cannot be."
Why laws fall short
For Naledi Masipa, campaigns manager at Gender Links, an NGO promoting gender justice across Southern Africa, the problem is not simply the absence of laws and policies.

"Having laws and policies does not automatically change what happens in communities and households," she told DW, adding that the entire support system must work, from reporting and policing to health services, psychosocial support and legal assistance.
If one part fails, she said, women continue to carry the burden. "The real test is whether a woman in an ordinary community feels safer."
Amnesty International South Africa also said the response must recognize the gendered nature of killings.

"Femicide itself is not recognized as a crime. It's just seen as another murder," said Tegan Snyman, a research assistant at Amnesty South Africa, noting that South Africa has declared gender-based violence and femicide a national crisis, but argues that the response needs dedicated resources and urgency.
A regional challenge
The neighboring country of Botswana has also struggled with high levels of gender-based violence.
Natasha Rampa, a permanent secretary in Botswana's Ministry of Youth and Gender Affairs, said that "at least 37% of women in Botswana have experienced violence in their lifetimes."
In June, Botswana and the United Nations launched a joint program focused on prevention, survivor-centered services and stronger institutions.

"Violence is unacceptable, and we must work together as a society to address this issue," Minister of Youth and Gender Affairs Lesego Chombo told parliament. He said that tackling gender-based violence (GBV) requires action beyond government.
Turning policy into protection
Zambia also faces persistent gender-based violence — despite laws and national programs aimed at tackling it.
Why are women still unsafe in South Africa?
Anne Mbewe-Anamela, executive director of the Non-Governmental Coordinating Council, which champions gender equality, said the response must put survivors at the center.

"GBV is deeply rooted in power, inequality, and social expectations," she told DW. "We can have strong laws, but if communities still believe violence is a private matter or a normal part of marriage, then survivors remain silent and trapped."

For activists across the region, the challenge is therefore not simply creating more policies. It is making protection, support and justice work in practice. And for families like Dineo's, that difference is painfully personal. Carol knows her sister will never walk through the door again.
She wants Dineo's daughter to grow up understanding that what happened to her mother was not normal and that women deserve to be safe.
"How do you explain to her … that your mother was brutally murdered …?" she said. "That is why you don't have a mother today."

articles.title: Putin consolidates grip on Russia as 49 Ukraine war veterans elected to parliament
articles.summary:
Pro-Kremlin party’s record victory in tightly controlled vote likely to be used as evidence country supports war

Russia’s new parliament will include 49 deputies who have taken part in the…

blocks.text: Russia’s new parliament will include 49 deputies who have taken part in the war against Ukraine, officials have said after a landslide victory by the ruling United Russia party in widely criticised elections.

The pro-Kremlin party won a record 355 seats in the country’s 450-seat Duma lower house of parliament, according to preliminary figures. The result further consolidates Vladimir Putin’s grip on power and gives United Russia a super-majority bigger than its previous 2016 record of 343 seats.

The polls are the first to be held since Putin’s 2022 full-scale invasion. United Russia’s general secretary, Vladimir Yakushev, said 86 veterans from Moscow’s “special military operation” were likely to have been elected. “This is quite a substantial contribution,” he said. He later revised the number to 49.

blocks.caption: As Russia counted the votes from its widely criticised election, Kremlin forces attacked targets in Ukraine, damaging the historic Zaporizhzhia National University.  Photograph: Ukrinform/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Putin’s press spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said the vote showed that Russians supported their longtime leader, who has ruled as prime minister or president since 2000. “These indicators, of course, point to the highest level of consolidation within Russian society around the head of state,” Peskov said.

Western governments denounced the polls held in Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine as a “sham”. Russia’s supreme court last month banned the only party that opposes the war, Yabloko, from participating, leaving liberal voters with no option to express discontent.

Kaja Kallas, the EU’s top diplomat, called the election “another major setback for Russian democracy”. “The Kremlin silenced dissent and shut out international election monitors,” Kallas wrote on X, adding: “The veneer of democracy is all that remains.”

The elections come amid speculation that Putin may announce a large mobilisation campaign this autumn, in an attempt to inject fresh momentum to Russia’s bogged down military campaign. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has suggested the Kremlin wants to recruit another 300,000 troops.

blocks.caption: Aftermath of a Russian drone attack in Zaporizhzhia. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: In recent months, Russia has escalated its bombardment, pummelling Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities with jet-powered attack drones. Ukraine has launched its own deep strikes, hitting Moscow’s oil refinery on Sunday, as part of what Zelenskyy has dubbed “long-range sanctions”.

Russia’s has also intensified its campaign to seize a string of cities in Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, including Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. So far, it has been unable to break through, with Ukrainian commanders reporting their own counteroffensive near the city of Lyman.

Inside Russia, criticism of the conflict is banned. Anti-war bloggers have been arrested and jailed. A local politician, Boris Nadezhdin, who previously tried to stand in presidential elections on a peace ticket, was barred from September’s elections and accused of being a “foreign agent”.

The other parties that won seats in this month’s poll all support the “special military operation”. They include the communists, who came second with 40 seats, the ultra-nationalist LDPR party, with 25, and the New People party, with 20. Chechnya’s leader, Ramzan Kadyrov, a Putin ally, was re-elected and said to have won more than 99% of the votes.

blocks.caption: A shopping centre, struck during Russia’s drone attack on in Zaporizhzhia. Photograph: Reuters/Stringer

blocks.text: Russia’s elections chief, Ella Pamfilova, said United Russia had won a resounding victory with 57.83%, with 95% of ballots counted, up from the 49.8% it won in the last parliamentary election, in 2021. She praised voters for resisting “psychological pressure”.

Overnight, Russia carried out what Zelenskyy called a “brutal, targeted attack” on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia. He said a nine-storey residential building, a university building, a shopping centre, and a boiler house were all damaged, with five people injured. A woman in Kharkiv region was killed in a drone strike.

Zelenskyy said: “Russia is not scaling back its escalatory actions and is signalling a readiness to expand the war. All this is happening against the backdrop of global stability already having been shattered by this war. We must continue to pressure the aggressor to bring this war to an end.”

articles.title: Merz vows to keep coalition together for Germany's 'democratic future'
articles.summary: The chancellor has come under increasing pressure after resounding state election defeats, but says the results "go far beyond my own person"

blocks.text: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz says he will keep his ruling coalition together for the sake of his country's "democratic future", following resounding defeats for his party in two state elections.

"We are determined to live up to the historic challenges our country is facing," Merz said, referring to the coalition between his Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party and the Social Democratic Party (SPD).

Merz's position has come under mounting pressure after Sunday's election results. In the north-eastern Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the most votes, with the CDU failing to reach the threshold to even enter the state parliament.
Meanwhile in Berlin, the CDU came second to the hard-left Die Linke party, with the AfD also making significant gains.
Speaking at the news conference on Monday, Merz described the result in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern as "a heavy blow".
"This election is a profound turning point. It is a dramatic, unprecedented result for the CDU in Germany," he said.
He however pushed back against the idea that his low popularity ratings were behind the election defeats.
"The reasons for these election results go far beyond my own person," he insisted.
Merz is under mounting pressure after months of poor approval ratings, and there have been rumours he could be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap.
Asked earlier on Monday how long Merz has left in office, the AfD's co-leader Alice Weidel told the BBC: "Pretty soon, he's going to leave."
The two local elections took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won a major victory.
