articles.title: House ends plenary debates on proposed 2027 COA budget
articles.summary: The House of Representatives on Monday terminated plenary deliberations on the Commission on Audit"s (COA) proposed 2027 budget, bringing it one step closer to inclusion in the General Appropriations…

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 6:47pm

The House of Representatives on Monday terminated plenary deliberations on the Commission on Audit’s (COA) proposed 2027 budget, bringing it one step closer to inclusion in the General Appropriations Bill.
Akbayan Party-list Representative Perci Cendaña moved to terminate the deliberations after less than two hours of interpellation.
Although he did not ask any questions, Cendaña expressed concern over the reduction in COA’s capital outlay.

“This is a critical part in their efforts to digitize and computerize the systems within this critical government agency. And I hope that at a certain point, we will be able to restore the necessary capital outlay for the COA,” he said.
Davao del Sur Rep. John Tracy Cagas sponsored COA’s proposed budget of P16.46 billion, inclusive of automatic appropriations.

Cagas said that, excluding automatic appropriations and considering only new appropriations subject to congressional approval, COA’s proposed budget totals P14 billion, 2.49% higher than its 2026 budget.

“The proposed budget is a vital investment in good governance. By equipping COA with the necessary resources, we are strengthening its capability to conduct rigorous audits, expand its workforce of dedicated state auditors, and adopt digital innovations that bring greater transparency to government transactions,” Cagas said.
“To starve COA of resources is to weaken our defenses against… corruption. To support COA is to fortify the integrity of our entire bureaucracy,” he added.

During the interpellation, Navotas City Representative Toby Tiangco questioned COA about its audit report on the House of Representatives, the Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE) of lawmakers, and the House’s allocation for supplies and materials.
Cagas said the plenary deliberations should focus on COA’s proposed budget.

“They are here to seek our support. As for the House budget as early as 2024 and 2023, to be fair to COA, their report is there and they have already provided it. If we have some speculation or suspicion, that’s not fair to COA, is it?” he said.
“They are doing their job, and it is reflected in the annual audit report. There is nothing being hidden there; it is open,” he added.
Tiangco clarified that he was not doubting COA and that he fully supported its proposed budget.
Cagas later said, however, that he would no longer answer questions regarding the House’s expenses in 2024 and asked Tiangco to submit his questions in writing.
Tiangco said his questions concerned COA’s audit report, which falls within the agency’s mandate.
“But if the distinguished sponsor no longer wants to answer any questions, then there is nothing we can do. Then we will stop asking questions,” he said.
Before the deliberations on COA’s budget, Tiangco had questioned why the plenary deliberations on the House of Representatives’ own budget were moved from September 24 to September 17.
His attempt to reopen the debate was denied.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Latest German election humiliation puts Merz on borrowed time as CDU unrest grows
articles.summary:
Chancellor acknowledges disastrous state election results but vow to push on is likely to further alienate voters, and his own party

•

blocks.text: Friedrich Merz called it a “disaster”, and that was even before the full scale of the catastrophe for himself and his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) came into view after Sunday’s state elections.

In what one outlet called a “power move”, the German chancellor made a highly unusual televised speech just minutes after polls closed in the states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, attempting to get ahead of the narrative with a pledge to stay on and fight for his economic recovery programme.

But as the results trickled in, it became apparent that the CDU had not only scored its worst-ever result in a state election, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, it had crashed out of a regional parliament altogether for the first time in postwar history with just 4.9% of the vote in the region on the Baltic coast.
The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) came out on top for the third time in a German state, drawing 38% against 35.5% for the centre-left Social Democrats, Merz’s federal coalition partner.

Although the AfD has little chance of taking power because of a “firewall” of non-cooperation agreed by the other main parties, the anti-immigration, Kremlin-friendly party could celebrate a further success in destabilising the German political establishment.

In Berlin, the CDU will almost certainly have to vacate city hall once the coalition negotiations wrap up after a stinging defeat to the leftwing Linke party, which is calling for the expropriation of corporate landlords to address a housing crisis.

Polls had been predicting the humiliating result for Merz’s conservatives, which came after a historic rout two weeks ago in the former communist state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the CDU scored just 17% to the AfD’s nearly 44%.

But the cumulative effect of these losses, coupled with Merz’s dire approval ratings and a far right with clear momentum, can hardly be exaggerated. Despite his vow to stay the course, many regard the German leader to be on borrowed time.

“Friedrich Merz is fighting for his political survival,” said the Berenberg bank’s chief economist, Holger Schmieding. “Although Merz has vowed to stay on as chancellor to spearhead the much needed pro-growth reforms, it will not be easy for him to contain the unrest within his party.”

Speculation was already rife after the Saxony-Anhalt race about a Kanzlertausch, or chancellor swap. But as long as none of the potential successors appears ready to wield the dagger, and Merz remains unwilling to step aside, a volatile deadlock will reign.
after newsletter promotion
Merz, 70, gathered the CDU leadership at the party headquarters in Berlin to watch the exit polls together late on Sunday.

Local media reported that some of those assembled loudly objected to the defiant, full-steam-ahead speech he planned to deliver regarding his programme, saying that it amounted to ignoring what voters were shouting from the rooftops with their choices.
Merz cancelled a planned trip to New York this week to speak before the UN general assembly, already anticipating he would need to be in Berlin to grapple with the state elections’ aftermath.
Now, more than ever, he will have his work cut out for him after just 16 months in office.

articles.title: As sea ice vanishes, Arctic communities like Tuktoyaktuk are losing their shoreline
articles.summary: Experts warn that the warming climate expands open-water seasons and melts sea ice leaving Arctic shorelines increasingly vulnerable to harsh waves. As the hamlet awaits federal response on expanded…

image.caption: Waves crash over Tuktoyaktuk's oceanfront during a severe August 2025 storm surge in this file photo. Forecasters issued coastal flooding warnings from Mackenzie Bay to McKinley Bay Sept. 14. (Dez Loreen/CBC)

blocks.text: North

Experts warn that the warming climate expands open-water seasons and melts sea ice leaving Arctic shorelines increasingly vulnerable to harsh waves. As the hamlet awaits federal response on expanded mitigation proposals, local leaders view current defences as a crucial measure to buy time for eventual planned relocation.
Shrinking sea ice leaves Tuktoyaktuk exposed as leaders weigh long-term protection and relocation plans.

A storm surge swept through the Beaufort Sea on Monday, sending a stark warning to low-lying Arctic communities like Tuktoyaktuk, N.W.T., about the mounting risks of climate change and coastal erosion.
While water levels receded quickly with no major structural damage, leaders say the hamlet was saved by pre-existing shoreline defences.

"The present disaster mitigation that was done before this year held its own, so we're fortunate this time through this short storm surge," said Tuktoyaktuk Mayor Vince Teddy. "We are grateful for that [funding] because it saved our community."
The Disaster Mitigation and Adaptation Fund (DMAF) is a federal program that helps communities build infrastructure to protect against climate hazards like flooding and erosion.

In Tuktoyaktuk, a hamlet of about 1,000 people on the shores of the Beaufort Sea, that protection includes a $54-million shoreline revetment project completed in July 2025 using boulders shipped from Inuvik to shield the harbour.

But experts warn that with the warming climate, the natural ice barriers that historically protected communities like Tuktoyaktuk are rapidly disappearing, leaving shorelines increasingly vulnerable to direct wave action over longer open-water seasons.
Joseph Kim, a researcher with the National Research Council of Canada, said in the past, sea ice would act as "a protective shield," but it is disappearing.
"As this open water season gets extended, you have much more time for storms to develop and impact the community," Kim said. "That leads to more flooding and more erosion on Northern shorelines."
Kim said a 2024 modeling study by the National Research Council found without sea ice protection, storm surges can reach two to three times higher than normal.

items: Tuktoyaktuk residents await funding to rebuild smokehouses after 2025 storm

blocks.text: Mauricio Carvallo Aceves, a climate adaptation researcher at the University of British Columbia, said warming ocean waters compound the problem: they thaw the underlying permafrost while waves mechanically strip away sediment.

“First of all, we have to remember that the coast is always changing and evolving,” said Carvallo Aceves. “That inherently poses a challenge because there is no such thing as a stable coastline, so to speak.”
Even after recovering from a severe storm surge in August 2025, Tuktoyaktuk continues to face coastal erosion due to the warming climate.
“One thing that we have to remember is that we really cannot stop the ocean. It will always win," said Carvallo Aceves.

According to Teddy, to secure long-term protection for the airport, inner harbour and fresh water reservoir, the Inuvialuit Regional Corporation submitted a joint funding application over the winter for Tuktoyaktuk and three neighbouring Beaufort Delta coastal communities: Sachs Harbour, Paulatuk and Ulukhaktok.
Teddy said the proposal remains under territorial and federal review as engineers and researchers compile scientific data alongside local traditional knowledge into a formal plan.
"Take all of that and we apply not only what we've learned over the last three years for DMAF, but also the traditional knowledge that's been there for generations," Teddy said.
Part of this involves exploring nature-based protective measures using local materials already present on the shoreline.
"We're looking at [adding] gravel and tundra on the shoreline just because that's what the shoreline is made of really; the topsoil is there, and the tundra is there," Teddy said.
Both Kim and Carvallo Aceves note that nature-based solutions can break wave energy naturally. However, short Arctic summer seasons leave tight windows for research and construction.
“Those are very difficult questions to answer partly because of just how localized it is,” Carvallo Aceves said. “We really need those kinds of studies to be done at a small scale.”
Teddy says that while shoreline reinforcement buys crucial time, every protective measure taken today is just one step in a larger plan.
The community's long-term goal remains relocation to safer ground on Inuvialuit lands. Preliminary discussions with government partners to that end continue.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Samanntha Lee is a multimedia journalist and CBC 2026 summer news scholar. She covers local and territorial news in Yellowknife. If you would like to share your story, you can reach her at samanntha.lee@cbc.ca

articles.title: Sara Duterte remained company director even after assuming VP post -- witness
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte remained one of the Board of Directors of Metro City Chow Foods Corporation until 2025 or even after she was elected and assumed office as Vice President, a witness from…

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 5:56pm

Vice President Sara Duterte remained one of the Board of Directors of Metro City Chow Foods Corporation until 2025 or even after she was elected and assumed office as Vice President, a witness from the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said Monday.

SEC Company Registration and Monitoring Department Director Gerardo Fernando del Rosario made the testimony during Day 27 of the impeachment trial of Duterte, saying the Vice President’s position in the said firm was reflected on Metro City Chow Foods Corporation submissions to the SEC.
“Ayon po sa GIS nila from 2022-2024, si VP Sara Duterte ay member pa rin po ng Board of Directors,” Del Rosario said, referring to General Information Sheet.
(Based on its GIS from 2022 to 2024, Vice President Duterte is a member of the Board of Directors [of Metro City Chow Foods Corp.)
Asked about the following year’s filing, the SEC official confirmed: “Member pa rin siya ng Board of Directors sa GIS ng 2025.”
(The GIS of the same firm showed the Vice President remained as one of the Board of Directors in year 2025.)

Asked by private prosecutor Erwin Matib to explain what a board does, Del Rosario described its authority over the corporation’s business and property, as well as its responsibilities to shareholders and government agencies.
On the board’s role in conducting the company’s business, Del Rosario replied, “Hindi po siya makakapag-conduct ng business kung wala po siyang Board of Directors.”
(A firm cannot conduct business without a Board of Directors.)
Prohibited under 1987 Constitution
Also on Monday, Del Rosario said the Constitution prohibits the Vice President from participating in any business as provided under Article 7, Section 13 of the Constitution.

During the same hearing, Del Rosario said that GenCorp. Industries Inc. (GenCorp), a firm declared by Vice President Duterte as one of her business interests in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN), did not list her as an incorporator or director based on the firm’s General Information Sheet and Audited Financial Statement submitted to the SEC.

Del Rosario made the confirmation when he was asked by prosecutor Eric Matib and later on by Senator Joel Villanueva if SEC records showed any involvement of the Vice President with GenCorp given that the Vice President listed it as one of her business interests in her 2023, 2024 and 2025 SALNs or during her term as Vice President.
“Wala po siya sa [company records ng] GenCorp,” Del Rosario said.
(Her name is not in GenCorp.)

Senator judge and Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian then quizzed Del Rosario as to possible scenarios which would explain the Vice President’s declaration of the firm as one of her business interest even if the company’s SEC submissions does not say so.
“Ano po ang posible na nangyari rito?,” Gatchalian said.
(What possibly happened here?)
Del Rosario then said that possibly, the Vice President could be behind the largest subscriber of GenCorp.

“If GenCorp has a corporate subscriber with a controlling interest…based on its GIS, it has corporate subscriber, JTC Group of Companies, which holds 55% of the company’s equity. If I am to give an example [scenario], maaring ang may-ari ng JTC ay si VP Sara, para magkaroon siya ng control dito sa GenCorp na kung saan hindi mag-aapear ‘yung pangalan niya [sa corporate records].
Del Rosario said that based on SEC records, JTC Group of Companies is represented by a certain Jaime T. Cruz.
“Yun po ang isang scenario; kung talagang siya ay may control ng JTC,” Del Rosario added.
(That is one possible scenario, if she is in control of JTC," Del Rosario added. — RSJ, GMA News

blocks.text: Tropical Storm Dujuan is skirting the coast of Japan and despite avoiding a direct landfall, is still expected to leave its mark. Dujuan briefly reached typhoon status on Friday before weakening to a tropical storm again on Sunday morning. But it is expected to restrengthen back into a typhoon by Tuesday morning. Sustained winds could reach 80mph (129km/h), with gusts approaching 100mph.

Although mainland Japan has avoided a direct hit, Dujuan’s track takes it across the Izu Islands, where evacuation warnings are in place. Heavy rain, flooding and landslide alerts are widespread, with high waves adding another threat to exposed coastal areas and islands.

Some exceptional rainfall totals are expected, with about 200mm (7.9in) possible along the southern coasts of the Chubu and Kanto regions in just 24 hours – roughly equivalent to the average rainfall for the entire month of September. The Tokyo metropolitan area is among the areas facing the heaviest rain, with some models suggesting nearly 90mm could fall within six hours on Monday evening. Further south, the Izu peninsula could receive more than 80mm in just three hours – 38% of the month’s usual rainfall in a single evening. Dujuan is expected to continue north-eastwards before dissipating in the north-west Pacific later this week.

The Atlantic hurricane season remains unusually quiet, despite Tropical Storm Fay developing south-west of the Azores over the weekend. Fay is not expected to strengthen further, extending the record for the latest first hurricane to form in a hurricane season during the satellite era. The previous date record was 11 September, set in 2002 with Hurricane Gustav and equalled in 2013 with Hurricane Humberto.

South-west Europe may get one last taste of summer with a blast of heat this week. Temperatures across Spain and Portugal will rise significantly above the monthly norm, to the low to mid 30s celsius. Even in north-west Spain, in Santiago de Compostela highs could reach about 35C (95F) on Tuesday, about 12C above the typical daytime high. Heading into the weekend, warmth will spread into central Europe, but most likely with less intensity than earlier in the week across the Iberian peninsula.

articles.title: Kids' repeated online exposure to school violence magnifies fear, confusion --NCMH
articles.summary: Authorities warned the public about the risks associated with young people repeatedly viewing violent online content about school shootings.

blocks.text: Following the latest fatal school shooting incident in Banga, South Cotabato, authorities warned the public about the risks associated with young people repeatedly viewing violent online content about school shootings.

The National Center for Mental Health (NCMH) emphasized on Monday that while social media plays an important role in disseminating information, excessive availability of graphic content on school violence, especially misinformation, can harm students, even those who did not experience the event firsthand.

“Social media can help disseminate information… However, social media can also magnify. Napapalala niya ‘yung fear, ‘yung confusion, and ‘yung emotional distress, especially when young people are repeatedly exposed,” NCMH Medical Center Chief Dr. Noel Reyes said on Bagong Pilipinas Ngayon.

(Social media can help disseminate information… However, social media can also magnify things. It worsens fear, confusion, and emotional distress, especially when young people are repeatedly exposed.)
“Lalong-lalo na ngayon ‘yung graphic video, photographs, ‘yung mga opinyon ng iba, speculations, and unverified reports,” he added.
(Especially nowadays with graphic videos, photographs, opinions of others, speculations, and unverified reports.)
Reyes said prolonged consumption of content related to school violence could foster a sense of ongoing threat that may trigger anxiety or intrusive memories in children.

“Even if the child is not present during the incident, repeated exposure may make that a threat. Parang ongoing pa [sa kaniya] ‘yung threat kasi parati siyang exposed doon. They may contribute to anxieties, sleep difficulty, and intrusive memories,” Reyes said.

(Even if a child was not present during the incident, repeated exposure can cause them to perceive it as an active threat. It feels as if the threat is still ongoing because they are constantly exposed to it. This can contribute to anxiety, sleep difficulties, and intrusive memories.)
The NCMH emphasized the importance of close parental monitoring and guidance, especially for children who spend significant time online.
Reyes advised parents to consider setting limits not only on screen time or internet access, but also on the platforms their children visit, engage with, and the content they consume.
He added that adults should be ready and willing to address questions or content that requires parental intervention, which includes explaining right from wrong and reporting harmful online content.
Preventive measures
According to the NCMH, while mental health literacy among Filipinos has noticeably increased, broader mental health promotion needs further reinforcement.

The agency pointed out that student-initiated school violence should not merely be addressed after a crisis occurs, but prevented beforehand by establishing a whole-of-community mental health support system.

“Unang-una po… there should be a mental health promotion for all students. This includes [having] a safe and nurturing school environment, school emotional learning, sustained anti-bullying programs, ‘yung mga responsible digital citizenship po, ‘yung mga parent education and training,” Reyes said.

(First and foremost… there should be mental health promotion for all students. This includes fostering a safe and nurturing school environment, social-emotional learning, sustained anti-bullying programs, responsible digital citizenship, and parent education and training.)
To promote mental health, the NCMH stated it is willing to launch school caravans to help expand mental health awareness and literacy across academic institutions.
Reyes noted that Filipinos are sometimes deterred from seeking help due to the stigma surrounding mental health in the country, which is often tied to shame.

“Sometimes kasi napipigilan ang pag-seek ng intervention because of stigma. Base po sa ating kultura na tinitignan po talaga nating mga kapwa Pilipino na ang karamdaman sa pag-iisip o kaguluhan sa pag-iisip ay senyales po ng kahinaan or kaya nagdudulot po sa kanila ng shame,” Reyes said.
(Sometimes, seeking intervention is hindered by stigma. Culturally, many Filipinos still view mental illness or psychological distress as a sign of weakness, or something that brings shame.)
“Hindi po ganon ang mental illness. Agaran po natin dapat tanggalin ang stigma upang ang intervention ay right time,” he added.
(Mental illness is not like that. We must immediately eliminate this stigma so that intervention occurs at the right time.)
In addition to the early identification of students in need of mental health assistance, the NCMH stated that schools must provide targeted support for these students.
This includes ensuring access to school counselors or caregivers, establishing preventive wellness programs, and maintaining partnerships with mental health institutions or referral centers.

The NCMH encourages individuals who need mental health support to call its 24/7 crisis hotlines (1553 or 0919-057-1553) or avail free online psychosocial support by scheduling sessions at www.ncmhusaptayo.com.
Parents, teachers, and peers are encouraged to closely monitor children and friends for significant physical and emotional behavioral changes that may signal emotional distress.
Emotional and physical red flags in children experiencing distress may include intense fear of school, nightmares, and stress-induced symptoms like headaches, tremors, or cold extremities.

Meanwhile, more severe indicators could include expressions of hopelessness, alcohol abuse, or self-harm, which all signal a critical need for immediate parental and professional intervention. — BM, GMA News

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 5:39pm
An attempt by Navotas City Representative Toby Tiangco on Monday to reopen the plenary debate on the budget of the House of Representatives was denied.
During the plenary session of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill, Tiangco questioned the changes of the budget hearing of the House from September 24 to September 17.

"Kaya po tayo nagbibigay ng schedule ng budget is para po makapaghanda yung mga members na magtanong. So kung ang budget ng House ay September 24 pa, natural po ang paghahandaan muna ay yung mga September 18, September 21. So mas logical kung doon po humugot," Tiangco said.

(The reason we provide the budget schedule is so that the members can prepare the questions they want to raise. So, if the House budget is scheduled for September 24, naturally, the members would first prepare for the September 18 and September 21 budget hearings. So, it would be more logical to draw from those instead.)
"So I'm asking for a motion for reconsideration to reopen the budget of the House and be presented to the plenary," he added.
However, Deputy Speaker Janette Garin denied Tiangco's motion, saying that Tiangco was unable to vote during the plenary debate of the budget hearing the lower chamber.

"Section 105 of our rules states, 'when a national report or motion is approved, adopted, or lost, a member who voted with the majority may move for its reconsideration on the same or succeeding session day'," Garin said.

"As we have conferred with the Secretary-General, the Honorable Toby Changco was on official travel abroad. Hence, with due courtesy, Hon. Toby Tiangco, your motion for reconsideration is out of order," she added.
The interpellation on the proposed P27.9 billion budget for Congress was terminated on Thursday, September 17.
The budget covers the Senate, House of Representatives, Commission on Appointments, and the House and Senate Electoral Tribunal. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: DOH debunks myths, shares facts about suicide
articles.summary: The Philippines observes Suicide Prevention Month every September to raise awareness about suicide prevention and help break the stigma surrounding mental health conditions.

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 5:22pm
The Philippines observes Suicide Prevention Month every September to raise awareness about suicide prevention and help break the stigma surrounding mental health conditions.

The Department of Health (DOH) on Monday conducted the "Mindful Media: Capacity Development on Responsible Reporting and Ethical Portrayal of Suicide" in Quezon City to strengthen responsible and evidence-informed media practices and promote compassionate and ethical reporting on suicide.
Here are some of the myths about suicide debunked by the DOH:
MYTH: Talking about suicide with someone who is suicidal is a bad idea and can be interpreted as encouragement.
FACT: Talking about suicide can help a person explore options and prevent suicide.
MYTH: Someone who is suicidal is determined to die.
FACT: They may be ambivalent about living or dying. Access to support can help prevent suicide.
"We urge them to address the situation and we want them to have access to available support," said Jason Roque, officer-in-charge division chief of the DOH Health Promotion Bureau.
MYTH: Most suicides happen suddenly without warning.
FACT: Most suicides are preceded by warning signs.
Speaking to the media, Roque said there are warning signs that may indicate that a person is at risk of suicide.
These warning signs may be seen in a person's words, feelings and actions.
Words: Expressing hopelessness, wanting to die or asking about suicide methods.
Feelings: Severe sadness, mood swings, unexpected rage and loss of interest.
Actions: Withdrawal from usual activities and isolation.
MYTH: Once someone is suicidal, they will remain suicidal.
FACT: Heightened suicide risk is often short-term and specific to a situation.
"Suicidal thoughts are not permanent. It is short term and specific to a situation," Roque said.
"It's not permanent for an entire life of an individual because because a person can be triggered by different situations in their life," he added.
These situations may include relationship concerns, financial problems, conflict, disasters, violence, abuse and loss.
MYTH: Suicide is an appropriate means of coping with problems.
FACT: Suicide is not a constructive means of coping with problems.
Roque said it is better to talk to family members and peers when dealing with problems.
MYTH: Only people with mental disorders are suicidal.
FACT: Suicidal behavior can indicate deep unhappiness but does not necessarily mean that a person has a mental disorder.
"There are so many things that can lead to deep unhappiness that may trigger a suicide attempt or the act of suicide itself," Roque said.
MYTH: Suicidal behavior is easy to explain.
FACT: Suicide is complex and cannot be explained in simplistic ways.
"It's not easy. It's difficult to discuss because you cannot easily talk about it. Discussing it can feel like you're walking on eggshells," Roque said.
To help avoid the stigma surrounding suicide, the DOH also presented the following terms that the public may use when talking about suicide:

items: Instead of "committed suicide," use "died by suicide" or "dying by suicide."
Instead of "completed suicide" or "successful suicide," use "died by suicide."
Instead of "failed suicide attempt," use "suicide attempt" or "self-directed violence."
Instead of "non-fatal suicide," use "suicide attempt."

Ex-Transport Minister Scheuer goes on trial for perjury

blocks.caption: Plans for a highway toll (Maut) in Germany have so far failed Image: Bernd Wüstneck/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A perjury trial against former Transport Minister Andreas Scheuer kicked off at the Berlin District Court on Monday.

Scheuer and his co-defendant Gerhard Schulz, a former state secretary, are accused of having lied to a parliamentary committee investigating a failed scheme some seven years ago to levy a highway toll on foreign motorists.
Both of them deny the charges made against them.
What are the charges against Scheuer and Schulz?

The two are accused of lying to the committee about having signed a contract with a company to run the toll operations despite knowing that the European Court of Justice (ICJ) was likely to declare the scheme illegal.

Scheur's Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of the Christian Democrats (CDU) currently led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, had devised a plan to levy tolls on all drivers but then compensate German motorists by reducing their motor vehicle taxes.
The scheme was shot down in 2019 by the ICJ for breaching EU rules.
But by that time, the Transport Ministry under Scheuer had already signed binding contracts with the operators who were to be tasked with executing the plan.
The German government was then forced to pay €243 million ($283 million at current exchange rates) in damages to the companies involved.
Jail sentences possible
The trial is planned to take place over 12 days, with a verdict expected on November 25.
If found guilty, the accused could face jail sentences ranging from three months to five years.

articles.title: Police officer and man injured in shooting outside Belleville, Ont., synagogue
articles.summary: A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire Sunday near a synagogue in Ontario as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. The man was hospitalized…

image.caption: Belleville police officers stand outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue Sunday night. The incident occurred on the street in front of the synagogue. Last night, the synagogue was taped off as part of the crime scene. (CBC)

blocks.text: Canada

A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire Sunday near a synagogue in Ontario as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. The man was hospitalized in life-threatening condition.
Shooting occurred as members of Jewish community gathered for Yom Kippur

A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire Sunday near a synagogue in the southern Ontario community of Belleville as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. The man was hospitalized in life-threatening condition.

Ontario's Special Investigations Unit said the exchange of gunfire happened near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, about 175 kilometres east of Toronto. Belleville police said the officer encountered the man around 7:10 p.m. and that both were taken to a hospital.

Police have not said what led to the shooting or whether the synagogue or Jewish community was targeted. They said there was no risk to public safety and asked people to avoid the area while officers investigated.
The Special Investigations Unit, the civilian agency that investigates serious incidents involving police, said it sent investigators to the scene.

items: 'Canada's civic compact is failing Jewish Canadians,' Carney says in speech addressing antisemitism

blocks.text: Belleville police said they would not provide further information while the investigation was underway.

I’m disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur.

My thoughts are with the Jewish community in Belleville and across Ontario, who have every right to…—fordnation
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the shooting took place outside the synagogue as people gathered for Yom Kippur.

"I'm disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur," Ford said in a post on social media.
Ford said Jewish people "have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear" and called for those responsible to be arrested and prosecuted.
"My thoughts are also with the police officer who was shot, along with their family and loved ones," Ford said.
Surge in antisemitism
York Regional Police said there was no known threat in the region but residents should expect increased patrols at places of worship.
Sunday's shooting comes months after Prime Minister Mark Carney warned that Canada was failing its Jewish community amid a surge in antisemitism.

Carney cited shootings at Jewish schools, firebombings of synagogues and attacks on community centers and Jewish-owned businesses. His government announced millions in additional funding to help faith-based institutions pay for security infrastructure, training and personnel.

Synagogues in the Toronto area have also previously been targeted by gunfire. In March, shots damaged the entrances of synagogues in Vaughan and Toronto. No one was injured. Police later arrested three suspects in connection with those shootings.

articles.title: Ed Davey rejects claims party is ‘sleepwalking into irrelevance’ under his leadership – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Lib Dem leader says he is proud of party’s record at Brighton conference

Ed Davey has urged Andy Burnham to deliver some “home truths” to Donald Trump when they meet at the…

blocks.text: Ed Davey rejects claims party is 'sleepwalking into irrelevance' under his leadership

Good morning. Ed Davey became Lib Dem leader in 2020, which means he is technically the longest-serving leader of a national party in the UK. (“Technically” because, while Nigel Farage only became leader of Reform UK in his current incumbency in 2024, he had led it before when it was called the Brexit party and, if you include Ukip, he has been leader of the anti-migrant, anti-EU right in British politics for more than 20 years.) After six years in charge, it is inevitable that some Lib Dems are starting to complain and, with the Lib Dem conference taking place in Brighton, Davey has been giving interviews this morning where he has had to respond to complaints from his critics.
The most vocal has been Julian Brazil, the leader of Devon county council, who told the BBC yesterday that the Lib Dems were “sleepwalking into irrelevance” with Davey at the helm.
Not surprisingly, Davey does not agree.
Asked about Brazil’s comments, the Lib Dem leader told BBC Breakfast:

double quotation markWe’ve grown really fast in recent years under my leadership. Record number of MPs. We’re running more councils than the Conservatives – councils up and down the country. [I’m] really proud of that record and it means when you have a bigger party, you can’t please everyone all the time.
And Davey was a bit more blunt when asked the same question on Sky News.

double quotation markI would say to the Devon councillor, we’ve now got six Liberal Democrat MPs in Devon. That’s not happened since the 1920s. We have a huge number of councillors across Devon and are leading the way in Devon, and I could go around the rest of the country. I happen to know Brazil. We’ve rarely seen eye to eye. So, all I would say is, we’re going to build on the success we’ve had.
I will post more from Davey’s interviews shortly.
There is more coverage here of what was happening at the Lib Dem conference at the weekend.
Here is the agenda for the day.

blocks.text: Davey urges Burnham to 'take a stand' when PM meets Trump in New York tomorrow
Ed Davey has urged Andy Burnham to deliver some “home truths” to Donald Trump when they meet at the UN tomorrow.
Asked how Burnham should treat the US president, Davey told Sky News:
double quotation markTake a stand, please. And the cosying up to him that was done by Keir Starmer absolutely failed miserably.
Davey praised Mark Carney, the Liberal Canadian PM for “standing up to Trump with success” and, referring to what he wanted to see from Burnham, he said:

double quotation markYou have to stand up to them. And this is a man who’s ruining our world. He’s ruining his own country, but he’s hitting people in our country. His disastrous war in Iran is leading to the hike in oil and gas prices, which means people are paying more for petrol and diesel. So if Andy Burnham is going to represent Britain’s interests and the interests of British people, he needs to tell Donald Trump some home truths, whether it’s on the economy and defence, whether it’s on Iran, whether it’s on NATO. I’m afraid, under President Trump, we no longer have a reliable ally in the White House ... You can’t trust this man. And I think, while he may want to choose his words slightly more diplomatically than I’m giving to you, he needs to stand up for Britain and British interests.

With Trump deeply unpopular in the UK, it is easy to see why Davey criticises him harshly. But prime ministers who have had to negotiate with Trump have tended to be more tactful and, in her preview of what is likely to happen when Burnham meets Trump tomorrow, Pippa Crerar, the Guardian’s political editor, says Burnham is not angling for a fight. She says:

double quotation markDowning Street insiders expect Burnham to be a bit more forceful [than Keir Starmer was] when he feels there’s a need to stand up for British interests. But there is no suggestion he will follow the more combative approach of Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister. Instead, one source said he would probably take a “third way” between Starmer and Carney, pushing back more than his predecessor publicly and privately, but avoiding open diplomatic warfare. A second source said the prime minister had three ambitions for Tuesday’s talks: bond with Trump, make the case for Ukraine, and avoid any drama.

articles.title: Merz insists he will stay as German chancellor despite heavy losses in state elections – Europe live
articles.summary:
CDU suffered heavy losses in two regional elections, including in home state of former leader Angela Merkel, where it polled just 4.9%

Good morning and welcome to our Europe live blog, where…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 11m agoOpening summary

blocks.text: Opening summary
Good morning and welcome to our Europe live blog, where we’ll start in Germany after a bruising night for Friedrich Merz’s party.

The German chancellor is staring down pressure over his leadership and authority after the CDU suffered heavy losses in two regional elections. For the first time in 77 years, it’s failed to enter a state parliament, in the former East German state of Mecklenburg- Vorpommern.
This was the home state of former CDU chancellor Angela Merkel; the party there last night pulled just 4.9% of the vote, losing more than half of its support.

Many of its voters have flocked to Alternative for Germany (AfD). The far-right, anti-migrant party gained 38% of the vote, doubling its share to now become the largest party in the state. This result comes just a fortnight after AfD romped to a majority in Saxony-Anhalt.
Merz called it a “disaster” last night in a public address, but vowed to stay the course and press on with his government’s reforms.

articles.title: Pakistan says strikes in Afghanistan killed '28 terrorists'
articles.summary: The Afghan border provinces of Kunar and Paktika were struck overnight. Pakistan said 28 militants were killed, Afghanistan said three civilians died. This follows soon after an attack on police in…

image.caption: Taliban officials accused Pakistan of targeting civiliansImage: Shafiullah Kakar/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pakistan conducted airstrikes on northeastern Afghanistan on Monday on what Pakistan's Ministry of Information described as suicide bomber training facilities.
It was the first Pakistani strike of its kind on Afghan territory since June, and followed soon after an attack targeting Pakistani police across the border in Kohat.
The uneasy neighbors reported seemingly conflicting casualty tolls.
What were the conflicting accounts on the strikes?
Pakistan's Ministry of Information and Broadcasting claimed online that the attacks had targeted terrorist training sites in Afghanistan with "precision and accuracy."

"Three targets were destroyed with precision including a Suicide Bombers training markaz [station], killing 28 terrorists alongside multiple suicide bombers. Large quantities of weapons and ammunition ... were also destroyed," the Ministry said.
The Taliban government in Kabul, meanwhile, claimed that three people were killed as it accused Pakistan of bombarding "civilian homes."
Afghanistan's deputy government spokesperson Hamdullah Fitrat said that the strikes took place in the Kunar and Paktika provinces.

Fitrat wrote on X that one strike hit at around 3:00 am Monday (2230 UTC, Sunday) in Kunar's Nurgal district and "completely destroyed" a house, adding that three people were killed and four other members of the family were wounded.
He said that two locations were also hit in the Paktika province, claiming that a shop and an unoccupied house were destroyed.
Neither side's assertions on the details of and casualties from the strikes could be immediately verified.

blocks.caption: The latest strikes threaten to shatter three months of relative calmImage: Shafiullah Kakar/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Strikes follow last week's militant attack in Pakistan

The reported strikes come after a suicide bombing and a 20-hour gun battle between militants and police on Friday, which took place at a district police headquarters compound in the Pakistani city of Kohat, situated near the Afghan border.
At least 31 people, including 16 police officers, were killed in the attack.
Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, a local militant group linked to the jihadist group Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility for the attack.
The Afghanistan-Pakistan conflict
Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan have been tense since the Taliban returned to power in 2021.
The latest strikes threaten to shatter three months of relative calm after former South Asian allies engaged in their worst clashes in years in February.
Pakistan declared that month that it was in an "open war” with Afghanistan, following a rise in militant attacks on civilians and security forces inside Pakistan.
Afghanistan launched retaliatory strikes after Pakistan carried out airstrikes inside Afghan territory and the cross-border fighting has since claimed the lives of hundreds of people.
Pakistan last mounted deadly airstrikes in Afghanistan in June.
Islamabad accuses Afghanistan of sheltering militant groups which launch attacks inside Pakistan's territory.
Main among these is the TTP, often referred to as the Pakistani Taliban and Baloch separatist groups from the border areas.
The Taliban has dismissed ​the allegations, saying that militancy in Pakistan is an internal problem.
Are Pakistan and Afghanistan heading for war?

articles.title: Germany's car crisis: Can the 35-hour workweek survive?
articles.summary: German carmakers want employees to work 40 hours instead of the current 35 without extra pay, arguing it would improve competitiveness. Unions strongly oppose the proposal and view it as an attack on…

image.caption: Germany's auto industry is shedding jobs faster than any other industrial sector in the countryImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany's famed automotive sector is facing a deep crisis, squeezed by high manufacturing costs, punitive US tariffs, intensifying competition from China and a difficult transition to electric vehicles.
Industry heavyweights such as Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz and BMW have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs.
The branch is shedding jobs faster than any other industrial sector in the country.

Volkswagen, for instance, is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW announced it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027.
Auto suppliers such as Bosch and ZF Friedrichshafen have also announced thousands of job reductions amid tough market conditions and global competition.
The legacy car industry is in crisis. How can it move on?

Germany's automotive industry is losing competitiveness as costs rise and production shifts abroad, said Ferdinand Dudenhöffer, director of the Center for Automotive Research (CAR) in the German city of Bochum.
"In 2018, the industry employed around 830,000 people. Currently, that number is below 700,000," he told DW. "We project that by around 2030, it will be 500,000."

Regaining competitiveness and securing jobs in the future will require an array of measures including lower production and energy costs, better logistics infrastructure and favorable tax conditions, he added.
Labor costs too high in Germany?
Auto industry executives agree that labor costs in Germany are too high compared to international rivals.
Labor costs in the country average $3,307 (€2,882) per vehicle, compared to $769 in Japan and $597 in China, according to a reportpublished by the consulting firm Oliver Wyman.
To trim labor costs, carmakers want employees in Germany to work 40 hours a week instead of the current 35 hours, without any increase in pay.
The 35-hour workweek has long been standard across much of Germany's automotive industry, having emerged from collective bargaining agreements negotiated in the 1980s and 1990s.
It reflects an era when Germany was highly competitive, said Dudenhöffer, adding: "That time is over."
Workers' unions, however, vehemently oppose longer working hours.

Christiane Benner, the head of the influential IG Metall trade union, said workers had already accepted wage cuts and other concessions worth several billion euros, yet were now being told that this was still not enough.

The union argues that German automakers are struggling with weak demand and underutilized factories, not a shortage of labor hours. "Not a single additional car will be sold just because the workforce works longer hours," the union announced.
IG Metall is holding demonstrations at more than 200 locations nationwide on September 21 to oppose job cuts and other measures affecting working conditions in the automotive sector.
VW is bringing out the axe
Can longer working hours save jobs?
The union is "fighting for relics from 20 years ago, forgetting today's reality," Dudenhöffer said.
The expert estimated that if carmakers were to move from a 35-hour week to a 40-hour week, personnel costs would decrease by 13%.
"We wouldn't be taking money away from employees, but we would be creating conditions that would make jobs possible in Germany, in the automotive industry, in the future," he underlined.

Stefan Bratzel, head of the Center of Automotive Management (CAM) in Bergisch Gladbach, said the 35-hour week represents a key achievement for trade unions in their collective bargaining history, so "conflict is inevitable" between management and unions.
On the other hand, more working hours for the same pay would mathematically lower labor costs per hour, he added.
"Ultimately, this raises the question of how the burdens of the current transformation are to be distributed between companies and employees," said Bratzel.
How can Germany's auto industry recover?
Experts say improving labor costs at German production sites is necessary, but it alone will not solve the industry's deeper structural problems.
"Working five hours more per week alone will not win the technological race against China," said Bratzel.

He stressed that, to restore their competitive edge, German carmakers need to deliver attractive and affordable electric vehicles, invest heavily in software and AI, and improve the efficiency of their development and manufacturing processes.
"German manufacturers must be at least as innovative and high-performing in technological terms as they are expensive by international standards," said Bratzel.
At the same time, he explained, Germany requires competitive framework conditions regarding energy, taxes, bureaucracy and infrastructure.
Could VW's Osnabrück car plant pivot to arms production?
Dudenhöffer echoed this view, saying that Germany must pursue difficult but necessary reforms.
"Germany can only be considered a viable option for its automotive industry and jobs if we regain our competitiveness," he said.
And for that, action is required on multiple fronts, including lowering labor and energy costs, adjusting taxes, and creating better logistics infrastructure, he added.

"But the coming years will be very tough," Dudenhöffer warned. "And they will become even tougher if we stick to the status quo and believe we can simply rest on the prosperity we enjoyed 20 years ago."

articles.title: US proposes AI safety mechanism in talks with China
articles.summary: US Treasury chief Scott Bessent said there had been "successful" talks with China on trade and AI. The talks come amid growing fears that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.

image.caption: Hopes of finding common ground on concerns over AI safety comes amid fierce competition between the two countriesImage: Bai Xueqi/Xinhua/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Top officials fro the United States and China have discussed a communication mechanism dealing with AI concerns between the two countries.
The talks on Sunday evening come ahead of a summit this week between US President Donald Trump and China's Xi Jinping and amid growing fears that AI poses an existential threat to humanity.
The discussion with a team led by China's Vice Premier He Lifeng also involved top US trade official Jamieson Greer and took place at JPMorgan Chase's New York headquarters.
What is AI's biggest risk: Speed or autonomy?
What did US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent say about the AI talks with China?
"We just had a very successful engagement with the Chinese on trade and AI," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters.
Bessent said the delegations spoke about a mechanism to communicate about AI issues, calling it the "US-China AI dialogue."
"The US has proposed that we have a notification mechanism between the two countries," Bessent said.

The US Treasury chief said that these notifications would be for potential "incidents" or an instance "that rises up to a national security level from AI," he said, adding that both sides have agreed to meet again.

"We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent said at the conclusion of the talks.
What has been reported in China?
Chinese state news agency Xinhua described the talks as "candid, in-depth, and constructive" on Monday.

"The two sides engaged in... discussions on key economic and trade issues of mutual interest, such as implementing the consensus from previous consultations and promoting bilateral trade and investment," Xinhua reported in a brief readout.
Xinhua added that Chinese and US officials also held a dialogue on "issues related to AI", with no further details provided.
AI fear machine?
Concern over the threat posed by AI
In recent weeks, leading AI firms have warned of the threat posed by unbridled AI development and the pace at which these threats could become a reality.
They have begun working on creating a standards body they say would regulate the industry amid rising fears about its dangers.

Late in August, more than 100 companies, including AI giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Perplexity, signed an open letter calling for a global effort to strengthen AI-powered cybersecurity threats.

That came after it emerged that OpenAI models had gone rogue and had hacked into a digital repository of AI technology. Anthropic conducted investigations to see if its own models had carried out similar attacks and found three incidents in which a Claude model and later identified a fourth incident.
America's AI boom: Who pays the price?
AI experts sound the alarm
Earlier this month, researcher Jacob Coxon, a former OpenAI employee, resigned from Anthropic, warning that AI companies were "gambling with our lives."
Former Google DeepMind researcher Bilal Chughtai echoed his concerns, warning that "AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome."
Trump has dismissed calls to better curb AI's development as "hoaxes" and a "conspiracy."
Trump's stance has been applauded by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose chipmaking company powers the vast majority of AI systems. Huang thanked the US president for "seeing through" the warnings on AI.

articles.title: Canada faces questions over treatment of Iranian conscripts as U.K, Australia take different approach

image.caption: Mostafa Tasbandi, 44, is one of what are believed to be hundreds of Iranians who received letters from the federal government informing them they may not be able to stay in Canada because of mandatory military service they completed in Iran as young men. (Submitted by Mostafa Tasbandi)

blocks.text: Mostafa Tasbandi lost his job last Thursday.

It's just one of the many ways his life has taken a turn since he and hundreds of other Iranians living in Canada received letters on Aug. 6 and 7 informing them they may be inadmissible to stay in the country because of mandatory military service they were forced to complete in Iran as young men.
"I don't have a future right now," Tasbandi, who lives in Halifax, told CBC News this week.

For years, Tasbandi, who arrived in December 2023, had been waiting for a work permit renewal, a situation that prevented his wife from getting a work permit of her own. His 11-year-old daughter has had serious trouble at school since she discovered her father's immigration troubles, he said.

Tasbandi, a computer engineer, isn't sure he will be able to renew his own work permit following his dismissal at work. His boss told him he was letting him go because the company didn't have enough work for him, but Tasbandi suspects a sudden decrease in his productivity due to the stress of his immigration situation had something to do with the dismissal.

"If I can't get another work permit, I don't have money to pay my bills and I cannot go back to my country because I am afraid. I'm stuck. What shall I do?" said the 44-year-old who has participated in several protests against the Iranian regime while in Canada. Iran has since undertaken campaigns to identify and punish citizens demonstrating abroad.

CBC reported last week that former conscripts of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and their family members increasingly face inadmissibility to Canada because of Ottawa’s designation of the IRGC as a terrorist organization. Men across the country who were forced into that military service now tell CBC they feel branded as terrorists by the country they sought refuge in.

They are calling on federal Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab to publish guidance distinguishing conscripts who were forced into service and didn’t commit any terrorist acts from full-fledged, regime-supporting members — similar to what the United Kingdom and Australia have done.

"Canada has a very aggressive policy vis-a-vis national security issues that leads to some decisions which I would say are absurd," said Lorne Waldman, a Toronto-based immigration lawyer representing nearly 40 former Iranian former conscripts targeted by the procedural fairness letters (PFLs).
'Why is Canada doing this?'

Tasbandi and five other Iranians who were forced into mandatory IRGC service in their late teens and early 20s tell CBC they self-disclosed the mandatory military service in their permanent residency applications and now feel penalized for their honesty.
"Why is Canada doing this? We trusted them. They’re treating us differently than other countries [would]," Tasbandi said.

In response to questions from CBC, a spokesperson for Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) said the department recognizes "that some individuals may have served as a result of conscription."

The department "cannot disclose details of our screening processes," spokesperson Mary Rose Sabater wrote in an email, adding the procedural fairness letters sent out in August provide "applicants with an opportunity to respond before a decision is made."

items: They came to Canada for safety. Now they’re suspected of supporting the regime they fled
They fled Iran after years of fear and protest. Canada's new asylum law has put them in limbo

blocks.text: But Yalda Ghani, an Iranian immigration consultant in Toronto, says several of her clients were deemed inadmissible before the August wave of procedural letters was sent out, despite having been conscripted and performing only menial tasks for the IRGC and are challenging the decisions in Federal Court.

"I have many clients who are scared to death, honestly," Ghani said. "They are afraid that if they become inadmissible in Canada, they will lose their chances for other countries, too, because this is a very serious thing to be labelled inadmissible under security and being a ‘member’ of a terrorist organization."
Canada designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps a terrorist organization in 2024, following the lead of the United States.
Every conscript CBC spoke with say they agree with the designation itself.
"I want Canadian immigration to … understand that we are not members of them and we were not members of them," Tasbandi said.
U.K., Australia recommend examining cases closely

The United Kingdom and Australian appear to have taken different approaches, where conscripts are not automatically considered "members" of an organization. In March, Australia's Parliament published guidance on the matter, saying authorities should distinguish involuntary conscripts from supporting members.

The U.K. government published similar guidance in August, stating military service is compulsory for men and that conscripts are unlikely to be required to commit acts "contrary to the basic rules of human conduct."

The six Iranians CBC spoke with for this story, who received PFLs in August, say they or their family members were randomly assigned to IRGC service among Iran's military and security organizations and were tasked with menial or administrative work. None were in a combat role, nor did they carry weapons, they said.

Tasbandi said that when he completed his service in 2008 and 2009, he was appointed to the guard's sports office, due to its substantial involvement in state sports, and was tasked with printing posters and booking appointments. He also briefly worked in a library. After he finished the service, he got an unrelated job in a refrigerator factory in his hometown of Mashhad.
The impact of the letters has extended beyond former conscripts themselves. In some cases, family members have also received procedural fairness letters because of a relative's past IRGC service.
Reza Rajaei, who came to Canada with his wife and daughter in 2022, said his wife and four-year-old daughter also received PFLs because they are part of his permanent residency application.
"What should I respond for her?" Rajaei said of his daughter. "She is four years old."
Samira Chahargoli, who lives outside Toronto with her family, said she also received a PFL because of her husband's compulsory military service in 2002, when he was 18 years old.
"We built a life in Canada. Canada is our home right now," Chahargoli said.
Iranian told he may have to leave Canada over past IRGC service

Without a specific policy, immigration officers and some Federal Court judges appear to be basing their decisions on a recent Federal Court ruling that upheld the inadmissibility of Mohammedreza Vadiati, an Iranian former IRGC conscript, according to Ghani and Waldman.
The Federal Court ruled in Vadiati v. Canada that mandatory service with Iran's IRGC can still count as "membership" for Canadian immigration purposes.
"That's the albatross hanging around our neck," said Waldman.

"The problem is now the immigration officers are relying on Vadiati and they're saying, 'Well, based on Vadiati, if you're a conscript, you're still inadmissible,'" Waldman said. "But the answer to that is there are a whole series of other legal arguments that should have been made that were not made in Vadiati."

Waldman says immigration officers should instead be basing their decisions on the Supreme Court's 2023 Mason decision, which requires immigration decision-makers to meaningfully consider the evidence and circumstances of each case.
Federal Court backlog
What remains unclear is why such a large number of people received letters advising them of their potential inadmissibility over the same two days in August.
Tasbandi belongs to a Telegram messaging group with 19,000 people in it. He says nearly 2,000 members of the group said they received one.
Waldman believes it may have been an attempt by immigration officials to clear a massive backlog in immigration-related Federal Court applications.

In June, the Federal Court published a news bulletin stating immigration proceedings could exceed 30,000 files in 2026, representing nearly five times the volume it handled before the pandemic caused "significant and sustained operational pressures" on the court.

articles.title: His Hyundai Santa Fe burst into flames on busy highway after repairs at dealership
articles.summary: Jason Pelletier was driving to work in June when his car suddenly caught fire. He managed to escape seconds before an explosion blew up its front end and, three months later, he's still waiting for…

image.caption: Jason Pelletier's Hyundai Santa Fe went up in flames in June, while on the road just north of Toronto. The car was a writeoff after the blaze, the cause of which is still under investigation. (Submitted by Jason Pelletier)

blocks.text: Three months after a "traumatizing" vehicle fire, Jason Pelletier is still waiting for answers — and hoping for more compensation — from automaker Hyundai.

On June 9, during the morning commute to work, the school principal was driving on a busy highway, just north of Toronto, when his Santa Fe suddenly caught fire. He saw thick black smoke and flames billowing from the hood. He says the engine and brakes were no longer responsive.
"I'm trying to cross five lanes of traffic on the 401 in morning traffic," Pelletier said. He says he initially struggled to open the door, but finally made it out of the vehicle.
"I got out and, 20 seconds later, there was an explosion," he said. "The whole front end blew up."

What Pelletier finds even more unsettling is that he had just taken his SUV to the dealership the day before. He had to replace a head gasket, a critical seal located between an engine's block and cylinder head that maintains combustion pressure and prevents coolant and oil from mixing.
He says he noticed a burning smell shortly after leaving the downtown Toronto dealership, but wasn’t too worried because the service manager said it might be from residue after the service.
He later sent text messages to the service manager, asking whether he should be concerned about the light smoke coming out from the hood.
Santa Fe catches fire on busy highway
The next morning, on his way to work, a message popped up on his vehicle’s touchscreen, warning of a "potential condition" with the engine control system and recommending a "full system check."
Pelletier sent a few more text messages — but the service manager did not reply before the engine burst into flames.
"They reached out and made sure I was alive essentially," he said.
Safety is 'top priority'
Hyundai Canada declined our request for an interview, but told CBC News in an emailed statement that safety is its "top priority."
"The circumstances surrounding this matter are still under review and we cannot comment further at this time," said Nitish Bissonauth, senior manager of corporate communications.

Joe Hakim, general manager of the dealership, stated in an email to Pelletier that Hycay Consulting Engineering had been commissioned to conduct a joint investigation with the insurance company to determine the cause of the fire.
Hyundai Canada did not respond to questions regarding other vehicle fires reported to the company or the preventive measures put in place in recent years.

Over the past decade — from Jan. 1, 2016 to Sept. 8, 2026 — Transport Canada received 1,140 reports of vehicle fires, across all makes and models. But it says there is no obligation to report these incidents to the ministry, so this number could be higher.
"Fires are about one in 2,500 cars in Canada," according to Murray Thomson, a combustion specialist and professor of mechanical engineering at the University of Toronto
"If you add it up across all of Canada, you have 10,000 vehicle fires per year. That is significant."

With 168 of the 1,140 reported fires, Hyundai accounted for roughly 15 per cent of incidents during this period. The Korean automaker ranks second, behind Ford. The ministry did not provide year-by-year data for each automaker.
A joint investigation by CBC Marketplace and Go Public, published in 2021, focused on seven cases involving Hyundai and Kia vehicles when engines had stalled or caught fire.
"If a car has recurring issues, that's obviously a concern," Murray said.

In 2023, Hyundai recalled more than 320,000 vehicles in Canada linked to a potential fault in the anti-lock braking system that could cause a fire. Pelletier’s Santa Fe was not affected by that recall but it was impacted by two others.

It was fitted with a Knock Sensor Detection System, which warns the driver if their engine is about to fail, in 2020 and, three years later, was fixed again because of a fire risk "even when the vehicle is stationary and the engine is switched off," as Hyundai warned in its safety recall.

items: 'My car's on fire': Drivers fear for their safety as years-long recall rollout drags on

blocks.text: Thomson says automakers remain responsible for the safe operation throughout a vehicle’s lifetime, but admits that it can be difficult when cars change hands. "There could be a system to track ownership more clearly, to link the current owner to the manufacturer directly," he said.

"That's what the whole recall system is about. Transport Canada plays a role too, because it tracks, collects information, and sometimes requests recalls or identifies issues that the manufacturer should respond to."

Transport Canada has conducted several investigations into parts and components of Hyundai vehicles, many of which have led to safety recalls. The federal ministry is currently investigating the trailer lighting module in 2019 to 2023 Santa Fe models, saying two reported fires may be linked to that part.

"In the majority of vehicle fires, the damage caused is significant, making it difficult to determine the exact origin and cause of the fire," the ministry stated in an email to Radio-Canada, adding that vehicle fires can result from various factors, such as inadequate maintenance, improper repairs or manufacturing defects. Arson is also included in its figures.
"Transport Canada does not have data that would allow it to reliably assign a specific percentage to the various potential causes of vehicle fires."
Lengthy claims process
Pelletier’s insurer paid him nearly $22,000 — the estimated value of the vehicle before the fire — on top of the cost of a rental car for one month.
But according to his own estimates, he has lost more than $5,000 worth of personal belongings, including AirPods, pairs of glasses, sportswear and accessories for his dogs.

That’s not to mention the many drag outfits, accessories and make up products that were in his SUV when it burned. The fire happened during Pride Month, a particularly busy time of year for his alter ego, Jezebel Bardot.
"I’m not trying to become a millionaire out of this. I just don’t want to be worse off than I was when I handed them the keys on Monday June 8th to have my car repaired," he said.

Three months later, the Toronto resident is astounded that his Santa Fe, currently stored in distant Oshawa, is still under forensic investigation. He wonders whether yet another recall could have prevented this ordeal.
"I'm certainly hoping that they're not knowingly gambling with people's lives."
In the meantime, he has decided to buy a new SUV — opting for a different brand. "I don't think you could pay me to drive a Hyundai at this point. And it's too bad from a guy who was a longtime fan."

The Residential Tenancies Act is updated with tighter deadlines for late rent repayment
Do you rent in Ontario? Here's what you need to know about new rental rules
A batch of changes to Ontario’s Residential Tenancies Act (RTA) comes into force on Monday, including shorter deadlines for tenants who landlords say have fallen behind on rent payments.
The RTA amendments, some of which were brought into force on July 1, come out of two bills — Bill 60 and Bill 97.
Earlier in the summer, they were described by a spokesperson for Ontario’s housing minister as being necessary to “restore balance and rebuild confidence in Ontario’s rental housing market.”
As of Monday, Sept. 21, here are the major changes that will impact both tenants and landlords:

items: If a tenant falls behind on rent and is issued what’s called an N4 eviction notice (a legal document demanding the money) the tenant now has seven days instead of 14 days to pay. If they don’t, the landlord can apply for an eviction.

Tenants who want to raise their own issues at an eviction hearing at the Landlord and Tenant Board, such as problems with their unit, now have to pay half of the rent they allegedly owe in order to do so.

The RTA now has a formal definition of “persistent late payment,” instead of leaving it open. It’s defined as rent being paid more than seven days late on at least three different occasions over any six-month period.

A landlord who evicts a tenant for their own or their family’s personal use with at least 120 days of notice no longer has to provide that tenant with compensation or the offer of an alternative unit.
Finally, if a landlord evicts a tenant for personal use, the intended new occupant has to move in within 60 days, or the eviction is presumed to be in bad faith.

blocks.text: Will this lead to faster evictions?

Ontario has billed the changes to the RTA as a way to address delays and backlogs at Ontario’s Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB), where non-urgent applications have been known to sit for months before being considered.
A spokesperson for Tribunals Ontario, which oversees the LTB, told CBC News it's been preparing for the RTA updates with “no impact anticipated on caseload or application processing times.”
But both landlord groups and some tenant advocates have questioned whether the changes will mean fewer LTB delays.
The halved deadline to pay back late rent “just means you can file the paperwork a little sooner at the LTB,” said Kayla Andrade, founder of the landlord advocacy group Ontario Landlords Watch.
“It doesn’t mean that you’re going to get your hearing any faster.”

The Small Ownership Landlords of Ontario group has raised similar concerns, arguing that the LTB should allow landlords to skip a hearing altogether for non-payment of rent disputes and instead be able to use a faster-moving mediation process.

Andrade is supportive of the formalizing of the definition of “persistent non-payment of rent,” telling CBC News that previously, “you didn’t know… exactly what the [adjudicator] would consider as persistent late payments. It’s good to have something concrete.”
Tenant advocates call changes a ‘smokescreen’
Tenant organizations have also argued that the RTA updates fail to address the cause of bottlenecks at the LTB.
In a release, the Federation of Metro Tenants' Associations said efficiency was merely a “smokescreen” for “eroding tenants' rights.”

Dania Majid, director of duty counsel for the Advocacy Centre for Tenants Ontario, told CBC News that her legal clinic is deeply concerned that the changes make it easier for tenants to be evicted. But that wouldn't necessarily happen faster, she said.
The switch from 14 to seven days to repay rent will “trigger more hearings. And that’s going to trigger a backlog,” she said.
New tenant union launches across Toronto
Majid says she expects a similar outcome from one of the earlier July 1 RTA updates, which halves the amount of time for tenants and landlords to request a review of an LTB decision.
“If you're not able to provide your materials in time at the LTB to request a review there, people are going to end up at the divisional court and that's going to create a backlog there,” she said.
Then there’s the requirement that tenants pay 50 per cent of the unpaid rent they allegedly owe in order to raise other complaints at their eviction hearing.
“Now the tenant has to file a separate application to raise these issues… when the entire matter could have just been handled at the same hearing,” said Majid
CBC News asked the Ministry of Housing how tenants can recover the money they paid before a hearing if it's found they don’t actually owe it. The ministry did not reply by publication time.

articles.title: Seven Ethiopian rebel groups form new alliance
articles.summary: The groups have been active in Ethiopia's most populous regions for years and now say they will work together.

blocks.text: Seven Ethiopian rebel groups have announced they have formed an alliance to remove the government in Addis Ababa and push for a transitional administration.

The alliance brings together the Fano militia in Amhara, the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and four other smaller groupings in a coalition named Alliance for Survival.
The groups accuse Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government of presiding over "war, genocide, mass destruction, and utter poverty", claiming Ethiopia is at risk of disintegration.
Federal authorities have not yet responded.
Ethiopia has faced years of armed conflict in Oromia and Amhara, the most populous states in the country.
There have also been renewed tensions in the northern Tigray region, where a two-year civil war left hundreds of thousands dead and displaced millions.
An African-Union peace deal ended that war in 2022, but there have been fears of a return to a full-scale conflict, with both sides accusing each other of violating that agreement.
Besides Oromia, Amhara and Tigray, the new alliance also includes groups based in three other regions - Ogaden, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz – making up a half of Ethiopia's 12 regional states.
Amhara's Fano group fought alongside federal forces during the Tigray war.
It however turned against the federal government in an armed insurgency less than a year after the war ended, after refusing government orders to disarm.
The government has been fighting the OLA since 2018.
The announcement of the Alliance for Survival coalition comes months after reports of an alleged alliance between TPLF and neighbouring Eritrea.
Abiy responded by saying he had faith in Ethiopia's "defensive capabilities".
"Even if others were added, we do not have an iota of fear regarding Ethiopia's sovereignty," he told lawmakers in July.

The country held a general election in June, with Abiy's Prosperity Party retaining its overwhelming parliamentary majority, despite the poll being overshadowed by conflict, accusations of repression and little participation by opposition parties.
The Fano and OLA rebel groups rejected the election and its results.
The Tigray region and its six million inhabitants were completely excluded from the poll.

Search and rescue authorities in the southern state of Kerala found three more dead bodies on Monday morning, taking the death toll from a flash flood to at least five.

Floods and rain-triggered landslides are a common occurrence in Kerala during the monsoon months, between June and November.
The state's Chief Minister VD Satheesan is set to arrive in the town shortly.
Meanwhile, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued orange alerts for six districts in the state on Monday morning, warning of more downpour.

An orange alert is the second highest in IMD's four-stage color-coded system, sitting just below the red warning. It tells local authorities and residents to 'be prepared' for heavy to very heavy rainfall in the region.
