articles.title: In cosmopolitan Berlin, elections still closed to foreigners
articles.summary: A quarter of Berlin residents will have no say in the German capital's city-state election because they lack citizenship. That's the highest proportion of residents excluded from the election yet,…

image.caption: Berliners head to the polls September 20 to elect a new state parliament. The anti-immigrant AfD party has been making significant gainsImage: Sonam Mishra/DW

blocks.text: Abdu, an Egyptian software developer, ended up in Germany's capital more or less by chance seven years ago. "I wouldn't say I chose Berlin," he told DW. "It was just that the company that offered me a job was here."

But now he loves it. The culture is "better than any other city I have experienced," he said. That's partly because of its diversity, but he also likes the way Berliners approach life. "They're more interested in living than just working," he said. "Here I feel life is more relaxed, and this also offers the opportunity for people to get more creative."

But there's plenty about the city that he's not particularly happy with, including Berlin's rapidly rising rental prices, and the notoriously opaque bureaucracy is a constant source of annoyance. "I myself would like to start my own business, but it is difficult because of all the bureaucracy," he said.

In general, Abdu is dissatisfied with Berlin's current government, a conservative-led coalition of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — but the trouble is, as a non-German national, he has no say in deciding whether it should stay in office or not. That is particularly frustrating at the moment, when the streets are bristling with campaign posters ahead of the election on September 20.
"We are people who pay taxes, but we don't have any representation at all, even on local level," he said. "The cuts to health care and German courses, for example, affect me directly."
Berlin initiative helps immigrant moms find their feet
Berlin: Bigger and more international

The German capital is growing and becoming more international. While the voting population in the upcoming election will be bigger than ever — mainly because the voting age has been lowered to 16 — so is the number of the disenfranchised.
Of Berlin's population of 3.9 million, a full quarter — around 976,000 adults — cannot vote because they don't have German citizenship. That number has doubled since 2011.

This is partly because of Germany's political structure. In Germany and across Europe, citizens of other EU countries can vote in municipal elections. In London, people from Commonwealth countries can do the same as long as they have UK residency. Spain, meanwhile, also has reciprocal voting agreements with several non-EU countries — in South America and elsewhere — that allow their citizens to vote in municipal elections, including for the mayors of Madrid and Barcelona.

Berlin's Sunday election is not a municipal one. Since Berlin is one of Germany's 16 federal states, it is holding a state election, which means that voting rights are more restricted. Berlin's municipal elections, where EU citizens are allowed to vote, only decide who governs the city's individual districts, and their political influence is limited.

The disenfranchisement is particularly acute in central Berlin. For that reason, Stefanie Remlinger, Green Party mayor in the district of Mitte, has organized a "symbolic election" for the non-Germans in her area — some 135,000 adults out of a population of 365,000. The initiative invites foreigners to vote at 15 ballot stations over a two-week period in early September to "raise awareness for the issue of voting rights for all."

"Mitte is an extremely heterogeneous district with a very international population," Remlinger told DW via video call from her office. "We have people from 170 different countries living here, and a lot of them don't have the right to vote. It's important to us to signal to those people that we value their opinions, that we see them."

blocks.caption: Around a third of adults in Stefanie Remlinger's district don't have German nationality Image: Annette Hauschild

blocks.text: Germany's 'rightward shift'

Getting people to vote in a meaningless election is a tough sell. Remlinger said she expected only a few hundred people to take part, and, anyway, she thinks the political climate in Germany is not exactly immigrant-friendly at the moment. Even in cosmopolitan Berlin, the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) is currently polling in second place, with nearly 20%.

"We as the Greens would liberalize voting rights even more, but I don't see the general debate in Germany going that way," she said. "We're fighting a rightward shift and a lot of hostility to immigration, and I think the chances of changing something on that issue right now are very bad."

To illustrate the state of the current debate, Remlinger mentioned a recent panel discussion she was part of, where a politician from the neoliberal Free Democratic Party (FDP) — a party that calls itself socially liberal — said voting rights shouldn't be opened to foreigners because they might start their own parties and take over the government. "And that from someone from the FDP!" said Remlinger, exasperated.

Abdu is also aware of this anti-immigrant shift in German politics. In fact, he said, that was one of the reasons he was considering leaving Germany altogether. "All the parties are trending right-wing, so it's getting more hostile," he said.
How Berliners are reshaping their city for the future
Is expanding voting good for the economy?

From an economic perspective, it might be considered a shame if qualified people like Abdu decided to leave Germany. The country lacks workers. The government estimates that the country will be short of about 440,000 workers by 2029, and even the AfD leadership claims it has nothing against immigrants who contribute to the economy.
Though some German cities and local authorities do have an elected advisory board for non-German residents, offering immigrants a real vote is frequently seen as a step too far.
Remlinger herself thinks that the best path to enfranchisement is not to offer foreign nationals voting rights, but to make it easier for immigrants to become German citizens.
That happens to be another one of Abdu's complaints about Berlin: "I applied for citizenship two years ago, and I didn't get any response," he said.

Germany has recently tightened citizenship rules again. Last year, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government reversed the three-year "fast-track" citizenship option introduced under his predecessor, Olaf Scholz. Still, the government did keep another of Scholz's reforms, which allows people to apply for citizenship after only five years of residency.
More and more Berliners are in fact becoming German: 2025 saw about 39,000 people naturalized in the capital, 17,000 more than in 2024.

That avenue is still closed for Abdu, but in the meantime, a little more political participation would go a long way. "If I could vote, I would reconsider leaving, to be honest, because then I could affect things, but now I'm just like a bank machine — they come to me and take half of my salary."

articles.title: Germany news: Doctors offer Oktoberfest flu jabs
articles.summary: Oktoberfest 2026 is underway but it's not just beer on offer in Munich this year; revelers can also get themselves a flu jab before heading to the tents. DW has more.
articles.byline: Matt Ford, Rana Taha, Timothy Jones

image.caption: Munich mayor Dominik Krause had the honor of tapping the first beer keg to officially open OktoberfestImage: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: September 20, 2026
O'piekst is!: German doctors offer Oktoberfest flu jabs

blocks.caption: Tightly packed groups of revelers raise trhe risk of the spread of illnessImage: Felix Hörhager/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Munich's annual Oktoberfest officially got underway on Saturday when the first beer keg was opened with the traditional cry of O'zapft is! ("It has been tapped!").
But another slogan is also being promoted in Bavaria this year: O'piekst is! ("It has been pricked!") — as doctors offer vaccine jabs against flu and Covid-19.

"With so many people coming together in such tight spaces in the beer tents, the risk of infection at Oktoberfest is higher," explained Christoph Spinner, head of infectiology at Munich's Rechts der Isar hospital.
Oktoberfest coincides with the start of the annual flu season, and Spinner warned that less than a third of people who are recommended a flu jab have actually had one.
Beatrix Zurek, a health expert from the city-led initiative München impft! ("Munich vaccinates!") said: "It's our job to go where people are. And that means: Oktoberfest."

articles.title: Why China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI development
articles.summary:
Beijing believes slowdown calls aim to lock in US advantage, and is pursuing a different balance between safety and pace

About two years ago, education entrepreneur Boris But had what he…

blocks.text: About two years ago, education entrepreneur Boris But had what he calls a “penny-drop moment” – that, like countless others in China, his company needed to embrace AI before it was made obsolete by it.
His clients, well-off parents looking to send their children to study overseas, had begun arriving in his office reeling off information and opinions gleaned not from rival firms, but from chatbots.
In response, he started developing his own AI study tool, concluding: “If you can’t beat them, join them.”
The pace and quality of AI development in China is second only to the United States, with the two superpowers locked in an intensifying rivalry as the stakes rise with each new model’s capabilities.
Analysts generally agree that frontier, or cutting-edge, US models are still some way ahead of their Chinese counterparts.

But over the last few weeks the mood music from Silicon Valley has been decidedly sombre, as insider after insider has warned of the potential catastrophes that could result from “loss of control” of the most advanced AIs.
And last Saturday Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei pitched a “worldwide pacing of the frontier” – something he said would “require cooperation with China”.
“China is definitely not receptive” to a slowdown on US firms’ terms, though, said Lian Jye Su from technology research group Omdia.
For the government, AI is a “core sovereignty capability”, and Beijing will not want to jeopardise the progress made in closing the gap with US frontier models.
“It sees these calls [for a slowdown] as a bid to lock in US advantage,” said Su.
Amodei made this explicit, mentioning China specifically when arguing it was key “to keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible”.
He advocated for measures including continued export controls to China on advanced chips and machinery – the existence of which some argue already amounts to a forced unilateral “pacing”.
China’s foreign ministry responded to Amodei’s piece by saying “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance”.
However, several analysts told the Guardian it would be a mistake to assume this suggested a rejection of the broader concerns raised by the essay.

This week China released the third iteration of its AI safety governance framework – a document that functions as a “mapping of the AI risk landscape and roughly what one should do about it”, said Gabriel Wagner, a researcher at Concordia, a Beijing-based AI safety consultancy.

Included in the updates are the risks posed by agents, the cybersecurity threats from frontier models and the issue of recursive self-improvement – an as-yet hypothetical scenario where AI becomes advanced enough to improve itself.
“In many ways, I think there is more common ground than people might assume between what Amodei is saying and what the Chinese government is saying,” said Wagner.
That contrasts with US president Donald Trump, who this week called fears AI could wipe out humanity a “hoax”.
Trump is set to meet counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington next week, with AI expected to make the agenda, though analysts are sceptical a major breakthrough will happen.
The ruling Communist party, finely attuned to risks to its political control, has been proactive in ensuring the new technology has developed within boundaries set by the state.
Centralised authority over critical infrastructure and commercial activity means China is generally better placed than the United States “to address any AI disaster”, said Omdia’s Su.
However, Chinese companies do less voluntary monitoring and evaluation work than US ones, said Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace (CEIP).
Neither government seems prepared for a loss-of-control incident like those outlined over the last few weeks, she said.
China’s regulation, though, is “iterative … they are quick to adapt and release new measures”, she added.
China has had an algorithm registry since 2022, but warnings on agents released this year suggest a switch in focus “from controlling what AI says to controlling what it does”, per Concordia AI.
Beijing also issued national regulations this year aimed at curbing emotional dependency on companion AIs.
At the same time, AI is being actively encouraged across the economy to promote growth, enshrining this goal in its latest Five Year Plan.

Local governments are offering funding and low rents to companies to help achieve this – entrepreneur But was recently invited to pitch his company, Hampshire Education, to a small city three hours from Shanghai set on establishing a reputation as a tech hub.
Factories across the country’s huge manufacturing base are being encouraged to convert their processes into the AI era.

“Safety and controllability are certainly major concerns, and they are actively discussed,” said a spokesperson for Black Lake Technologies, an industrial agent platform that says it has worked with 40,000 factories globally.
“But in manufacturing, these concerns tend to be much more concrete and operational … what companies care most about is whether the AI is reliable.”
Daily life in China is already highly digitised, with traditionally less discourse around data privacy helping with widespread adoption.
For example, digital health service A-fu, which features AI chatbot versions of prominent doctors trained on real clinical studies, recently hit 150 million users.
“Most people treat AI as an already-useful everyday tool, not an abstract threat, so the practical attitude is to live with it,” said Ni Tao, founding editor of tech website yangtzeer.com.
“There is real anxiety about jobs and misinformation, but it coexists with a strong belief that China must master AI rather than slow down.”

articles.title: Germany: Is it possible to replace the chancellor?
articles.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz's record-low approval ratings have emboldened his opponents. There are three ways to remove a chancellor from office in Germany.

image.caption: Sixteen months into office, Friedrich Merz has record low approval ratings, triggering a debate abour his futureImage: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: It is the hot topic this week in Berlin: Does German Chancellor Friedrich Merz still have the backing of his own party, the Christian Democrats (CDU), and the coalition partners, Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD)? Will he be ousted? How would that work? Can he just step down?

Support for the chancellor has reached a record low: In the latest Deutschlandtrend representative survey, conducted by pollsters Infratest-Dimap for German public broadcaster ARD in early September, only 13% of respondents said Merz was doing a good job.
In early September, Merz's CDU suffered a resounding loss in the state of Saxony-Anhalt's parliamentary election, seeing the party's result halved from the 2021 election.
The election result has reinforced criticism of Merz, even from within his own ranks, and his communication style, which frequently alienates his audience.
But Merz remains chancellor. What are the options to change that? Germany's constitution, the Basic Law, grants the position a strong standing. German chancellors are not so easy to unseat.
Option 1: Resignation

Merz himself can decide to resign for any reason. That would not necessarily mean the end of the coalition government he leads. An example: In May 1974, then Chancellor Willy Brandt of the SPD resigned after a spy from communist East Germany (DDR) was discovered to have been working in his inner circle. The governing parties, the SPD and the business-oriented Free Democrats (FDP), quickly agreed to continue their alliance.

Only 10 days later, Finance Minister Helmut Schmidt, also of the SPD, was elected as the new chancellor. To do this, an absolute majority of all lawmakers in the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, was needed (not only those present during the vote). This majority is called the "chancellor majority". Schmidt achieved the necessary majority, eventually got reelected and remained head of the German government for 8 years.
How likely is Merz to step down? Today's chancellor seems determined not to give up.
Option 2: A constructive vote of no-confidence

If a new majority were formed through alliances in the Bundestag or if a chancellor fell so far out of favor that their own supporters no longer believed in them, the instrument of a "constructive vote of no-confidence" could come into play. That means the majority of lawmakers vote in favor of a new candidate for chancellor.

An example: Helmut Schmidt of the SPD, lost the support of his junior coalition partner, the FDP, in 1982. The FDP wanted to push through changes to economic policy, which Schmidt rejected. They joined forces with the conservatives from the CDU and CSU, and jointly put CDU leader Helmut Kohl forward as a new chancellor. He won a majority in parliament, replaced Schmidt and moved into the chancellor's office where he remained for 16 years.

The probability of this happening in Merz's case is very remote. The conservatives and Social Democrats do not want to end their coalition. There is no clear rival candidate for Merz. North Rhine-Westphalia's State Premier Hendrik Wüst of the CDU is seen as a possible successor, but has not made a step forward. Besides: The CDU is usually very loyal toward its political leaders; ousting the chancellor via a vote of no-confidence on the open stage of the Bundestag is simply unthinkable for most conservative lawmakers.
Option 3: A confidence vote

Germany's parliament cannot simply dissolve itself and call new elections. Lawmakers can, however, call a confidence vote on the chancellor and his government. Several chancellors have already used this mechanism, coupling it with a vote on a contentious issue.

As chancellor in November 2001, Gerhard Schröder (SPD) put forward a confidence vote in the Bundestag and linked it with the question of whether his government should deploy the German military to Afghanistan to support the NATO mission led by the United States following the September 11 attacks. Schröder won, remained in office and continued with his military policy.
Merz has already said he sees no point in calling for a confidence vote. There are also no signs of large breakaway movements from members of his coalition in Parliament.

If a chancellor loses a confidence vote, the Bundestag can be dissolved and fresh elections called. Following the defeat in the Bundestag, the chancellor can ask the German President to dissolve parliament and call voters to the polls. The president is not obliged to do so, but usually does.
It seems that Merz has ruled out this option. Neither the SPD nor the conservative Union (of CDU/CSU) are interested in calling new elections at a time when their approval ratings are low.
So will the government remain the same? Right now, it seems so. However, things have been so dynamic in recent days and weeks in Berlin political circles that nothing should be ruled out.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Two killed in 'massive' Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow region, says Russia
articles.summary: An oil refinery was also reportedly hit in Moscow, and flights were suspended at two capital airports.

blocks.text: At least two people have been killed and six injured in a "massive" overnight Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, Governor Andrei Vorobyev has said.

Vorobyev said 249 drones had been shot down, and he reported fires in several residential houses. A local warehouse was also ablaze. In the capital Moscow, an oil refinery was damaged, and flight restrictions were in place at two airports.
Earlier, a Ukraine official said seven people, including two children, were killed in Russian attacks in the Kyiv and Sumy regions on Saturday.
Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes, targeting energy-generating and transport facilities, as well as major logistics hubs.

In a post on Telegram on Sunday, Vorobyev said a 44-year-old woman was killed in Sofyino after a drone hit a three-storey residential building. Another five people - including two children - were injured, he said.
In the Orekhovo-Zuevo district, an elderly man died after a private house was hit, the regional governor said.
Videos have emerged on social media purportedly showing explosions in the night skies in the Moscow region, and of a burning warehouse. The footage has not been verified by the BBC.
Meanwhile, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said a drone struck a building near one of the capital's boulevards and a facility at an oil refinery was damaged.
He earlier said that 152 drones heading for Moscow had been shot down.
Sheremetyevo - Moscow's biggest airport - warned passengers about "temporary restrictions" in place, while at the capital's Vnukovo airport all arrivals and departures were halted.
In Ukraine, a mother and her two small children, a boy and a girl, were killed in Saturday's Russian attack in the city of Fastiv, Kyiv regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.
He added that several private houses were also damaged.
In the north-eastern Sumy region, four people were killed when a Russian drone hit the car they were travelling in, top local official Oleh Hryhorov said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title: Cultural treasures are being destroyed by war, and people want justice
articles.summary: A cauldron of conflicts is bubbling across the world, with cultural monuments being destroyed. These people are fighting against it.

blocks.text: August was a brutal month for Ukraine. Russian aerial attacks increased significantly, launching thousands of drones. Kyiv was intensely bombarded, as were the southern cities of Mykolaiv and Odesa. Amid the destruction and loss of life, Odesa reported damage to six Unesco-protected sites, including the salmon-pink 19th Century Alexandru Sturdza House.
It raised again the question of why it is so hard to hold actors accountable for the destruction of buildings and objects with real cultural significance.
In the last month alone, Ukraine's Ministry of Culture reported that 148 cultural heritage sites were recorded as damaged or destroyed, including in Odesa.

Several Ukrainian activist groups have tried to get accountability by lodging complaints with the International Criminal Court (ICC) against Russia over cultural destruction and looting, but no indictments have been issued.

Bijan Rouhani, a senior researcher at the Endangered Archaeology in the Middle East and North Africa project, says that the legal framework may be strong on paper but in practice it almost inevitably falls short. "No state actor has ever been tried for this offence. The obstacle is no longer evidence. We have satellite imagery, remote sensing and monitoring teams. The obstacle is jurisdiction and political will."

Looking at the cauldron of conflicts convulsing the world, the question is ever more pressing as to whether effective action is possible to stop the damage being done or ensure accountability when it does.
A casualty of war
The conflict in Ukraine is just one of the panoply of wars in recent years that have revealed once again the disastrous impact of conflict on cultural heritage.

Tareq Abu Dayyeh sells craftwork, souvenirs and antiquities in Gaza. The Great Omari Mosque features on many of the items he sells. It represents the very identity of Gaza - charting its history through the building's many manifestations from ancient pagan temple to Byzantine church to Seventh Century mosque to Crusader Cathedral and then back to being a mosque.
The Great Omari Mosque was all but destroyed in an Israeli strike in 2023. The Israeli military said the strike was targeting Hamas.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Great Omari Mosque in Gaza was largely destroyed in an Israeli strike in 2023

blocks.text: Image source, LightRocket via Getty Images
The Great Omari Mosque in Gaza was largely destroyed in an Israeli strike in 2023
Now Dayyeh says his heart is broken every time he sees the ruins. "When your past is destroyed, you have no present."

The war in Gaza has claimed tens of thousands of lives and an estimated 200,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed by Israeli bombardment. But despite the overwhelming death and devastation, such cultural losses run deep.
This is a sentiment expressed throughout history by people living through war.
In Sudan, Lebanon, Yemen and Iran, the alarm has been raised time and time again.

More than 100 sites in Iran are reported to have been damaged during the aerial war launched by the US and Israel back in February. They include the Unesco-listed Golestan Palace in the capital, Tehran, and Naqsh-e Jahan Square in Isfahan.
The civil war in Sudan has further imperilled one of the ancient wonders of the world - the Meroe Pyramids, built during the flourishing civilisation of the Kingdom of Kush.

Unesco, which designated Meroe as a World Heritage Site in 2011, has warned that the fighting has halted all preservation work there, leaving the fragile ancient structures prey to erosion from the encroaching sand and vegetation.
A difficult task

In response to the massive destruction of World War Two, the first-ever international treaty exclusively dedicated to protecting cultural heritage during armed conflict was adopted in The Hague in 1954.
It applies to monuments and architecture, but also works of art and books, requiring states to safeguard and respect cultural property and refrain from any actions that might endanger it.
Since the Hague Convention, there have been several additional moves to strengthen protective measures for cultural heritage.

A Second Protocol to the Convention in 1999 said that any site that has been placed under enhanced protection due to its immense cultural significance must not be made a military target even if it is being used in such a way as to have become a 'military objective' - unless there is no other feasible way of ending its use in that way.

When the International Criminal Court was established in The Hague in 2002, part of its remit was to bring accountability for deliberate attacks in war against buildings of religious, artistic and educational value as well as historical monuments, which had been defined as war crimes.
But this has been a complex and difficult task.

So far, only one case has been successfully brought at the ICC. Ahmad al-Faqi al-Mahdi was a jihadist militant leader in Mali who was found guilty of directing attacks that destroyed mausoleums and a mosque in Timbuktu. He was sentenced to nine years in prison.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ahmed al-Faqi al-Mahdi remains the only person successful prosecuted for this by the ICC

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Ahmed al-Faqi al-Mahdi remains the only person successful prosecuted for this by the ICC

Rouhani says that without the full backing of the major powers and a genuine commitment to international law and its enforcement, the world will simply keep watching the same devastating pattern repeat itself.

"For most governments, heritage is a secondary concern, unless it becomes useful for propaganda," Rouhani says. "The Hague Convention requires states to build protection into their military rules and to respect cultural property abroad as well as at home. Looking at the scale of damage in recent conflicts, it is difficult to conclude that these obligations are taken seriously."

In conflicts from Ukraine to Iran to Gaza, where schools and hospitals are seen as permissible military targets by combatants, how likely is it that a museum or pile of ancient stones, however freighted with beauty and history and memory, will be spared?
Heritage ambulances

In an isolated position in open countryside, a museum dedicated to the 18th Century Ukrainian philosopher and poet Hryhoriy Skovoroda was destroyed by Russian shelling during an overnight attack in 2022. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said it had left him speechless: "Targeted strikes against museums - not even terrorists would think of this. But this is the kind of army we are fighting against."
The building was set ablaze and a caretaker was injured, but much of the collection had already been removed.

Joe Biden, then the US president, said that Russian President Vladimir Putin was not only trying to take over Ukraine, but "literally trying to wipe out the culture and identity of the Ukrainian people".
That pattern has been repeated across much of the frontline in Ukraine where local organisations have worked with international groups to try to safeguard their national heritage from Russian attack.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A museum dedicated to the 18th Century Ukrainian philosopher and poet Hryhoriy Skovoroda was destroyed in a Russian attack

blocks.text: A museum dedicated to the 18th Century Ukrainian philosopher and poet Hryhoriy Skovoroda was destroyed in a Russian attack
One international group that's played a big role is the Aliph Foundation, which was set up in Geneva in 2017 to protect and repair cultural heritage.
Alexandra Fiebig, a project manager with Aliph, says that her group provided millions of dollars in funds to Ukrainian museums scrambling to move their most valuable items to safety.

This has involved the use of what she describes as 'heritage ambulances': "These vehicles that have specialised equipment and space with specialised teams and equipment, they were in the beginning travelling a lot to affected museums that were damaged through military action."
Now, she says the teams also check on the artefacts that were transported in great haste to safer places to make sure they remain in good condition.

Blue Shield International is a group that operates in multiple war zones, working with armed forces and local heritage officials to such an extent that it's come to be known as the Red Cross for culture.
Dr Emma Cunliffe, the head of operations for the group, says Ukrainians are risking their lives to protect their heritage.

"They are taking great measures to document the damage even when they are risking their own lives to do it. In fact one of the things we really see is that the government is taking huge steps despite the many many competing priorities and the struggles they are facing."
Other conflicts have seen civilians take similar measures to protect their culture.

In February 2015, Isis turned its attention from hacking down ancient statues and artefacts in Mosul in northern Iraq to ransacking its written heritage as its fighters laid waste to the city's much treasured public libraries. They burned the Central Library and destroyed or stole many thousands of books - many of them rare manuscripts that told the story of the city.

blocks.caption: Image caption, After seizing Mosul in 2014, Isis burned books in the city's Central Library

blocks.text: Image source, The Asahi Shimbun via Getty Images
After seizing Mosul in 2014, Isis burned books in the city's Central Library

"These were not simply books or shelves, they represented decades of knowledge and research and formed an important part of the intellectual heritage of Mosul University and the wider community… Within days, everything was gone," Dr Mohammed Jasim Mohammed al-Hamdani says. The main library in Mosul has played a key role in his life - to such an extent that he is now the director there.

"Seeing it destroyed felt like losing a part of myself. Many people in the city had a story connected to the University of Mosul and therefore the loss felt very close to home. And this is why when that part of Mosul was liberated from Isis, young people, old people rushed to the library to save what they could."
A lucrative trade
The obverse of communities taking it into their own hands to protect cultural property is the looting of those same sites.
Again, this is a byproduct of war that dates back to the dawn of history.

Cunliffe says that understanding the reasons for looting - which can vary from place to place - is a necessary starting point: "That might then in turn result in greater sanctions, greater prosecutions to take it seriously as a threat." She says that it's important if possible to convey a sense to local communities that by assisting this, they are selling their own heritage.
In Iraq and Syria for example, both during and after the Isis rampage, looting of priceless artefacts was carried out on an industrial scale.
The precious objects were spirited out and trafficked abroad, including to the US.
A years-long investigation by the US Justice Department traced and tracked the smuggling routes and resulted in thousands of looted artefacts being returned to Iraq.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The looting of priceless artefacts in Iraq intensified during the Isis rampage

blocks.text: The looting of priceless artefacts in Iraq intensified during the Isis rampage
In Europe and elsewhere, co-ordinated, multi-national police and customs operations take place regularly, seizing large numbers of stolen antiquities and arresting some of the traffickers.
But the trade remains highly lucrative and the plethora of conflicts provides ever more opportunities.

In Sudan, the national museum in Khartoum was stripped of its treasures in 2023 when it came under the control of one of the warring factions, the RSF, which loaded them onto trucks and left the display rooms bare.

As in other conflict zones like Ukraine, specialised training has been provided for those involved in trying to recover the antiquities, which has had some success. But much of the museum's display - which told the story of the region over thousands of years - may have disappeared for good.
Slim chance of deterrence
The challenges of trying to limit the scale of destruction and looting of cultural heritage are huge.
At an international or state level, there are regulations in place, but putting them into practice in a timely fashion is difficult enough - and often there isn't even the will to attempt this.
Local initiatives backed by organisations like Aliph and Blue Shield International can make a difference on a small scale.
But if - as seems the case right now - the chances of anyone facing consequences for destroying a heritage site are close to zero, then there is all but no real deterrent.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Khaled al-Asaad was killed for refusing to give up Palmyra's secrets

blocks.text: Image source, Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images
Khaled al-Asaad was killed for refusing to give up Palmyra's secrets

"What would change the calculation is not harsher sentences," says Dr Bijan Rouhani, "but a real prospect of being named - arrest warrants for the commanders who authorise these strikes, prosecutions in national courts under universal jurisdiction, and targeted sanctions on named individuals. Those measures don't require a new treaty. They require states to be willing to use the instruments they already have, against allies as well as adversaries."
Of all the recent attempts to erase the cultural past embodied in stone, Palmyra in Syria still stands out. Isis blew up temples there and might have done far worse if it had not been defeated.

One man became emblematic for standing up to them. For 40 years, the archaeologist Khaled al-Asaad had been the principal custodian of Palmyra. He was in his eighties when Isis descended on the ancient city.

They captured him and tortured him to try to find out where its most valuable artefacts had been hidden. When he refused to tell them, they beheaded him in a public square and hung his corpse from a traffic light.

Al-Asaad was celebrated across the world as a heroic defender of culture against the forces of darkness. He was awarded the Order of Civil Merit in Syria and in Palmyra, a school was named in his honour.
But nothing is free from political complications.
Years later, under the new authorities in Syria, his name has now been removed from the school.

articles.title: Israeli president pardons combat medic who shot dead wounded Palestinian attacker
articles.summary:
Elor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter of man who stabbed soldier continues to divide country

Israel’s president has pardoned a combat medic who shot dead a badly wounded…

blocks.text: Israel’s president has pardoned a combat medic who shot dead a badly wounded Palestinian attacker who had stabbed a soldier in the occupied West Bank, in a case that divided the country a decade ago.

Elor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter and his release after serving two-thirds of his 18-month sentence drew enormous attention in Israel, where military service is compulsory for most Jewish men.
In his first interview after his release, Azaria said he would “act exactly the same, because that’s how I needed to act”.

Azaria had approached Abdel Fattah al-Sharif as he lay on the ground, unarmed and badly hurt, after stabbing a soldier in the city of Hebron. A mobile phone video captured Azaria shooting al-Sharif in the head.

The office of president Isaac Herzog said in a statement on Saturday that he acted on the recommendation of defence minister Israel Katz. The statement cited the time that had passed, and the spirit of the approaching Yom Kippur, or Day of Atonement, holiday as among the factors in the decision.

Herzog’s office also said that Azaria, who was 20 when he was sentenced, had “expressed his sorrow” in his request. The statement noted that in an earlier request, he called his gunshot an “operational error”.
In a separate statement, Katz called it a “right, humane and fitting decision” and said Azaria had been in a “complex operational mission”.
But the military’s chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, had said in a letter to the defence minister that the pardon should not be granted, Israeli media reported.

The conviction was a rare case of a military court ruling against a soldier for deadly action taken in the field. Top generals had pressed for his prosecution, while many in the Israeli public supported Azaria at a time when there had been a series of stabbings and car-ramming attacks by Palestinians or Israeli Arabs. Some supporters protested outside his trial.

On Saturday, Israel’s hard-line national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said in a statement that “cancelling the criminal record of someone who killed a terrorist makes me emotional and very happy”.
Some Palestinians and human rights groups had described Azaria’s sentence as far too lenient. Prosecutors had sought a sentence of three to five years.
The statement by Herzog’s office on Saturday said that his decision “does not constitute a reassessment of the case”.
The divisions over Azaria’s case led to public polling and political pressure that led the defence minister at the time, Moshe Ya’alon, to resign.
After the verdict, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for Azaria to be pardoned.
After the sentencing, the Palestinian government minister in charge of prisoner affairs, Issa Karaka, called it a “joke”.

articles.title: Summer of 2026 broke records in Europe, and caused deaths
articles.summary: The summer of 2026 was not only the hottest on record in Europe, it also saw a record number of people die. More than 16,000 are thought to have died because of the heat in Germany alone.

image.caption: Older people are more vulnerable to extreme heat Image: Joel Saget/AFP

blocks.text: The summer (June to August) of 2026 was the warmest in Europe since records began, beating the record set in 2003, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service,

Not only that, Germany's DWD weather service says that there was an "unprecedented" number of hot days this year. "On average across Germany,there were about 22 hot days with temperatures of at least 30 degrees Celsius and about five very hot days with temperatures of at least 35 degrees Celsius," the DWD wrote in in a press release at the end of August.

The estimated number of heat-related deaths also reached unprecedented levels, with at least 16,300 people dying by the end of August, even if few of them died directly because of the heat, but rather as a consequence of underlying health conditions exacerbated by the heat.

The figures were compiled from a statistical correlation between the number of deaths recorded by Germany's Federal Statistical Office and the temperatures measured by the DWD during a specific period.

Heat-related deaths in Germany are more likely if the average weekly temperature reaches 20 degrees Celsius or more. This is the average of all hourly temperatures recorded in a week, including at nighttime.

This year, the average weekly temperatures in the country rose above the 20-degree mark several times. It was particularly hot at the end of June, when the average weekly temperature reached above 26 degrees between the 22nd and 28th of the month.
Why Europe's extreme summers are getting worse
Excess mortality during heat waves

Though it is not possible to determine a cause of death using statistics, researchers and medical professionals have a good understanding of how heat affects the human body, and there is widespread consensus that excess mortality during heat waves is possible.

"It was not just the high temperatures on the thermometer that were important, but also how long the heat lasted and the fact that it hardly cooled down at night," said Andreas Matzarakis, professor of environmental meteorology at Freiburg University.
Many people have trouble sleeping on hot nights. Yet, getting enough sleep is important so that the body can recover from the heat and stress of the day.

Matzarakis said that the severity of heat stress was not related solely to air temperatures. Humidity, solar radiation and wind also played a role — and what is known as the 'felt' temperature. He said that humidity and still air could place a heavy strain on the body, even in moderate temperatures.
Powerful El Nino set to bring extreme weather
Underprivileged most vulnerable

The less privileged members of society were also among the most vulnerable, said Martin Röösli, environmental scientist at the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute in Basel. "They are more likely to live in homes that are not well insulated or are more likely to work outdoors."

A large proportion of those who died because of the heat probably had only a short life expectancy left, due to their age and medical conditions, but Röösli said that there was a consensus that "some of the deceased could have lived for a long time and were simply in a fragile state at the time of the heat wave."

For Alexandra Schneider, a meteorologist and epidemiologist at the Helmholtz center in Munich in southern Germany, the deaths that occurred during the heat waves were very likely not only because of the "harvesting effect," which describes "how a heat wave causes very vulnerable individuals in particular to die a few days or weeks prematurely."

Had this been the case, there would have been a deficit of mortality in the following weeks, which did not happen. Thus, she believes, a significant proportion of those who died could have lived on for months or even years.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Houthis claim attack on Saudi capital after smoke seen rising near Riyadh airport
articles.summary: The King Khalid International Airport incident caused hours of flight disruptions and comes amid an escalating conflict with Houthi rebels in Yemen.

blocks.text: Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen say they carried out drone and missile attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh and energy sites on the country's Red Sea coast.
A column of black smoke was seen rising from what appeared to be fuel tanks near the Saudi capital's international airport on Saturday, hours after air raid alerts were issued.
It was the first time residents had been given an alert and urged to stay indoors since a recent escalation in the conflict with the Houthis.
There has been no official comment from Saudi authorities.

In a statement posted online, Houthi military spokesman Yahya al-Sarea said a "large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones" had been used to attack "sensitive sites" in Riyadh and Aramco state oil and gas company facilities in Yanbu on the coast.
He added that the attacks were "in response to the Saudi enemy's criminal attempts" to target the Yemeni capital Sanaa.
Earlier, Sarea had accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out 300 strikes across Yemen during the past week.
The Houthis are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.
They have attacked targets inside Saudi Arabia on several occasions in recent months, and said this week that they were responsible for downing a Saudi fighter jet over Yemen.

According to an unconfirmed report from AFP news agency, quoting military sources on both sides of Yemen's civil war, fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces claimed 48 lives on Saturday.
The Houthis said 31 of their fighters had been killed while government sources said their side had lost 17 soldiers, according to the news agency.
On Friday, the International Organization for Migration, a UN body, reported that the number of people displaced as a result of recent fighting had passed 104,796, external.

A number of apparent explosions were heard in Riyadh and major problems were reported at King Khalid International Airport earlier on Saturday, with the tracking website FlightRadar24 reporting delays and cancellations., external
An AFP journalist reported that firefighters could be seen trying to extinguish the flames of a burnt-out fuel tank belonging to Aramco.
The Saudi Civil Defence had sent out phone alerts overnight warning of potential danger in Riyadh and other regions, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning.
Residents told AFP on condition of anonymity that they had heard what sounded like a round of explosions echoing through the city after the alerts.
"I heard the alarm, then my windows shook," said a resident of northern Riyadh, 27. "It was definitely scary. I was not expecting this."
The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to a key shipping route used by the Gulf state to export to Asia and Europe.
The group said the naval blockade was in retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled north-western Yemen.
Saudi vessels have relied on that stretch of the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.

On Friday, investment banking giant JP Morgan said it was struggling to predict how oil prices would be impacted by the war, telling investors in a rare note that "we simply don't know how to model the endgame".

articles.title: German-Russian relations at freezing point
articles.summary: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine destroyed the once-close relationship between Moscow and Berlin. Yet the far-right AfD is calling for a normalization of relations.

image.caption: Chancellor Friedrich Merz (left) has described Russian President Vladimir Putin as "perhaps the worst war criminal of our time"Image: picture alliance

blocks.text: For many years, Germany and Russia had a perfect partnership.

Russia supplied cheap energy, which helped German industry succeed in exporting its goods worldwide. This partnership began in the early 2000s. On the German side was Chancellor Gerhard Schröder from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), followed later by Chancellor Angela Merkel of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Their counterpart was Vladimir Putin.

Even when Russia annexed the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea in 2014, business continued as usual. It was then that the agreement to build Nord Stream 2, a direct gas pipeline between Russia and Germany designed to bypass Ukraine was signed. At the time, other European countries and the US warned that the pipeline would provide Russia with powerful leverage.

The warnings proved to be correct. On February 24, 2022, Russian tanks rolled into Ukraine. German hopes for a stable European order, the democratization of Russia, and the continuation of its lucrative business model were shattered.
Hundreds of fake posts target German elections
How could so many German politicians be so wrong?

"Shortly before the invasion, the widespread view was that there were no rational grounds for an attack on Ukraine, because the economic, military, and political costs to Russia of starting a war would be far too high," Russia expert Mario Baumann of the German Council on Foreign Relations told DW. "People [in Germany] had projected their own rationality onto Russia. They underestimated the regime's imperialist and revisionist ambitions."

After that, nothing in the bilateral relationship was ever the same again. Chancellor Olaf Scholz(SPD) spoke of a Zeitenwende (epochal shift) in foreign and security policy, in the days after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine began.

Since then, the German armed forces have expanded. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said the following year, "We must become capable of waging war," a statement that critics still say was an escalation of tensions.

Germany ended its decades-long energy dependence on Russia and shut down Nord Stream 2. In September 2022, the pipeline was blown up. The Federal Prosecutor's Office suspects a Ukrainian group was responsible.
A series of EU sanctions have long since reduced Russian-German trade relations to a minimum. Government cooperation in culture, science, and education has also practically ceased to exist.
A new low point
While the German government under Scholz initially hesitated to take dramatic steps on military aid to Ukraine, Friedrich Merz, then the leader of the opposition, stepped up his rhetoric.

"Ukraine must win the war. Russia must lose the war," he said in 2024 as leader of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group in parliament. In 2025, as chancellor, he then spoke of Russia's "economic exhaustion," which the West must "help bring about." But that has yet to materialize. To this day, Russia has shown no serious willingness to compromise.
Why Putin turned to ex‑German chancellor as a peace broker

Meanwhile, Germany is feeling the consequences of its military support for Ukraine. The German government has long suspected Russia of being behind cyberattacks on government agencies and critical infrastructure.

So when an armed drone was discovered and defused in August 2026 at Leipzig Airport close to Ukrainian transport aircraft — which transport a large portion of the military aid to Ukraine — the government was certain: For the first time, it publicly blamed the Kremlin.

A Russian cultural center in Berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn were closed, which the German government said were being used as espionage centers. Moscow responded by closing the Goethe Institutes and the German consulate in St. Petersburg.

Putin has denied Russian responsibility for the Leipzig incident, calling it a "serious mistake" to blame Moscow, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov even described the accusations as the "beginning of a real war." But Baumann says: "We shouldn't give in to the fears being stoked, because they are part of Russia's strategy to weaken Germany and Europe."
AfD wants to resume relations with Russia

The German government is also facing domestic pressure as the far-right Alternative for Germany(AfD) has made gains in regional elections and is rising in the national polls. The AfD would prefer to end support for Ukraine and normalize relations with Russia, including deals on oil and gas. High fuel prices in Germany have only made the issue more explosive.

"German support for Ukraine worries many people," said Sven Leunig, political scientist at the University of Jena in Thuringia, following the election in the neighboring state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won the September 6 election by a landslide. However, he noted, "it is less a fundamental rejection of the support itself than a reaction born of fear. People want to 'stay out' of the conflict so as not to be drawn into it more deeply themselves."

In the latest ARD Deutschlandtrend survey, 42% of respondents believe military aid to Ukraine has gone too far. "If public support weakens over the long term, the government will eventually have to respond," says Leunig.
Carry on or change course?

So far, the German government is sticking to its course, as Merz made clear once again following the AfD's election victory. But opinions on how to deal with Russia and the war in Ukraine differ not only among politicians but also among political scientists and experts.

Johannes Varwick of Halle University in Saxony-Anhalt believes it is long past time for a change of course: "German and European policy toward Ukraine resembles a mix of platitudes and wishful thinking," Varwick told DW. "It is high time for a course correction, and Germany should exert pressure on Ukraine to move closer to the latest American proposals, which aim for a compromise and could thus possibly bring about a political solution."

Baumann, on the other hand, argues: "Supporting Ukraine remains the best investment for safeguarding German and European interests. The government has recognized this and should stick to this course and continue to communicate it as such." However, it is important that Berlin act in concert with its European partners.

The war in Ukraine has now lasted longer than World War I. And there is no end in sight. Hopes that Russian-German relations will return to the way they used to be seem illusory for the foreseeable future.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Thick smoke seen near Riyadh airport after air-raid alerts in Saudi capital
articles.summary:
Authorities also issued warnings for Jeddah and Yanbu, a major industrial port and home to vital oil facilities

Flames and a large plume of black smoke were seen rising above Riyadh airport…

blocks.text: Flames and a large plume of black smoke were seen rising above Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Saturday after the government sent air-raid alerts to citizens by phone overnight warning of aerial attacks.

Explosions were heard in the capital and firefighters battled to extinguish the flames of a burning fuel tank emblazoned with the logo of the Saudi oil company Aramco near the city’s King Khalid international airport.
It is the first time the government has issued such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with the Iran-backed Houthis in neighbouring Yemen escalated in July.
Residents told Agence France-Presse that hours after the alert, they had heard what sounded like another round of explosions echoing through parts of the Saudi capital.
According to tracking website FlightRadar24, there are “major problems” at the airport and it has been listed under its maximum disruption index.
“In the direction of the airport, we saw black smoke and fire,” one resident told AFP, speaking on condition of anonymity.

The Saudi civil defence force sent air-raid alerts overnight on Friday to residents of Riyadh, Jeddah and other cities including Yanbu, a major industrial port which is home to critical oil facilities.
The all-clear was given shortly afterwards, but residents were encouraged not to gather in crowds.

The UN security council condemned the continued ​Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia in a statement on Friday. It said they had included attacks that affected civilian and energy infrastructure and had injured civilians, including women and children.
It also condemned the Houthis’ military offensive in Yemen, where nearly 105,000 people have fled their homes, the International Organization for Migration said on Wednesday.

The security council’s 15 members called for “practical cooperation” to prevent the Houthis from acquiring arms, military training, financing and other military-related assistance needed to carry out their attacks. They stressed that all countries must enforce the UN arms embargo against the group.

The Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had foiled unspecified “criminal attempts” ⁠in the Yemeni capital of Sana’a, blaming Saudi Arabia and vowing a response. The group also says the Saudi air force has conducted hundreds of airstrikes against it in recent days.

The Houthis recently seized control of strategic the Red Sea islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish. Earlier this month, the group captured the port of Mokha and Perim island in the Bab al-Mandab strait, fueling fears the world could face a second oil supply crisis.

articles.title: Men deported from US bound and beaten in Equatorial Guinea detention hotel, lawyers say
articles.summary:
Group trapped at Hotel Bamy after US removal as rights groups sound alarm over poor conditions and violence

Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were…

blocks.text: Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers.

The men – one from Egypt and one from Eritrea – were then taken to a prison. About 30 detainees from the US remain trapped at a hotel in the outskirts of the coastal city of Malabo after being deported from the US. Detainees have said they believe the men were beaten for telling the press and human rights advocates about the poor conditions and violence inside the hotel, and that they are haunted by flashbacks and terrified they will be retaliated against next.
Human rights advocates and experts have warned for months that conditions at the Hotel Bamy – a run-down establishment that has served as a detention center for US deportees – are dangerous.

The US has sent at least 66 people from different African countries, Cuba and Brazil to Equatorial Guinea, which has received $7.5m as part of a deal to cooperate with the US deportation program. The Trump administration has pursued dozens of similar deals with countries to take in immigrants that the US cannot deport directly to their home countries, where judges have deemed they would face torture or persecution. In the past, the US government allowed those people to live and work in the US indefinitely.
The Trump administration, however, has sought instead to expel them to third countries where they have no ties, do not speak the local language and have no legal status – trapping them in limbo.

Advocates have been especially concerned for deportees sent to Equatorial Guinea, where the authoritarian government is notorious for human rights abuses, including torture, according to the US state department. Detainees held at Hotel Bamy have told the Guardian that armed guards keep watch over them 24/7, and that they have not been provided any medical care or even fresh clothes since arriving there. One of the detainees, who has a severe stomach hernia that requires visits to the hospital to drain his stomach due excessive fluid build-up, said he has been unable to see a doctor since arriving at Hotel Bamy.
Other detainees have managed to obtain medication for HIV, diabetes and other conditions via human rights lawyers, but remain fearful that access to medications will be arbitrarily cut off.

The two men who were tortured – Ahmed Soliman, 31, of Egypt, and Samson Birhane, 47, of Eritrea – have since been transferred to a prison in Malabo. Multiple witnesses recounted that the police officers shouted, “Where is the phone? Where is the phone!” as they beat the men, who had initially been accused of breaking a mirror at the hotel before they were pulled aside and arrested.

The beating, which occurred on 11 September, followed the release of a video first reported by Reuters showing conditions at the hotel and the violent behavior of the guards. The detainees had been using cellphones to communicate with lawyers and the media about the conditions they were facing.

blocks.caption: Equatorial Guinea police point gun at migrants deported by Trump administration - loop

blocks.text: In the video taken by Soliman, which lawyers shared with the Guardian, authorities are seen pointing guns at the deportees. A Cuban man asked the officer for the return of his confiscated mobile phone ​so he could contact relatives and a ​lawyer, but was ignored. When officers noticed Soliman filming the exchange with his mobile phone, multiple officers rushed at him and others standing nearby, pointed their guns, and told Soliman to remain on his knees with his hands up for 10-15 minutes.

In another video, Soliman was able to film authorities forcibly sending US deportees to Ethiopia, where they are likely to face torture. When deportees resisted going with authorities, officials gave them the option to “go back to their home country” or “go to prison”. At least 12 people have been returned by Equatorial Guinea to their home country, where they face persecution.

In May, human rights experts at the United Nations issued a rare public appeal asking Equatorial Guinea to halt plans to return deportees to their home countries and to comply with international human rights standards and avoid refoulement, or the expulsion of people to countries where they face persecution.

“This is a human rights catastrophe,” said Bella Mosselmans, director of the Global Strategic Litigation Council, who represents several of the deportees at Hotel Bamy. The US and Equatorial Guinea “must be held accountable for the atrocities they are committing”, she added.

In the week since Soliman and Birhane were beaten, police have also been searching the other detainees’ hotel rooms for cellphones, and have confiscated them. They have also barred lawyers from seeing the deportees. Authorities have told the 29 US deportees who remain at Hotel Bamy that they may never see Soliman or Birhane again, according to lawyers. One detainee who witnessed the beating said authorities treat them as if they are “blanks” who “don’t even exist”. Another detainee said an officer told her: “You will disappear from the earth. I am the law.”
Witnesses said they feared for the lives of Soliman and Birhane, who came to the US as children.

Soliman is a gay man from Egypt who had lived in Phoenix for most of his life. He had a green card, but lost status after he was convicted of drug possession. He served time for his crimes, and in October, a judge had determined he would face persecution and torture if he were to return to Egypt due to his sexuality.

Birhane had come to the US as a refugee when he was 13, but lost status after a conviction for robbery when he was in high school, in 1988. He was allowed to remain in the US after a judge ruled he faced torture in Eritrea, and had been regularly checking in with Immigration and Customs Enforcement as required.

Lawyers for the deportees shared copies of multiple emails they had sent to the US embassy in Equatorial Guinea alerting them to threats and violence against those detained at Hotel Bamy, but those messages have gone unanswered, they said. In July, amid a lawsuit challenging conditions for deportees, the African Commission issued an urgent interim order instructing the government of Equatorial Guinea to refrain from deporting, transferring, or relocating deportees against their will.
The US Department of Homeland Security did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.
A spokesperson for the state department said: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”
The agency did not respond to questions about whether it was aware of how Equatorial Guinea was treating US deportees, nor would it acknowledge whether any measures have been taken to intervene.
“As a general matter, we do not comment on the details of our private diplomatic communications with other governments,” the spokesperson said.
